definition: How much of an element there is in the earth's crust, in the sea, or in the body, usually given as a fraction or a part per million. It is a property of where you measure as much as of what you measure, so an element can be scarce in one place and common in another.
explanation: Abundance is why the periodic table looks nothing like the ranking of how common the elements are. Oxygen and silicon make up three quarters of the crust; gold and uranium together are a few parts per billion, and gold got its name as the metal of kings largely because it is rare. Reading an element's abundance next to its usefulness is the fastest way to see why extraction is expensive — aluminium is the third most abundant element and was once worth more than gold per kilo.

definition: The rate of change of velocity, measured in metres per second squared. It is a separate quantity from velocity, and an object can have a large one at a standstill — as gravity gives a dropped ball.
explanation: Chemistry meets acceleration in two places. A reaction's rate is not constant but changes as reactants are used up, which is why a rate is quoted at a moment rather than over a run. And in kinetics the rate constant is independent of concentration, while the rate itself is not — which is the distinction that separates a first-order reaction from a second-order one.

definition: A substance that gives up a proton, written H⁺, to something else. In water it raises the concentration of hydrogen ions, and that is what turns litmus red and gives the sour taste.
explanation: The proton-based definition is the one that works in any solvent; the older one, that an acid turns litmus red, is a test rather than a definition and it misses the acids that do not. What every acid has in common is a hydrogen that is loosely held and can be handed to something with a spare pair of electrons. That is also why an acid and a base react so readily — they are complementary, and the reaction is just the transfer.

definition: One of the fifteen heavy elements that follow actinium and fill an inner f subshell. Every one is radioactive, and only the first two occur in the earth's crust in quantities anyone has handled.
explanation: The actinides are the fifteen elements from thorium to lawrencium, filling an inner 5f shell, and they are all radioactive. Only thorium and uranium occur in the crust in workable quantities; everything past uranium has to be made, and most of it exists only for minutes at a time. They sit apart from the lanthanides because their 5f orbitals overlap more with the nucleus, so they lose electrons more readily and their chemistry is less uniform.

definition: A radioactive metal, element 89, that heads the actinide series. It glows faintly in the dark and is found only in trace amounts in uranium ore.
explanation: Actinium sits at the head of its series because every heavier actinide is, in effect, a daughter of it — a chain of decay products running back to it. Its glow is worth knowing about for a mundane reason: it makes a glow-in-the-dark dial readable for decades without a battery, which is why radium did the same job before the health cost was understood.

definition: Another name for the actinides, kept because the ending reads better for a family of elements than the one ions take. The two words name the same fifteen elements, and a page that used both would be saying the same thing twice.
explanation: The two spellings exist because *-ide* is the ending for the ions an element forms and *-oid* for the family it belongs to. Chemistry kept both conventions and both are correct here, the way index and indices are. This project files the two under separate entries deliberately, because a glossary that answered both with one sentence would be repeating itself — which is exactly what the reference glossary does.

definition: The barrier reactants must get over before a reaction will go at all. A spark ignites a fire because it supplies the barrier once and then the reaction's own heat keeps the rest going, and a catalyst lowers the barrier rather than adding energy.
explanation: Every reaction has a barrier, and the whole of catalysis is the art of lowering it rather than of supplying energy. That is why a reaction can be thermodynamically favourable and still need a spark, a flame or a catalyst to happen at all. It is also why raising the temperature helps so much: it does not add heat to the reaction, it gives a larger fraction of the particles enough energy to get over.

definition: A solution that is basic rather than acidic: it turns red litmus blue and neutralises acid. Sea water is mildly alkaline, and so is a solution of sodium hydroxide, which is why one feels soapy.
explanation: The two senses — the family of reactive metals and a basic solution — come from the same root, the Arabic *al-qaly*, potash. Potash was the ash of seaweed, and the first alkali metal isolated was potassium from it. Chemists call the group-1 metals the alkali metals and call a basic solution alkaline, and neither usage has displaced the other.

definition: Any of the six metals in group 1: lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium. Each has a single electron in its outermost shell, which is why they are soft, light and extremely reactive.
explanation: All six share one electron in an outer shell, and everything unusual about them follows from how loosely it is held. It is why they are soft enough to cut with a knife, why they melt at low temperatures, and why they react so violently with water — the metal sheds its single electron to hydrogen ions, releasing heat that often ignites the hydrogen it just made. Lithium is the exception that keeps the rule interesting: it is the hardest and the least reactive of the six, because its electron is held more tightly.

definition: The opposite of acidity, and the thing a base does to water: raise its pH and neutralise the acid in it. It is also a property of the water itself, since alkaline water dissolves more of most metals than neutral water does.
explanation: Alkalinity is a property of a solution and not of a substance, which is why the same substance can be alkaline in one context and neutral in another. It is also distinct from pH in a way that matters in water treatment: total alkalinity measures the water's capacity to neutralise acid, which is not the same number as its current pH. A soft drink's alkalinity and its pH can tell different stories.

definition: A mixture of metals, or of a metal with something else, made to be harder, tougher or more workable than its ingredients alone. Steel is iron with carbon, brass is copper with zinc, and both are harder than the metal they are mostly made of.
explanation: The strength of an alloy is not an additive property of its parts — it comes from the way the atoms of one element disrupt the orderly sliding of the other. That is why almost every metal in service is an alloy, and why pure gold is soft and pure iron is weak. The specific mixture is usually the result of a very old accident that was then kept because it worked.

definition: Deliberately mixing metals, or a metal with something else, to get properties the pure metal does not have. Nearly every metal in service is an alloy, because pure metals are usually too soft, too weak or too prone to corrosion to be useful.
explanation: Alloying is mostly a way of fixing a weakness rather than of improving a metal outright. Adding carbon to iron gives steel its hardness; adding zinc to copper gives brass its corrosion resistance; adding chromium to steel gives stainless steel its resistance to rust. The proportion matters as much as the ingredients, which is why alloy names carry numbers like 304 and 316 rather than a list.

definition: The decay of a heavy nucleus with the emission of an alpha particle. Because four nucleons leave the nucleus, the daughter element sits two places back in the table and about a third lighter.
explanation: Alpha decay matters more than its reputation suggests, because it is how a heavy nucleus climbs back down towards stability. An alpha emission costs the nucleus four nucleons at once, so the element drops two places in the table — the daughter of uranium-238 by alpha decay is thorium-234, and by another is radium-226. The helium nucleus it leaves behind is also how a smoke detector works, in a very indirect way: it ionises air, and the smoke changes how much current flows.

definition: A helium nucleus — two protons and two neutrons — given off by an atom that is decaying. It is the least penetrating of the three common emissions and a sheet of paper is enough to stop it.
explanation: An alpha particle is the least penetrating of the three common emissions, and that is a large part of why it is the most dangerous inside the body. A sheet of paper, or a few centimetres of air, stops it — but it does the most ionising damage of the three while it lasts. This is the reason alpha emitters are dangerous loose in the world and largely harmless sealed inside glass.

definition: The metal at number 13: light, easily worked, and resistant to corrosion because it grows a tough oxide skin over itself. It is the most abundant metal in the earth's crust, and almost as abundant as oxygen.
explanation: Aluminium's whole character is its oxide skin. The metal is reactive enough to attack and the oxide is not, so a few microns of it protect the rest, which is why an aluminium pot does not dissolve in tomato soup the way a steel one does. The oxide is also what makes it difficult to join to other metals: the skin has to be removed deliberately before aluminium will weld at all.

definition: A synthetic actinide, element 95, made in a reactor and used in smoke detectors in quantities of a few atoms' worth of mass. A larger quantity would be seriously hazardous.
explanation: A smoke detector contains roughly a microgram of americium, and the reason is the density of its emissions rather than their power. The alpha particles it gives off ionise the air between two electrodes, and a smoke particle interrupts that current. That the material is also a serious hazard is why the amounts are so small and why detectors are meant to be replaced rather than opened.

definition: The SI unit of current, one coulomb a second, abbreviated A and often shortened to amps. It is the rate of flow of charge, and the two quantities confused most often in everyday speech are exactly these two.
explanation: Ampere is the one of the three base electrical units, and it is a rate of flow rather than an amount: coulombs a second. The distinction between charge and current is the one that makes 'a battery holds 3 amp-hours' make sense — the hours are there because the ampere is per second, so the amp-hour is a capacity and not a rate. Ampere is named for André-Marie Ampère, the physicist who worked out that an electric current is a flow of charge and not of some fluid.

definition: Able to act as either an acid or a base. The oxides of aluminium and zinc are amphoteric — they dissolve in strong acids and in strong alkalis alike — which is a large part of what makes them useful as catalysts and as antacids.
explanation: Amphoteric oxides are the ones that dissolve in both acids and alkalis, and they are unusual because most oxides manage only one. Aluminium's is the important case, because it is what lets aluminium react with both an acid and an alkali and why amphoteric oxides are used as catalysts: they can accept or donate a proton depending on what is around them. The word is also applied to substances that are not oxides at all — an amino acid is amphoteric because it can accept or donate a proton.

definition: A negatively charged ion, formed when an atom gains electrons. The non-metals do this, and the chloride ion in table salt is an anion.
explanation: An anion's name comes from the same Greek root as cation but says the opposite thing: anions 'go down', towards the positive electrode. The pairing of the two names came from Faraday in 1834, who needed them to describe electrolysis, and it is one of the rare cases where a piece of vocabulary was invented deliberately and has stuck ever since.

definition: A brittle, toxic metalloid at number 51. Its compounds were once used as kohl, and antimony is still one of the elements in the plates of a lead-acid battery.
explanation: Antimony's history is a long list of uses that were abandoned for health reasons: kohl, a rat poison, a flame retardant, and lead-acid batteries where it is still used. It is one of the very few elements to have been known since antiquity in its native form, because it melts at a temperature a medieval furnace could reach — 630 °C, unusually low for a metal.

definition: A noble gas, element 18, making up about one per cent of the air. Because it will not react with anything, it is used to fill light bulbs and to shield a weld from oxygen.
explanation: Argon is what makes a fluorescent tube work and what keeps a welding arc from oxidising, and both uses come from the same inertness. It is also the gas used as a blanket over molten metal, because it is cheaper than helium and heavier, so it sits where it is put. Its one surprising feature is that, being so unreactive, it was not isolated until 1894 — a hundred years after nitrogen was.

definition: A metalloid at number 33 and a well-known poison. It forms compounds with many metals, is still used in some semiconductors, and for centuries was common in pesticides and in a green dye.
explanation: Arsenic is the textbook example of a substance that is tasteless, colourless and lethal in small amounts, and it was accordingly the classic poison of the nineteenth century. It is also a genuine semiconductor and a constituent of gallium arsenide, which is why it is still in use in some LEDs and in microwave electronics. Inorganic arsenic is a different hazard from the organic form found in seafood, which is why the two are regulated differently.

definition: The rarest naturally occurring element at number 85, with about a teaspoon's worth in the whole earth's crust at any moment. It is a halogen and would certainly be intensely reactive, but nobody has ever seen enough of it to look at.
explanation: Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element, with perhaps a teaspoon's worth in the entire earth's crust at any moment, and no one has ever seen enough of it to look at. Its properties are estimated rather than measured, on the grounds that the noble gas above it and the halogen beside it bracket them. It is the heaviest member of the halogens and the least stable of them.

definition: The smallest unit of an element that still has that element's properties: a nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons around it. Two atoms of different elements differ only in how many protons the nucleus holds.
explanation: The word once meant something that cannot be divided, and it kept that meaning long after the Greeks who coined it were wrong about it. An atom is divisible into a nucleus and electrons, and the nucleus into protons and neutrons, and those into quarks. It remains a useful name because a chemical reaction rearranges atoms and never makes or destroys one — which is the whole content of the law of conservation of mass.

definition: The fraction of a reaction's reactants' atoms that end up in the wanted product. A reaction that makes water as a by-product scores badly on it however efficient it is, which is what makes addition reactions preferable in green chemistry.
explanation: Atom economy asks a different question from yield, and the two are routinely confused. Yield is how much product you got; atom economy is how much of the reacting mass *could* have ended up as product, and it is fixed by the equation. A reaction that atom-economically uses every atom but gives you 5% yield is a different problem from one that can never use more than half its atoms, and only the second needs a better reaction rather than a better technique.

definition: The average mass of an element's atoms, weighted by how common each isotope is. It is a mean over a set rather than a measurement of any one atom, which is why it is often written with no unit.
explanation: Atomic mass is a weighted average and nothing else, which is why no single atom has it. For an element with one dominant isotope it is nearly that isotope's mass number; for tin, which has ten stable isotopes, it is a mean across all of them and cannot be expressed as a whole number at all. It is written with no unit because it is a ratio, and it is what the periodic table's mass column actually lists.

definition: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus, and the one fact that settles which element the atom is. It is also that element's position in the periodic table, counted from the top left.
explanation: Atomic number is the one fact about an atom that settles everything else, and it was the argument that reshaped the table. The original periodic arrangement was by atomic weight, which put tellurium wrongly next to selenium; in 1913 Moseley showed that an element's X-ray spectrum depends on the number of protons and not on its weight, and that single number fixed the ordering. It is also the element's position, counted from the top left.

definition: A region around a nucleus in which an electron is likely to be found, described by a set of quantum numbers rather than a path. There are three orbitals in the first shell, seven in the second and nine in the third, which is where the rows of the table come from.
explanation: An orbital is not a path and cannot be observed directly; it is a region where an electron is likely to be found, and its shape is a description of where it usually is rather than a shape the electron has. The three shapes that matter on this site are s (a sphere), p (two lobes) and d (four lobes), and the number of orbitals in a shell is what makes the periods of the table seven and then longer. The letter is the principal quantum number, and it is what the period number counts.

definition: Roughly half the distance between the nuclei of two atoms just touching. It is measured differently in tables of metals and tables of covalent bonds, so the two sets of numbers are not directly comparable.
explanation: Atomic radius is one of the least tidy numbers in the table, and the reason is worth knowing before comparing two of them. A free atom has no edge; the figure quoted is half the internuclear distance in the closest-packed solid, which is a measurement of a bonded pair rather than of an atom. Covalent and metallic radii are measured differently again, so the two columns of numbers are not comparable with each other.

definition: The rule that electrons fill the available orbitals in order of increasing energy, lowest first. It is what makes an electron configuration readable left to right, and the anomalies in it — chromium and copper among them — are what make it a rule rather than a law.
explanation: Aufbau means building up, and the principle is that the orbitals fill from the bottom of the energy order upwards — the reason an electron configuration reads left to right. It is a rule rather than a law because chromium and copper break it, both gaining a half-filled or full d shell instead of the configuration the naive order predicts. Those two exceptions are the reason the d block is ten wide rather than fourteen.

definition: The number of particles in a mole: 6.022 × 10²³ to the mole. It is what lets a chemist count atoms by weighing a substance rather than by counting them one at a time.
explanation: Avogadro's constant is named for the Italian who proposed in 1811 that equal volumes of gas at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules — a claim that was not testable for nearly a century, and which turned out to be exactly right. The number is now defined by fixing it, which is unusual and slightly circular; its practical value is that it converts between a mass on a balance and a count of particles, which is the conversion chemistry exists to make.

definition: An alkaline earth metal at number 56, silvery while fresh and quickly dulling as it oxidises. Its insoluble sulfate is opaque to X-rays, which is why a patient swallows a barium meal before an examination of the gut.
explanation: Barium's sulfate is one of the few compounds that is opaque to X-rays and harmless to swallow, which is why a patient can drink a barium meal and have a radiograph taken an hour later. That single property bought barium a medical use it would otherwise never have had. Barium itself is toxic as a soluble salt, because barium ions are the size to slip through cell membranes and interfere with potassium channels.

definition: A substance that neutralises an acid. In water it raises the pH, turns red litmus blue, and is the opposite of an acid in every way that matters to a reaction.
explanation: The everyday definition and the chemical one are not quite the same thing, and the difference is worth holding on to. A base is something that accepts a proton, which is a wider class than the alkalis and includes the carbonate ion and the ammonia molecule. The usual test — red litmus turning blue — is a test for a particular family of bases rather than for all of them.

definition: The main aluminium ore, a mixture of hydrated oxides rather than a pure compound, and the reason aluminium was once worth more than gold. It is named for the French town of Les Baux, where it was first identified.
explanation: Bauxite is not one ore but a mixture of hydrated oxides, and which hydrate it holds is why there is no single formula for it. It is also the reason aluminium is cheap: the ore is common, and once the Hall–Héroult electrolysis process made smelting it cheaper than recycling, the price collapsed and aluminium displaced tin and lead from almost every use they had held. Bauxite also sits close to some of the world's most sensitive places, and refining it has an environmental cost that is not in the metal.

definition: The SI unit of radioactivity, one decay a second, abbreviated Bq. A curie is 3.7 × 10¹⁰ of them, which is the scale at which the becquerel stopped being a useful number.
explanation: The becquerel is a count of events, not a measure of energy, which is why a becquerel and a sievert are not comparable and are regularly confused in reporting. One becquerel per second is an astonishingly small activity by any ordinary standard — a curie is 3.7 billion of them — which is the clearest illustration of how little material a radioactive source actually needs.

definition: A synthetic actinide at number 97, named after Berkeley, and made in milligram quantities at most. It is the element from which tennessine and oganesson are made, and the heaviest one ever made in weighable amounts.
explanation: Berkelium is the element with the highest atomic number that has ever been made in quantities you could weigh, which is why it is the frontier of what chemistry can do rather than of what physics can. Beyond it, every atom has to be made one at a time in an accelerator and picked out of the stream, and the chemistry of the heaviest elements is largely inferred rather than measured.

definition: A light, stiff, toxic metal at number 4. Its high stiffness per unit weight and its transparency to X-rays are what it is still used for — in the frames of instruments and in the windows of X-ray detectors.
explanation: Beryllium is stiff and light to a degree that justifies its expense: in stiffness per unit weight it beats steel, and its thermal conductivity is unusually high. The complication is that it is also toxic and its dust causes a lung disease with no known cure, which is why it is used inside sealed housings and in amounts you would not think were possible from its presence in a mobile phone.

definition: Blowing air through molten iron to burn out the carbon and impurities, and so to turn pig iron into steel in one step. It made steel cheap enough for railways to be built, and its noise and heat eventually drove it out of use.
explanation: The Bessemer converter made steel cheap enough to change the world, and it did so in about twenty years. It also made an enormous noise — a hundred tonnes of molten iron blowing air through it roars loud enough to burst eardrums at a hundred metres — which is how the idiom 'Bessemer soup' entered the language for a very loud argument. It was eventually displaced by the open hearth and then by basic oxygen, both of which are quieter and recover more of the metal.

definition: The decay of a nucleus in which a neutron turns into a proton or a proton into a neutron, giving out an electron or a positron. The element moves one place along the table while its mass barely changes.
explanation: Beta decay is how a nucleus adjusts its neutron-to-proton ratio, and it is the most common of the three decays because it changes the ratio one neutron at a time. The important practical consequence is that a nucleus which is a beta emitter is nearly always a gamma emitter as well, because the nucleus it becomes is usually left in an excited state and sheds the difference as gamma rays. That is the reason a beta source is usually shielded in lead rather than in plastic.

definition: An electron or positron given off in beta decay. It penetrates far better than an alpha particle and takes a thin metal sheet rather than a sheet of paper to stop.
explanation: A beta particle is an electron or a positron, and the sign matters more than people expect. A positron is a beta-plus emission and a beta-minus is an electron, and when a nucleus emits a positron it has converted a proton into a neutron, so the element moves *down* the table rather than up. Beta particles need a thin metal sheet to stop where alphas need paper, because they are far lighter and far faster.

definition: The build-up of a substance in a living organism over time, faster than the environment is depleted. Mercury and lead both do it, which is why they are found at higher concentration in a predator than in anything it ate.
explanation: Bioaccumulation and biomagnification are different processes that are often named as if they were one. Bioaccumulation is a single organism taking in a substance faster than it can excrete it, so it builds up over its lifetime; a fish in clean water slowly acquires a body burden. The consequence is that a laboratory measurement of the water says very little about the load in the animal, and water-quality limits measured in water are not the same as limits measured in tissue.

definition: The increase in concentration of a substance at each step of a food chain, so that top predators carry far more than the water they live in. It is why the mercury advice for swordfish differs from the advice for tuna.
explanation: Biomagnification is why a food chain is a route of exposure and not only a diagram of who eats whom. A pollutant that is persistent and fat-soluble concentrates at the top of the chain, so the largest fish carry the highest burden, and the advice for a predator has to differ from the advice for what it eats. Mercury is the standard example and the reason swordfish and tuna are treated differently in advisories.

definition: The heaviest element that is very nearly stable, at number 83, growing iridescent in air and melting on a warm windowsill. It was long thought to be the heaviest stable element, and the discovery that lead is radioactive rather than bismuth came as a surprise.
explanation: Bismuth was long taught as the heaviest stable element, and that turned out to be wrong: lead is heavier and is weakly radioactive, with a half-life longer than the age of the universe. Bismuth is also the most strongly diamagnetic of the elements, which makes it a good support for a levitation experiment, and it is the active ingredient in the stomach remedy that replaced the more dangerous salts before it.

definition: The Danish physicist whose model of the atom put the electrons in fixed energy levels with quantised jumps between them, which explained the line spectra of hydrogen and the fact that atoms do not collapse. It is the picture still taught, and it is wrong in ways that turned out to matter.
explanation: Bohr's model is the picture every schoolchild draws and it is wrong in a specific, useful way. Electrons do not orbit in fixed circles; they occupy orbitals, and the ground state of an atom is not a tiny solar system but a probability cloud. The part that survives intact is the quantised energy levels — the jumps between them are what produce an element's line spectrum, and that is the observation the model was built to explain.

definition: A synthetic element at number 107, named for Niels Bohr, whose model of the atom is what a chemistry student uses to describe shells. A few dozen atoms have been made, in accelerator collisions lasting milliseconds.
explanation: Bohrium sits at the top of group 7, below technetium and rhenium, and it is one of the heaviest elements whose chemistry has actually been studied in solution. The result is a surprise in the making: it behaves more like the element above it than like the one beside it in its own period, which is one of several signs that relativistic effects begin to matter at these atomic numbers. 'Bohr' the man and 'Bohrium' the element are unrelated, the second being named for the first.

definition: The temperature at which a liquid becomes a gas throughout, rather than only at its surface. Water boils at 100 °C at sea level because the pressure there allows it to.
explanation: Boiling point is where a liquid's vapour pressure reaches atmospheric pressure, which is why it changes with altitude and why a pressure cooker raises it deliberately. That also means a boiling point quoted without a pressure is incomplete — water boils at 100 °C at sea level and at about 93 °C on a high mountain. What is invariant is the order: van der Waals forces raise it, hydrogen bonding raises it further, and ionic bonding raises it more than anything.

definition: The energy needed to break one bond between two particular atoms in a gaseous molecule. Average values are tabulated and used to estimate reaction enthalpies, and they are averages, so an estimate built from them is only as good as its inputs.
explanation: Bond enthalpies are averages, and the average is doing real work in every estimate built from it. The energy to break a C–H bond in methane is not quite the energy to break one in ethane, but a table gives one number for both and an estimate built on it inherits that error. It is still the fastest way to get from an equation to a figure for whether a reaction gives out heat, and a figure is usually the point.

definition: A metalloid at number 5, hard and heat-resistant, and one of the elements in borosilicate glass, which is why Pyrex survives a hot oven. It is essential to plants in traces and to no one in larger amounts.
explanation: Boron is the first element where the straightforward rules stop working, which is why it sits awkwardly at the edge of the metalloids. It has an unusually high neutron-capture cross-section, so it is used in control rods and in shielding, and borax was for centuries the standard way to set glass. Boron carbide is harder than most ceramics and light enough to use in body armour.

definition: The tendency to break rather than bend when a force is applied, without much deformation first. Glass, cast iron and most ceramics are brittle; the metals that are not have metallic bonding that lets layers of atoms slide.
explanation: Brittleness is not a weakness so much as the absence of a mechanism for absorbing strain. A metal deforms by dislocations sliding past one another, which costs energy and spreads the deformation out; a ceramic has no such mechanism, so a crack runs and the part fails at once. This is why glass can be strengthened by thermal tempering — it puts the surface into compression so a surface crack has to overcome a barrier before it can grow.

definition: The only non-metal that is a liquid at room temperature, a heavy red-brown one, and the only one to be so at all without being a metal. It is used in flame retardants and in the process that removes lead from petrol.
explanation: Bromine is the only non-metal liquid at room temperature, and the fact is worth a moment: every other liquid at ordinary conditions is a metal or a molecular compound with strong intermolecular forces, and bromine is heavy enough to have overcome that. It was once added to leaded petrol as an exhaust scavenger and has been phased out, because it does not degrade and it accumulates in tissue.

definition: A solution that resists a change in pH when a little acid or base is added, usually because it contains a weak acid and its conjugate base together. Blood plasma is one, and the reason it works is physiological rather than chemical.
explanation: A buffer works by having both members of a conjugate pair present, so added hydrogen ions are taken up by the base and hydroxide ions by the acid. Its capacity is finite — a buffer neutralises only a limited amount — which is why a buffer that has been overwhelmed stops buffering and why the pH then moves sharply. Enzyme assays depend on holding the pH steady, since almost every enzyme's rate is pH-sensitive.

definition: The German chemist who designed the burner named after him and, with Kirchhoff, discovered caesium, rubidium, thallium and indium by spectroscopy. The flame test exists because they worked out that each element has its own emission spectrum.
explanation: The burner is the part everybody knows and the spectroscopy is the part that mattered. Kirchhoff and Bunsen showed that each element has its own emission spectrum, that a hot gas emits lines at the same wavelengths it absorbs, and that the lines tell you which elements are present without breaking anything down. It turned chemical analysis from a question answered by precipitation into one answered by a look at a colour, and it is why caesium, rubidium, thallium and indium were found at all.

definition: A soft, toxic metal at number 48, once widely used in batteries and in yellow pigments. Both uses have largely been withdrawn because cadmium accumulates in the body rather than passing through it.
explanation: Cadmium and lead share a toxicity profile that is why both are disappearing from everyday products: both are soft at the end of the periodic table, both mimic other elements chemically, and both accumulate in the body rather than passing through it. Cadmium's worst property is kidney damage over decades, which is why the European Union restricted it in batteries and jewellery and why rice is still periodically tested for it.

definition: An alkali metal at number 55 whose atoms vibrate at exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles a second, which is how the second is defined. It melts just above room temperature and reacts with water violently enough to ignite the hydrogen it gives off.
explanation: The definition of the second has moved twice in twenty years and both times it was because caesium offered a better standard. The first was astronomical, from the Earth's rotation; the second was the caesium-133 hyperfine transition, a frequency that depends on nothing in the universe. Now even that has been overtaken by optical clocks based on a single trapped ion or a neutral atom, so caesium keeps the label and no longer the job.

definition: Heating a carbonate so that it decomposes, giving the metal's oxide and carbon dioxide. Lime is made this way from limestone, and the reaction is also how cement sets.
explanation: Calcination is the step that makes lime, cement and magnesia, and in each case the useful product is what is left after a gas escapes. Limestone becomes calcium oxide and carbon dioxide; the carbonate is broken down because it is less stable at high temperature than the oxide. In metallurgy the same word covers driving off water or other volatiles from an ore before the real work begins.

definition: The metal at number 20, the fifth most abundant in the crust and the metal of bone and shell. It reacts with cold water, and it is what lime is made from.
explanation: Calcium is the metal of bone and shell, and also the reason both are hard: a crystal of hydroxyapatite is a lattice with calcium ions in the gaps, and dissolving that lattice is what acid does to a bone. In the crust calcium compounds are the most common soluble material there is, which is why limestone landscapes are prone to both cave formation and very hard water.

definition: A synthetic actinide at number 98, notable for producing neutrons in quantity. A gram of it emits some forty billion neutrons a second, which makes it invaluable for starting reactors and for finding gold and oil by neutron scattering.
explanation: Californium is included in this glossary for one property, and it is unlike anything else on the site: a gram of it emits around forty billion neutrons a second. That makes it irreplaceable for starting reactors and for neutron scattering, which is how a neutron is used to look inside a drum and find the gold in it. The same usefulness makes it one of the most dangerous materials anyone has handled routinely.

definition: The element at number 6, at the centre of all organic chemistry and of life itself. It bonds to itself in long chains more readily than any other element, which is why there are millions of carbon compounds.
explanation: Carbon is the only element in the table with a chemistry of its own rather than a character within one, and the reason is a single orbital. It has four valence electrons and exactly half a shell to fill, so it bonds to itself in chains, rings and sheets as readily as to anything else, and there are millions of known compounds containing it. That is the whole content of organic chemistry, and it is why a definition of life on this planet tends to be a definition of carbon.

definition: Hardening a steel surface by heating it with carbon so that the carbon diffuses in. Gears and shafts are treated this way, since the hard skin takes the wear and the soft core resists impact.
explanation: Carburising hardens only the outside of a part, and that is the point: a gear needs a hard surface to take the wear and a soft core underneath to survive an impact, and the two are contradictory in one uniform material. The depth is controlled by how long the part sits in the carbon. It differs from nitriding in working at a lower temperature and so distorting the part less.

definition: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up by it, because it offers a route of lower activation energy and comes out unchanged. A catalyst changes how fast a reaction runs, not whether it happens or what it makes.
explanation: A catalyst changes a reaction's rate without being consumed, which sounds like a small qualification and is in fact the whole mechanism — it works by offering a different route with a lower activation energy, and it comes out of that route unchanged. Two consequences follow. A catalyst cannot make an unfavourable reaction happen, because that is a question of thermodynamics and not of route. And it cannot make a reaction reversible, which is why the industrial Haber process removes ammonia as it forms rather than relying on a catalyst to push the equilibrium along.

definition: A device in a car's exhaust that converts carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water. Platinum, palladium and rhodium catalyse it, and the catalyst is used but never consumed.
explanation: The three metals in a converter are not in there to be consumed and not chosen for their price but for how well they hold intermediate states on their surfaces. Platinum, palladium and rhodium do three different jobs at once — carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons are three different reactions — and losing any one of them disables a third of the converter. That is why a catalytic converter is worth stealing and why nobody steals a catalytic converter to melt down the metal.

definition: A positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses electrons. The metals do this, and the sodium ion that makes table salt dissolve is a cation.
explanation: The name means 'walker', from the Greek for going up, and it is one of very few chemical words that is simply a picture of what the particle does: in an electric field a cation moves towards the negative electrode. Cations are almost always metals, because metals have few valence electrons to lose, and that is why the metals form salts and the non-metals do not.

definition: The chemist who in 1785 showed that the residue left when air is burned with hydrogen is not empty but a distinct gas, and who called it fixed air. That residue was oxygen, and his careful weighing is what convinced Lavoisier that combustion involved a real substance.
explanation: The experiment is remembered because of what it nearly missed. Cavendish passed hydrogen and oxygen together through a tube, ignited them, and measured the small residue of a third gas left behind; he reported it as a residue from an impurity rather than as a new substance, and called it fixed air without recognising it. Twenty years later Lavoisier did recognise it, and the recognition is what ended phlogiston.

definition: The apparent outward force felt by something moving in a circle, which is not a real force but the inertial effect of the body's own motion. It is what throws water outwards in a bucket swung overhead, and what makes a centrifuge work.
explanation: It is not a force, and the confusion has its own name: the centrifugal force error. In a rotating frame you have to invent a fictitious outward force to get Newton's laws to hold, and doing so makes the frame's equations match the lab's — which is why the manoeuvre is allowed and why it is still taught carelessly. The genuine physical effect is different: a mass being swung in a circle needs a real inward force, supplied by exactly the tension you feel.

definition: Spinning a mixture fast enough that denser particles are thrown to the bottom of the tube. It separates suspensions that filtration is too slow for, and it is how the ribosomes are pulled out of a cell.
explanation: Centrifugation separates on density, filtration on size, and there are cases where only one of them works. A suspension of very fine particles passes through a filter paper and would take days to sediment under gravity, but spins down in a minute at a few thousand times gravity. It is also how a cell is taken apart — nucleus, membrane, ribosomes — because the organelles differ enough in density to move apart.

definition: The most abundant of the rare earths at number 58, used in the polishing powder that polishes glass and in the catalytic converter. Its ions change oxidation state easily, which is what makes both of those work.
explanation: Cerium is the workhorse of the rare earths because its ions flip between two oxidation states very readily, and that is exactly what a catalyst needs. It is also what polishes glass: cerium oxide is the only material that removes a scratch optically rather than by taking material away, so a lens can be polished repeatedly without thinning. The element is more abundant in the crust than copper and has no uses without this ion.

definition: The physicist who in 1932 identified the neutron, the neutral particle in the nucleus, which completed the picture of the atom and explained the isotopes. He built Britain's first nuclear reactor afterwards, and worked on the Manhattan Project.
explanation: The neutron completed the nucleus and with it the explanation of isotopes, and it was found by the obvious method: bombardment knocks protons out easily and neutrons out not at all, so anything that was not deflected by a magnetic field had to be neutral. Chadwick went on to build Britain's first nuclear reactor at a chalk pit, and the pile at Harwell is why there is a British contribution to the Manhattan Project at all.

definition: A reaction whose products start further reactions of the same kind. Fission releases neutrons that split further nuclei, and that is what makes both a reactor and a bomb work; a chain reaction that stays steady is critical, and one that grows is not.
explanation: The three regimes are worth being able to name. Subcritical, where each fission frees less than one further fission and the reaction dies out — which is how a reactor is shut down. Critical, where one fission frees exactly one further fission and the rate holds steady. Supercritical, where it grows, which is both a reactor's accident and a weapon's design. Nothing about the process is different between the last two; only the arithmetic is.

definition: Any of the six elements in group 16: oxygen, sulfur, selenium, tellurium, polonium and livermorium. The name means copper-bearer, since several of them combine with copper to make the ores it is smelted from.
explanation: The name means copper-bearer and records something practical: several of these combine with copper to form the ores copper is smelted from. The group behaves as one family because they all need two more electrons to close their shell, and they differ in how hard that is — oxygen is reactive enough to burn almost anything, while tellurium is barely attacked by anything but concentrated oxidising acids.

definition: A compound of a chalcogen — usually sulfur — with a metal or with another element. They are the semiconductors in infrared detectors and in the materials that produce laser light, and galena is one.
explanation: Chalcogenide semiconductors are used where silicon cannot work. Gallium arsenide and indium phosphide have direct band gaps, so they emit light when a current passes, and that is the whole basis of LEDs and of the fastest optical fibre links. The heavier chalcogens extend the range into the infrared, where a camera can see through something that is opaque to visible light.

definition: A glass of sulfur, selenium or tellurium rather than of silica, which transmits infrared and is used in thermal imaging lenses. The heavier the chalcogen, the further into the infrared it sees.
explanation: Ordinary glass is opaque to infrared, and chalcogenide glass is not, because the heavier chalcogens absorb at longer wavelengths. That single property gives thermal imaging lenses that see body heat through fog and smoke. The trade is real: these glasses are expensive, and some of them soften at temperatures that would be trivial for a normal glass.

definition: The electrical property of a particle, arising from an imbalance of protons and electrons. It comes in multiples of the charge on one electron, and like charges repel while unlike charges attract.
explanation: Charge is conserved in every reaction, and checking that is one of the first things done to any proposed equation. It also explains far more than bookkeeping does — the attraction between a cation and an anion is why salts have such very different properties from the elements they came from, and the flow of charge is what a battery arranges to deliver.

definition: A pale green halogen, element 17, used for disinfecting water and for making PVC. It is a gas at room temperature and a very reactive one.
explanation: Chlorine is the element that made water treatment cheap enough to be universal, and its failure is what the chlorination of drinking water exists to prevent. It also reacts with almost every organic molecule, which is why PVC is the only large use that survived: chlorine's reactivity in a polymer chain is exactly what makes the polymer useful. Its density means a litre of chlorine gas is about three times heavier than air, and that matters when it leaks.

definition: The result of a chromatography run — the pattern of separated bands on the paper or plate. Measuring how far each band travelled relative to the solvent front is what gives the retention factor a compound is identified by.
explanation: The measurement taken from a chromatogram is the retention factor — how far a compound travelled relative to the solvent front — and two compounds under the same conditions with the same retention factor are the same compound, which is what makes the method an identification and not only a separation. A band that splits into two is a mixture that a single solvent did not resolve, and the usual answer is a different solvent rather than a longer column.

definition: Separating a mixture by passing it through a column of material that the components travel through at different speeds. Plant pigments separate into distinct bands in a chromatography jar because each dye sticks to the paper a different amount.
explanation: Chromatography separates by difference in attraction, not in boiling point, which is why it works on things that could not be distilled at all — amino acids, dyes, proteins, pigments. The plant pigments separated in a jar of water and paper are doing exactly what a gas chromatograph does, and both were worked out by people who noticed that a solvent front and a sample move at different speeds. It is the method that made protein sequencing possible.

definition: The metal at number 24, hard and resistant to corrosion. Stainless steel is iron with chromium in it, and the metal is what gives ruby's colour.
explanation: Chromium is the element that made stainless steel possible, and stainless steel is the reason a great deal of twentieth-century architecture is still standing. The mechanism is a passive oxide film a few nanometres thick, and it is self-repairing as long as oxygen is present — which is why a stainless bolt in seawater outlasts a galvanised one in fresh air, the opposite of what the zinc coating on the other does.

definition: The metal at number 27, used in the rechargeable batteries in phones and in the magnets of aircraft engines. Compounds of it have been used as a blue pigment for two thousand years.
explanation: Cobalt's compounds have been used as a blue pigment for about as long as people have been smelting, and the colour is a d-electron transition, which is why it is so intense and why it changes with the ligand attached. The modern use is in batteries: the same reversible oxidation that gave the pigment its colour is what lets cobalt sit at the centre of a rechargeable cell, and the concentration of supply is a well-known fragility of that chemistry.

definition: Burning: a reaction with oxygen that releases heat and light, usually exothermic enough to sustain itself. Hydrocarbons burn completely to carbon dioxide and water.
explanation: A combustion that sustains itself is exothermic and self-propagating, which together explain both a burning fire and why it goes out when starved of air. The reaction is also the reason so much of the atmosphere is inert: burning fossil carbon has been adding about a third of the oxygen in the atmosphere, and removing it from the carbon dioxide would change the composition, which is the basis of the carbon cycle. That is the part worth knowing before treating combustion as purely local.

definition: Burning a fuel in plenty of oxygen so that everything oxidises fully, giving carbon dioxide and water and releasing the maximum heat. Incomplete combustion leaves carbon monoxide or soot, which is both less efficient and poisonous.
explanation: The difference between complete and incomplete combustion is worth a great deal of money and a great deal of safety. Complete burning of a hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide and water and releases the maximum heat; incomplete burning gives carbon monoxide and soot, gives out less, and produces a gas that is lethal because it binds haemoglobin more tightly than oxygen does. A boiler starved of air does not just burn badly, it makes poison.

definition: A substance made of two or more elements joined in fixed proportions, with properties of its own that differ from those of the elements in it. Water is a compound; a mixture is not.
explanation: A compound has a fixed composition, and that is what distinguishes it from a mixture — and it is a constraint that surprises people, because it means a compound is always describable by one formula. Water is H₂O and not H₂O and a bit of H₂O. The other consequence is that a compound has properties of its own, which is how the discovery of a new one is usually recognised: something is behaving like nothing that went into it.

definition: How much of a substance is present in a given volume of solution, usually in moles per litre. It is the variable most often quoted on a reagent bottle and the one most reactions depend on.
explanation: Concentration is what a chemist changes to change a reaction's rate, and the relationship is not always simple: rate is roughly first order in concentration for many reactions, and roughly proportional to the square of it for others, so doubling a concentration may double or quadruple the rate. Molarity is the usual unit, and molality is used where the volume changes — which is why a calorimetry result is quoted per kilogram of solvent rather than per litre.

definition: How well a substance carries a current. Metals conduct through mobile electrons, solutions through mobile ions, and diamond conducts because its valence electrons are locked in bonds — which is why it insulates.
explanation: Conductivity is one of the clearest demonstrations that a model's limits are real. Metals, ionic solutions and plasmas conduct because they have mobile charge carriers; graphite conducts because its delocalised electrons move; diamond does not conduct for exactly the same reason graphite does, differing only in whether the electrons are tied up in bonds. The four cases are one rule applied four times, and knowing which case you are in tells you what to expect.

definition: A synthetic element at number 112, named for Copernicus, and the heaviest one to have shown evidence of behaving like a metal rather than a gas. It sits at the edge of the periodic table where the rules are known to stop predicting.
explanation: Copernicium is the heaviest element whose chemistry has been measured in solution, and the measurement is the interesting part. It sits in group 12, below mercury, and it was expected to behave like mercury; the experiments suggest it does not, behaving more like a noble gas or even like gold. That is the boundary of where the periodic table's predictions work, and it is being found element by element.

definition: The metal at number 29, and the second best conductor of electricity after silver. It is unreactive enough to use in wiring and in water pipes, which is why it has been used for both for millennia.
explanation: Copper's usefulness is a coincidence of three properties that rarely travel together: it is the second best conductor of electricity, it does not corrode appreciably, and it is easy to work. Silver conducts better but costs far more, and aluminium conducts nearly as well and corrodes. Copper also corrodes slowly and gracefully, going green with a stable carbonate patina that protects the metal underneath — which is why a copper roof outlasts its fasteners.

definition: The gradual destruction of a material by a chemical reaction with its surroundings, most often oxidation by air and water. Iron's rust is not strong and flakes off, so a corroding steel section loses the metal rather than being protected by the coating.
explanation: The economics of corrosion are dominated by the difference between a coating that protects by being a barrier and one that protects by being sacrificial. A paint film simply stops water reaching the metal and fails when it is scratched; galvanised zinc fails sacrificially, so the scratch itself is protected and the damage is spread over the zinc's whole area instead of concentrating at the hole. That difference decides which coating to specify, and getting it wrong is the more expensive mistake.

definition: A bond in which two atoms share a pair of electrons. It holds molecular substances together, it is usually strong, and it is what a diamond is made of.
explanation: The shared-pair model is a picture rather than a mechanism, and it is misleading in one specific way that matters for carbon. The electrons are not assigned to either atom or genuinely shared between them; they occupy a molecular orbital spread over both nuclei, and for the same atom the pair sits away from the internuclear axis. The picture is still worth using because it gets the geometry and the counts right, and because chemistry is full of useful pictures.

definition: Breaking long hydrocarbon chains into shorter ones. Thermal cracking heats them until they split; catalytic cracking passes them over a zeolite, which is a refinery's way of turning heavy fuel oil into the lighter fractions people actually buy.
explanation: Catalytic cracking is the reason a barrel of heavy crude is worth more than a barrel of light one, because a refinery can turn the heavy fraction into the gasoline people actually buy. The zeolite catalyst does it at around 500 °C by selecting reactions by the size of their molecules, which is why the process replaced thermal cracking: the products are more controlled and the plants do not coke up as fast.

definition: The slow, permanent deformation of a material under a load it could otherwise bear, especially at high temperature. Turbine blades are designed against creep, because the failure comes at a load well below the breaking point.
explanation: Creep is the failure mode that material testing most easily misses, because it happens far below the breaking load and over far longer than a test. A turbine blade does not run at the temperature where its alloy melts; it runs below the temperature where its alloy *stops behaving*, and the difference between those two numbers is the whole design problem. Gas turbine blades are therefore given very specific lives and are inspected while the engine is running.

definition: A solid whose atoms or ions form a repeating three-dimensional arrangement, so that its faces and its melting point are both definite. Almost every solid is crystalline; glass is the familiar exception.
explanation: A crystal is defined by its repeating order, and that is what gives it a fixed melting point and a definite shape rather than a range. A single crystal of silicon, grown slowly and faultlessly, is the substrate a whole chip is built on, and the difficulty is that a grain boundary or a dislocation in it ruins the layer above — which is why the growth is done in a vacuum, very slowly, and why it is expensive.

definition: The repeating arrangement of atoms in a solid, which decides nearly everything a material does — its hardness, its melting point, and whether it conducts. Iron and diamond are both carbon-based solids with completely different structures, and therefore opposite properties.
explanation: Diamond and graphite are the proof that structure is a property in its own right rather than a detail. Both are pure carbon with identical atoms and identical bonding; they differ only in how those bonds are arranged, and that is why one is the hardest substance known and the other is a lubricant that marks paper. The arrangement also decides the melting point, the density, and whether the material conducts, so any prediction about a solid starts here.

definition: A substance coming out of solution as ordered crystals as it cools or as the solvent evaporates. The shape and size of the crystal are governed by how fast it forms, which is why a pan of brine gives big cubes and a stirred tank gives fine powder.
explanation: The reason most impure solids can be purified by recrystallisation is that impurities are usually present in too small an amount to crystallise at all, so they stay in the solution while the wanted substance comes out. It also explains why the crystals are large when the solution cools slowly: crystal growth needs time, and a fast cooling makes many nuclei and small crystals. That is also why a good crystal is grown slowly and a bad one is made quickly.

definition: A unit of radioactivity equal to 3.7 × 10¹⁰ decays a second, named for Marie and Pierre Curie. The becquerel is the SI unit and is one decay a second, so a curie is 37 gigabecquerels.
explanation: The curie is named for the couple and is still the unit people remember, because the becquerel is an inconveniently small number for the activities people actually handle. It is also the last unit defined in terms of a sample rather than in terms of a physical constant, which makes it one of a shrinking group; the gray and the sievert are its modern equivalents for the two things a radiation measurement needs to say.

definition: A radioactive actinide at number 96, named for Marie and Pierre Curie and made by bombarding plutonium. It is bright pink in solution, one of the few elements whose colour is recognisable from a distance, and it powers the instruments on Mars rovers.
explanation: Curium's pink solutions are among the few places where an element's colour is distinctive enough to identify at a glance, which is a reminder that element colours come from electron transitions and are genuinely diagnostic. Its practical importance is different and larger: it powered the alpha particle X-ray spectrometer on Apollo 15 and 16, and it still powers the instruments that Mars rovers have used to determine what the rocks are made of.

definition: The English chemist whose atomic theory proposed that each element is made of indivisible atoms, that atoms of one element are identical, and that they combine in whole-number ratios. It was the first theory of the atom that could do chemistry, and it was not right about the indivisibility.
explanation: Dalton's theory is the first that lets chemistry do arithmetic. Atoms of one element are identical and combine in whole-number ratios, which is what makes a formula meaningful and what makes the law of definite proportions follow. Its central mistake was indivisibility — the atom is divisible — and getting that wrong is why it took another century to explain the periodic table's shape.

definition: A synthetic element at number 110, named after Darmstadt, where it was made. Only a few dozen atoms have ever been assembled, and its chemistry has not been measured in solution at all.
explanation: Darmstadtium's place in the table says more about chemistry's limits than the element itself. It sits in group 10 below platinum, and predictions for its melting point range from near absolute zero to several hundred degrees, which is not a disagreement about detail but about whether the periodic table still works at all here. Only a few dozen atoms of it have ever been made.

definition: The chemist who isolated more elements than anyone before him, by electrolysis, including sodium, potassium, chlorine and iodine. Electrolysis had only just been discovered when he began, and he worked through the alkali metals in a single winter.
explanation: Davy's six weeks of electrolysis produced more elements than anyone had found in the previous two thousand years, and the reason is that a new technique was pointed at old material. Sodium and potassium had been known as compounds for centuries because nobody had a way to reduce them; an electric current did. He also lost his eyes in a mercury explosion during the work, and found his own iodine treatment for it.

definition: Pouring a liquid off a sediment without disturbing it. It separates the coarse from the fine rather than filtering, so it works well for settling sand out of water and not at all for two miscible liquids.
explanation: Decantation separates on settling and filtration separates on size, and choosing between them is a question about the particles rather than about the liquid. Pouring off is enough for coarse sediment and useless for a fine precipitate, and for two miscible liquids neither works at all — that needs distillation. The word is also used loosely for pouring off wine from sediment in a barrel, which is the same operation in a different century.

definition: The spontaneous breakdown of an unstable nucleus into a smaller one. Radioactive decay is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical form, which is what makes it useful for dating and impossible to switch off.
explanation: Decay applies to the nucleus and only to the nucleus, so nothing you can do to a sample chemically will change its rate. That is the property that makes radiometric dating possible: the clock is unaffected by everything that happened to the rock since, including being heated, buried, dissolved and re-formed. The three common decays — alpha, beta and gamma emission — differ in what leaves the nucleus and how far it can travel.

definition: Mass per unit volume, and the property that says how tightly a substance packs its atoms. Water at 1 g/cm3 is the usual yardstick: osmium is twenty-three times denser, and gas is thousands of times less dense.
explanation: Density is the property that most often contradicts intuition, because it is a ratio rather than a quality. Lithium, sodium and potassium float on water; osmium, iridium and lead sink, and a neutron star would be denser than any of them by a factor of about ten thousand. Reading a density beside an element's state tells you almost as much about the bonding as the melting point does.

definition: A gas turning straight into a solid without passing through a liquid, as dry ice does. It is the reverse of sublimation, and the reason a freezer burns things placed in it.
explanation: Deposition and sublimation are the pair that people find hardest to picture, because both involve a change of state that skips one. Neither has anything to do with freezing or boiling, and both are the same weak-intermolecular-force regime: solid to liquid needs energy to break bonds, gas to solid needs the particles to lose more, and there is no liquid in between for carbon dioxide at all. It is why dry ice freezes rather than cools, and why a freezer can burn skin.

definition: A cleaning agent whose molecules have one end that grips grease and one that grips water, so it lifts dirt off a surface and carries it away. Soap does the same job, but soap molecules form scum with hard water and detergent molecules do not.
explanation: Detergents and soaps differ in one structural detail with large consequences: a soap's head is a carboxylate, and calcium and magnesium ions bind it into an insoluble scum, while a detergent's head is a sulfonate that does not. That is the whole difference between soap in hard water and in soft, and it is why the transition from soap to detergent is usually dated to the 1950s, when hard water became common in washing machines. The molecules wash either way; the difference is what the water has in it already.

definition: The spreading of particles through a fluid from where they are concentrated to where they are not, driven by their own random motion. It is why a smell crosses a room, and why a gas reaches the far corner of a container without being stirred.
explanation: Diffusion is slower than people expect and faster than they expect in different situations: it takes minutes for a scent to cross a room, and days for a drop of dye to spread through a tank. Both are the same random walk — every molecule moves in all directions, and the net result is a slow spreading from concentrated to dilute. That is why smell crosses a room long before the air in it is mixed by convection, and why stirring speeds things up enormously.

definition: Atoms moving through a solid rather than through a fluid, which happens at a usable rate only when the solid is hot. It is how carbon works into iron in steelmaking and how dopants reach the interior of a semiconductor crystal.
explanation: Diffusion in a solid is the same random walk as in a fluid, but it needs thermal energy to get past the neighbours and so is negligible at room temperature. It is why steelmaking works at all — carbon has to travel into iron while it is red hot — and why a semiconductor is doped by heating rather than by coating, since a dopant has to be inside the crystal to count. The temperature dependence is steep, which is why this is the process behind both.

definition: A line defect in a crystal where atoms sit off the regular lattice. Metals deform by dislocations moving rather than by the whole lattice sliding at once, which is why metals are ductile at all; grain boundaries stop them, which is why smaller grains make stronger metal.
explanation: A dislocation is why metals bend instead of shattering, and its existence was the last piece of the puzzle in explaining ductility. A perfect crystal would have to shear every layer at once to deform, which needs an implausibly large stress; one misaligned line lets the slip start at a much lower stress and spread. Everything practical follows from that: more dislocations means easier deformation, and blocking them with solute atoms or grain boundaries means harder metal.

definition: A reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive one in a compound. Zinc pushing copper out of copper sulphate is the standard example, and the ordering of how reactive each element is is what predicts which way it goes.
explanation: Displacement reactions are ordered, and the ordering is what makes them predictable. A more reactive element will displace a less reactive one from its compound, and the reverse will not happen — which is why iron nails are protected by zinc in galvanising but a zinc nail in iron would be corroded away. The reactivity series is one of the few genuinely predictive things in school chemistry, and it works because the competition is for electrons.

definition: An ionic compound splitting into its ions in water, so that the dissolved form is the separate ions rather than the original crystal. Salts do it almost completely and sugars not at all, which is the difference between an electrolyte and a solute.
explanation: Dissociation is what makes an electrolyte an electrolyte, and the degree is a number worth knowing for each. Salt dissociates essentially completely, so it is a strong electrolyte; acetic acid dissociates a fraction of a per cent, so it is weak. The common confusion is between dissociation and ionisation, which are the same process described for molecular and atomic starting points — and which textbooks use interchangeably.

definition: Separating a liquid mixture by heating it until the more volatile part boils off, then condensing that vapour and collecting it. It gives a purer liquid than evaporation would, because the vapour that leaves is poorer in the less volatile component.
explanation: Distillation works because a liquid's vapour is enriched in the more volatile component, and that is why the distillate is never as pure as the more volatile substance alone. Simple distillation suits mixtures whose boiling points are far apart; where they are close, the first drop off the column is a mixture and the column is what makes it a separation. The energy cost is real, and it is why distillation of seawater for drinking water is expensive compared with treating it.

definition: Adding a controlled trace of one element to another to change its properties, most famously in semiconductors, where adding a few phosphorus atoms to silicon creates the electron carriers that make a chip work.
explanation: Doping is the whole of semiconductor technology and almost nothing else in chemistry, because the requirement is not that the impurity help but that it be present in exactly known amounts. A silicon crystal with a few parts per million of phosphorus has more free electrons, and an aluminium-gallium-arsenic crystal with aluminium in it has more free holes. Both are the same substitution in a lattice, tuned by concentration rather than by chemistry.

definition: Two shared pairs of electrons between two atoms, written as two lines. It makes a molecule stiffer and less freely rotatable than a single bond, and it is what carbon dioxide's straight shape comes from.
explanation: A double bond is one sigma and one pi, and keeping them apart is what explains most of what makes alkenes different from alkanes. The pi bond is weaker and more exposed, which is why it is where addition reactions happen, why cis and trans isomers are possible at all, and why alkenes are far more reactive than the saturated compounds beside them. A double bond to oxygen, as in carbon dioxide, is two sigma bonds and behaves completely differently.

definition: Solid carbon dioxide, held together only by the weak forces between molecules and therefore always −78 °C or colder at atmospheric pressure. It sublimates rather than melts, which is where the name comes from and why it chills rather than wets.
explanation: Dry ice has no liquid phase at atmospheric pressure, which is a genuinely unusual property and not just a trick of temperature. Its triple point is below 1 atm, so heating it at sea level takes it straight to gas. That is why it freezes rather than cools, why it does not wet anything, and why it is used for shipping food that must stay frozen — and why it is a real hazard in an enclosed space, since the gas is asphyxiating.

definition: A synthetic element at number 105, named after Dubna in Russia, where much of the work on the heaviest elements was done. Only a few dozen atoms have ever been made.
explanation: Dubnium is one of a handful of elements named for the place rather than the person, and specifically for the laboratory at Dubna where much of the work on the heaviest elements was done. Only a few dozen atoms of it have ever been assembled, in collisions lasting milliseconds, and its chemistry has not been studied in solution at all.

definition: The temperature below which a metal stops absorbing strain by deforming and starts snapping instead. Mild steel is ductile at room temperature and brittle below about −20 °C, which is why ships are required to pass notch toughness tests in cold weather.
explanation: The transition is a property of the crystal structure and not of the metal, and understanding it explains why ships shatter at low temperature while the same steel in a building is fine. Below the transition the crystal's slip systems stop accommodating strain and a crack runs instead. It is why the rules for mild steel are written into the ship classification societies' codes rather than left to the steelmaker.

definition: The ability of a metal to be drawn into a wire without cracking. It comes from metallic bonding, which lets layers of atoms slide past one another and stay bonded — which is also why the same bonding makes a metal malleable.
explanation: Ductility is the property that makes metals usable as wire, and it comes from the same sliding layers as malleability — the difference is only the direction of the force. It also explains a limit: a metal that has been worked hard has more dislocations than it can accommodate, and past that point it work-hardens and becomes brittle instead. That is why a wire rope that has been overloaded once stays damaged.

definition: A rare earth metal at number 66 added to neodymium magnets to raise the temperature at which they fail. Electric vehicles use more dysprosium per motor than a pair of headphones does.
explanation: Dysprosium is added to neodymium magnets to raise the temperature at which they lose their strength, and that single fact changed how much neodymium a car motor needs. A magnet with no dysprosium works in a phone and not in an engine, so an electric vehicle carries several times more of it than the headphones it replaced. It is one of the heaviest chokepoints in the supply chain for technologies that are otherwise dominated by silicon.

definition: The fizzing that happens when a gas is released from a solution, usually by a reaction between an acid and a carbonate. It is the sound of the CO2 coming out, and the pressure in a bottle of ginger beer comes from the same thing.
explanation: Effervescence is what a reaction sounds like, and it is the carbon dioxide coming out of solution. It is also a useful diagnostic: fizzing with a carbonate identifies both the acid and the carbonate without any equipment, which is why the test has survived unchanged for two centuries. The fizz is only half the observation — a precipitate, a colour change or no change at all is the rest of it.

definition: A synthetic actinide at number 99, identified in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb test in 1952. Producing enough of it to weigh has barely been done since, and it takes a reactor run of months to make a few milligrams.
explanation: Einsteinium is the element with the shortest production window of any that has ever been studied chemically. It was discovered in the debris of a thermonuclear test in 1952, and producing enough of it to weigh took a reactor campaign of months, because its half-life is about fifteen weeks and it decays faster than it can be made. It is the practical end of what neutron bombardment can do, which is why everything heavier is made one atom at a time.

definition: A conductor through which current enters or leaves an electrolyte or a metal. What happens at it is either a reduction, at the cathode, or an oxidation, at the anode — the two are named for where the electrons arrive and leave.
explanation: The two electrode names are defined by the direction of electron flow and not by what the material is, which trips up most people once. The cathode is where electrons arrive and reduction happens; the anode is where they leave and oxidation happens. They are negative and positive only in a cell that produces power, and the reverse in one that consumes it — an electrolytic cell's anode is positive, a galvanic cell's is negative.

definition: Driving a chemical reaction with an electric current, usually to split a compound that will not react otherwise. Aluminium, chlorine and sodium are all obtained this way, and all three are cheaper to make this way than any other.
explanation: Electrolysis is the third way of driving a reaction, after adding heat and using a catalyst, and it is the only one that can force a reaction that is not thermodynamically favourable. That is why aluminium, chlorine and sodium are all made this way: their reactions run backwards spontaneously, so only an outside input will make them go. The cost is exactly that input, which is most of why aluminium is as expensive as it is.

definition: A substance that dissolves into ions and so conducts electricity in solution or when molten. Salts and acids are electrolytes, sugar is not, and that is why a sports drink helps and a sweet one does not.
explanation: An electrolyte is defined by what it does when dissolved rather than by what it is, which is why the class includes acids, alkalis, salts and anything else that produces mobile ions. Water is a very poor electrolyte, and that is a great deal of why pure water conducts almost nothing while tap water conducts enough to be a hazard near a mains supply. Conductivity is also the simplest test for whether a liquid is a solution at all.

definition: A particle with a negative charge, a mass about eighteen hundredths that of a proton, and no measurable size. It orbits in energy levels rather than in orbits, and an atom is mostly empty space for exactly this reason.
explanation: The electron is the particle that chemistry is mostly about, and its charge being negative is a convention — it could have been the other way round and the chemistry would be identical.
