What is not conventional is its mass, at about one eighteen-hundredth that of a proton, which is why an atom is mostly empty space and why a nucleus can be hit with a fast alpha particle without the atom noticing until it is nearly there.

definition: The energy released when a gaseous atom gains an electron. Chlorine's is high enough to be worth measuring, which is why it reacts so readily, and the noble gases' are negative — they give an electron back rather than keeping it.
explanation: Electron affinity and electronegativity are related and routinely confused. Electronegativity is a comparative scale for pulling shared electrons in a bond; electron affinity is a measured energy for gaining an electron as a free gaseous atom. They correlate but do not agree, and the clearest divergence is the noble gases: their electronegativities are usually left undefined because they do not form bonds, and their electron affinities are negative because they give the electron back.

definition: A record of which energy levels and orbitals an atom's electrons occupy, written in the Aufbau notation: [Ar]4s2 3d6 for iron. It explains the shape of the table, the number of columns in a period, and why two elements in the same column behave alike.
explanation: An electron configuration is the shortest statement of why the periodic table has its shape, read in three ways at once. The principal quantum number is the period, the subshell being filled is the block, and the group is the outer shell's occupancy. The irregularities are where the table's symmetry breaks — chromium and copper are the famous ones, and the f-block's apparent interruptions are really the lanthanides and actinides lifted out to keep the table printable.

definition: How strongly an atom pulls shared electrons toward itself in a bond. Fluorine is the most electronegative element and caesium the least, and the spread across the table is the reason bonds are ionic at one end and covalent at the other.
explanation: Electronegativity is a scale rather than a measurement, and that is worth being clear about because it is quoted to two decimal places as though it were exact. It is defined by contrast — Pauling set fluorine at 4.0 and derived the rest from bond energies — so it says how much more one atom pulls than another and nothing on its own. The trend across and down the table is solid; the third decimal place is not.

definition: The energy gained by one electron crossing a potential difference of one volt, about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ joules. It is the natural unit for atomic and nuclear physics, because the electronvolt is defined through the electron rather than through a mechanical standard.
explanation: The electronvolt is the natural unit of atomic and nuclear physics for a reason that is entirely practical: the electronvolt is defined through the electron and through a volt, and in both of those fields the electron and the volt are the things you can measure. It is also why it is the unit for ionisation energies and binding energies on this site rather than the joule — the numbers would run to twenty digits.

definition: Moving charged particles through a gel by applying a field, so that smaller ones travel further and the mixture separates into bands. It is how DNA fragments are compared, and the technique that made the Human Genome Project readable.
explanation: Electrophoresis works because DNA is charged and moves in a field, and the gel is a molecular sieve that separates by size as well as by charge. The result is the ladder everyone recognises: bands at intervals, each one a fragment of a particular length, with a marker lane beside it for scale. It is the technique that turned sequencing from slow and manual into something a machine does, and it is why a genome is a set of fragments before it is a sequence.

definition: A substance whose every atom has the same number of protons, which is the one thing that defines it. It is the largest number of distinct kinds of matter in ordinary use, and no chemical reaction can turn one element into another.
explanation: The definition of an element is a count — the number of protons in the nucleus — and everything else about it follows from that number. Two atoms with the same protons are the same element whatever else differs, which is why isotopes are still that element. And because no chemical reaction changes a nucleus, no reaction can turn one element into another: transmutation needs a particle accelerator or a reactor.

definition: A mixture in which droplets of one liquid are held apart in another that they will not dissolve in — milk, where fat is dispersed in water. It is not a solution, and it separates on its own given time or a little heat.
explanation: An emulsion is not a solution, and the distinction is the practical one: the droplets are large enough to scatter light and large enough to coalesce given time. That is why milk separates if you leave it, and why a skin cream is made by whipping rather than by dissolving. Emulsifiers stop the separation by sitting at the interface and giving the droplets something to hold on to.

definition: A process that takes heat in from its surroundings rather than giving it out. Dissolving ammonium nitrate into water is cold enough to be useful, which is why it is used in instant cold packs.
explanation: Endothermic and exothermic are about heat flow, not about temperature, and the distinction is worth keeping separate from whether a reaction feels hot or cold. A dissolving process can be endothermic and cool, an evaporation is endothermic and cools you, and a reaction can be exothermic and end at a lower temperature than it started at if it did more work than it released. The sign convention is about the system's heat content, not about what your hand feels.

definition: The capacity to do work or to cause change, measured in joules. Chemical reactions involve it as bond energy, as motion of the particles, and as heat.
explanation: Energy comes in forms that convert into one another, and the total is conserved. Chemistry's contribution is the way it is stored in bonds: breaking a bond always costs energy and forming one always releases some, and the difference between those two numbers is a reaction's enthalpy. That is the whole mechanism behind combustion, behind why a reaction runs, and behind why an explosive is a substance that stores a great deal of energy in very unstable bonds.

definition: A quantity of heat content, written as ΔH for a change and measured in kilojoules per mole. A negative ΔH says a reaction releases heat and a positive one says it has to be supplied, which is the difference between exothermic and endothermic.
explanation: Enthalpy is the thermodynamic quantity that survives constant pressure, which is the condition almost every reaction is actually run at. The H itself is not directly measurable and never needs to be; only differences between states matter, and every published enthalpy is a difference. The subscript for standard conditions means one bar and a stated temperature, and because it is usually 25 °C that temperature is worth looking for before comparing two numbers.

definition: The heat a reaction gives out or takes in at constant pressure, written ΔH. A negative value means exothermic and a positive one endothermic, and Hess's law says the total is the same whether the reaction runs in one step or several.
explanation: The sign convention is worth one line's attention, because it is the sort of thing that gets remembered backwards. A negative ΔH means the system gave heat out; a positive one means it took heat in. Bond breaking always costs energy and bond making always releases it, and the net of the two is the reaction's ΔH — which is why breaking a bond in a step releases heat overall if the bonds made are stronger than the ones broken.

definition: A measure of how many ways the energy in a system can be distributed among its particles, written as ΔS for a change. It tends to increase on its own, which is one of the two reasons a reaction may run at all.
explanation: Entropy is often described as disorder and that shorthand does more harm than good, because it is really a count of the ways energy can be distributed among the particles. It tends to increase in an isolated system, and that — not a preference for neatness — is the second half of the answer to why reactions go. The phrase 'entropy always increases' is about a system plus its surroundings, not about the system alone.

definition: A protein that makes a particular reaction go much faster by offering a route with a lower barrier, and which is unchanged by having done it. Enzymes are what make digestion work at body temperature rather than at the several hundred degrees a reaction would otherwise need.
explanation: Enzymes are remarkable for their specificity and unremarkable in principle: they are proteins with a shape that fits one substrate, and they work by holding it so that the barrier is lower. That is why they are sensitive to heat and to pH, since both change the protein's shape. It is also why a reaction that needs no enzyme in a flask with nothing alive in it still needs an enzyme in a cell — the enzyme is providing the route, not the energy.

definition: A state in which a reversible reaction is going forwards and backwards at the same rate, so the proportions stop changing even though nothing has stopped. It is a state of balance rather than of rest, which is the distinction the word dynamic exists to make.
explanation: The word people misuse most is reversible: a reversible reaction does not mean one that undoes itself on request, it means one that can go in either direction. At equilibrium both directions are still happening, at equal rates, and the composition stops changing while nothing has stopped. A closed bottle of a carbonated drink is heading towards equilibrium with a very small amount of dissolved carbon dioxide, and shaking it moves it away from that state.

definition: The ratio of products to reactants once a reversible reaction has settled, at a given temperature. It is fixed for that reaction at that temperature and says how far the reaction goes — not how fast it gets there.
explanation: The equilibrium constant is fixed by the reaction and the temperature and by nothing else — not by how much you started with, not by how much catalyst you added, not by the volume. A large value means the products are favoured and does not mean the reaction is fast. And because the constant depends on temperature, a reaction that is exothermic will have a smaller constant at higher temperature, which is the quantitative version of Le Chatelier's principle.

definition: A rare earth metal at number 68, and the amplifier element in the optical fibres that carry the internet across oceans. Adding it to the glass lets a signal be regenerated every so often rather than degrading to noise.
explanation: Erbium's amplifier ions make long-haul optical fibre possible, and the mechanism is worth understanding because it is a neat trick. A weak signal coming down the fibre excites the erbium ions in the glass, which then emit light of their own at exactly the same wavelength — so the signal comes out stronger without being converted to an electrical signal and back. It is the reason a fibre can run across an ocean without being regenerated at intervals of a few kilometres.

definition: A reaction in which an acid and an alcohol join and split off water, making an ester and often smelling strongly of fruit. It is reversible, so industrial batches push the balance over by removing the water as it forms.
explanation: Esterification is a condensation reaction: an acid and an alcohol join and a molecule of water comes off. That it is reversible is a nuisance industrially and a feature in the laboratory, because it means an ester can be hydrolysed back to its parts. The equilibrium can be pushed towards the ester by removing the water as it forms, and driving off the volatile alcohol works too, which is how the reaction is run at scale.

definition: A rare earth metal at number 63 whose compounds are red and blue phosphors, used in screens and in anti-counterfeiting ink. It is also the element whose sharpness of 4f emission makes it a probe for chemical reactions.
explanation: Europium is the element that made euro banknotes and television screens harder to counterfeit, and in both cases by the same property: it is one of the very few elements whose emission has sharp, atom-like lines rather than a broad band. A broad glow is easy to imitate with an ordinary phosphor; a set of narrow lines at known wavelengths is effectively a fingerprint. That sharpness comes from its 4f shell being shielded from its surroundings.

definition: The lowest temperature at which an alloy is fully liquid, below which it is solid whatever its composition. It is what makes a solder melt sharply at one temperature instead of over a range, and it is why a eutectic alloy can be a liquid at all.
explanation: A eutectic is what makes a solder and a casting alloy work, and it is a minimum rather than a compromise. At the eutectic composition the alloy melts at a temperature lower than either of its components does alone, so a solder melts sharply and quickly instead of going through a mushy range. That is why solders are close to their eutectic and why the melting point of an alloy is not the melting point of its ingredients.

definition: A liquid turning into vapour at its surface, at any temperature, as the fastest molecules escape. It is why a puddle dries on a cool day, and it continues below the boiling point because the molecules are not all equally energetic.
explanation: Evaporation happens at any temperature because the molecules in a liquid are not all equally energetic — some are always at the surface moving fast enough to leave. What evaporates is therefore enriched in the lighter and faster molecules, which is the basis of isotopic separation by distillation and of the smell of a spill spreading further than the spill. Boiling is evaporation with the rate raised until bubbles form throughout rather than only at the surface.

definition: A process that gives heat out to its surroundings. Combustion is the obvious one, and an exothermic reaction is often self-sustaining because the energy it releases is what keeps the next part going.
explanation: Exothermic releases heat, and the release is often what keeps the reaction going: the heat from burning gas is what ignites the gas above it, which is why a fire propagates upward and why it needs a continuous supply of fuel rather than one match's worth. It is also why exothermic reactions run harder as they heat, which is a runaway in a reactor and a mechanism in a flame.

definition: Getting an element out of the ground or out of a compound, and the sequence of processes that concentrate it and reduce it. The energy cost of extraction is why an abundant metal is not always a cheap one.
explanation: Extraction is usually a redox reaction in which a metal is reduced from its ore, and the choice of reducing agent sets the energy cost. Carbon is used because it is cheap, which is why every metal above carbon in the reactivity series is extracted with it; aluminium needs electrolysis because nothing cheap enough will reduce it, which is the same fact as its position in the series. Where an ore is already oxidised it needs only melting and a flux.

definition: The unit of electric charge, about 96,485 coulombs, and the charge carried by one mole of electrons. It is what lets electrolysis be calculated rather than guessed, since a known charge moves a known amount of substance.
explanation: The faraday ties charge to amount of substance, which is what makes electrolysis calculable rather than empirical. One faraday of charge deposits one mole of a singly charged ion, so the mass deposited is proportional to the charge passed and to the ion's molar mass — and Faraday's laws, both of them, follow from that single fact. The unit matters practically: a chemist running an electrolysis thinks in faradays per mole.

definition: Failure of a material under repeated loading well below its strength, and the reason bridges, aircraft and bicycles are designed to cycle their loads. It happens in metals and polymers alike, and no static test reveals it.
explanation: Fatigue is the failure that static testing cannot find, and it is why bridges, aircraft and bicycle frames are designed to cycle their loads rather than merely to hold a maximum. A material under cyclic load fails at a stress well below its breaking strength, and it fails without warning and often well before any visible change. Testing is therefore destructive and statistical, and a design's life is quoted as a number of cycles at a given amplitude.

definition: A synthetic actinide at number 100, and the heaviest element that can be made by neutron bombardment rather than by smashing nuclei together. Everything beyond it has to be made in a particle accelerator, which is why the two techniques matter.
explanation: Fermium is the heaviest element that can be made by neutron bombardment rather than by smashing nuclei together, and that boundary matters more than the element does. Neutron capture is slow and produces several atoms at once; heavy-ion collisions produce one wanted atom in a spray of a hundred unwanted ones. Everything past fermium — a quarter of the periodic table's heaviest end — can only be made the slow way, or not at all in useful quantity.

definition: Separating an insoluble solid from a liquid by passing the mixture through something porous that the liquid gets through and the solid does not. It separates by size, so it will not separate two dissolved substances from one another.
explanation: Filtration separates by particle size and does nothing at all to separate two things that are genuinely dissolved, which is why filtering seawater does not make it drinkable. It also fails on particles too small for the pores, which is why a fine precipitate may pass through filter paper and be described as passing through the filter — that phrase almost always means the precipitate was too fine, not that the paper is faulty.

definition: Nuclear fission: a heavy nucleus splitting into two lighter nuclei, releasing neutrons and energy. The neutrons it throws off can split further nuclei, which is what turns one event into a chain reaction.
explanation: Fission is worth separating from fusion as the release of energy from a change in binding energy per nucleon, which is the whole of both. Heavy nuclei have more binding energy per nucleon than medium ones, so splitting them releases some; light ones have more than the heaviest, so fusing them releases some too. Both releases come from the same iron-group maximum, and that is why the curve of binding energy per nucleon rather than total mass is the diagram to look at.

definition: Heating a sample and looking at the colour its flame turns, which identifies certain metals: sodium gives yellow, potassium lilac, copper green. It is the quickest way to tell the alkali metals apart, since all of them burn.
explanation: The flame test is the oldest analytical technique that still works and needs no instrument beyond a burner. Each metal has a characteristic emission because its electrons have characteristic energy gaps, and the sodium yellow is so strong that a trace of it masks whatever else is in the sample — which is why potassium samples are viewed through cobalt glass. It identifies alkali and alkaline earth metals and little else.

definition: A synthetic element at number 114, named after the Flerov Laboratory in Dubna. It sits below lead in group 14, and experiments have suggested its chemistry departs sharply from the element above it — the beginning of an island of stability whose edge this is.
explanation: Flerovium is where the periodic table's predictions stop being useful. It sits below lead in group 14 and every simple extrapolation says it should behave like lead and be heavier, denser and still metallic; relativistic calculations suggest it may instead be gaseous or even a solid at room temperature, with chemical properties resembling a noble gas. It is one of the experimental cases for the 'island of stability' whose edge it sits on.

definition: A pale yellow halogen, element 9, the most electronegative element there is and the most reactive of all the non-metals. Its compounds are used in non-stick coatings and in the refrigerant that replaced CFC gases, and in toothpaste in the form of fluoride.
explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative element there is and it shows. It is the only element that reacts with every other one, including the noble gases and the metals that resist everything else, and it reacts violently: it will set asbestos alight and it cannot be handled in glass at all, because it attacks the glass. The Teflon and the non-stick coating are its compounds, and tooth decay is a battle against one of them.

definition: A substance added to a melt to lower the melting point of the impurities or to combine with them so that they float off. Its job is to gather what you do not want into something you can discard, rather than to filter anything.
explanation: A flux's job is not to melt the metal but to deal with what is in it. It combines with the impurities to form something with a low melting point, and that slag floats off the denser metal — so the process is a chemical one, not a straining. Borax is a domestic flux for soldering, and limestone is the flux that makes a blast furnace work, carrying the silica out of the ore as slag.

definition: The smallest whole number of ions in a compound that comes back to the compound's neutral charge. It is written as a formula rather than as a molecule because ionic solids have no discrete molecules — sodium chloride is a lattice, not a pair of particles.
explanation: The formula unit exists because ionic solids do not have molecules. Sodium chloride is a lattice extending as far as the crystal goes; there is no discrete pair of sodium and chloride to count, so Avogadro's number of sodium ions pairs with Avogadro's number of chloride ions and the smallest whole formula that comes back to neutral is NaCl. Molecular compounds do have molecules, and use the term molecular mass instead.

definition: Distilling a liquid mixture through a column that lets the more volatile component rise and condense while the other runs back down, repeating it many times. It separates substances whose boiling points are close, which simple distillation cannot manage.
explanation: A fractionating column gives the separation its selectivity by making it happen many times over. Vapour rises through packing, condenses, falls back, re-evaporates; the more volatile component accumulates towards the top and the less volatile runs back down. That repeated equilibrium is what lets it separate liquids whose boiling points differ by only a few degrees, which simple distillation cannot do at all.

definition: The least stable of the first hundred elements, at number 87, with a half-life of under half an hour. It is the last member of the alkali metals and the rarest naturally occurring element, present in the crust only a few grams at a time.
explanation: Francium is the rarest naturally occurring element and the least stable of the first hundred, with a half-life under half an hour. At any moment there is perhaps thirty grams of it in the entire earth's crust, and it is produced continuously in minute quantities by the decay of actinium. It is the last of the alkali metals and nothing useful has ever been made from it, which is a legitimate reason it is on this list and a common source of questions.

definition: An atom or molecule with an unpaired electron, which makes it very reactive and usually short-lived. They come apart under light or heat, and they are what starts the chain reaction in burning and the damage done by radiation.
explanation: A free radical is what is left when a bond breaks evenly, one electron to each fragment, and the two unpaired electrons are what makes it so reactive. Radicals are the mechanism of nearly every chain reaction: a radical is generated, it reacts to make two more, and the chain continues. That is combustion, it is the damage done by radiation on tissue, and it is why antioxidants are added to food that must keep.

definition: Joining two light nuclei into a heavier one, releasing enormous energy because the product is more tightly bound than the parts. It is the reaction that powers the sun and that thermonuclear reactors are trying to reproduce under control.
explanation: Fusion is the reaction that makes the light from the sun and it requires temperatures of about a hundred million degrees to start, which is why it has not been practical on Earth for the reasons it is obvious. It also produces no long-lived waste and needs a great deal of fuel, since a fusion reaction involves nuclei far lighter than fission's — deuterium and tritium, weighing about five atomic mass units between them.

definition: A rare earth metal at number 64 that is strongly paramagnetic, so its compounds are used as a contrast agent in MRI scans. It has the highest neutron capture cross-section of any element, which is why it is used in nuclear reactor control rods.
explanation: Gadolinium has two unrelated extremes and is used for both. As a free ion it has more unpaired electrons than any other element, which makes it strongly paramagnetic and useful as an MRI contrast agent; as a metal it has the highest neutron absorption of any element, which makes it a control rod material. Few elements have two such different applications resting on the same unpaired-electron configuration.

definition: The main lead ore, a sulfide of lead, recognisable by its metallic lustre and its cubic crystals. It was called galena from the Latin for lead ore, and it is the commonest of the sulfide ores.
explanation: Galena is the main lead ore and one of the few minerals you can recognise on sight: bright metallic cubes with a perfect cleavage. It was the first semiconductor used in a device, a crystal detector in a radio, and lead's value as a mineral is very largely why Roman silver and lead production was so large. It is also the principal ore of silver in many deposits, because silver frequently substitutes for lead in galena.

definition: A metal at number 31 that melts at 29.8 °C, so a warm room turns it to liquid, and it has one of the widest liquid ranges of any element. Its oxide gallium arsenide is what LEDs were made from for decades.
explanation: Gallium's most famous property is a party trick: it melts at just under 30 °C, so a spoon made of it melts in a warm hand, and a sealed gallium sample can be carried in a pocket through winter and used in summer. Its serious use is as a dopant in gallium arsenide, and it is the metal that makes low-power LEDs possible, because the direct band gap means the light comes out instead of the energy becoming heat.

definition: Coating steel with zinc so that the zinc corrodes in its place and the steel does not. The protection is sacrificial rather than a barrier, which is why a scratched galvanised bucket still does not rust at the scratch.
explanation: Galvanising is the clearest case on this site of sacrificial protection, and the distinction from painting is the whole point. A paint film is a barrier, so the moment it is scratched the exposed steel rusts from the hole outward. Zinc is more reactive, so it corrodes in preference, and the scratch is protected for as long as the zinc around it lasts. The protection therefore spreads outwards from the damage rather than concentrating at it.

definition: Electromagnetic radiation given off by an excited nucleus, which is the most penetrating of the three common emissions and the least ionising. It needs lead rather than paper to stop, and it is what makes radiotherapy possible and nuclear waste dangerous long after it stops being hot.
explanation: Gamma radiation is the most penetrating and the least ionising of the three common emissions, and that combination is why it dominates both medicine and waste disposal. It passes through the body and damages cells well beyond where it deposits energy, which is what makes a gamma source dangerous to be near and what makes it useful for imaging a tumour from outside. In waste it is the reason a spent fuel assembly needs cooling and shielding for years before it is safe to handle.

definition: A state in which particles are far apart and move freely, so that a gas fills its container and has no shape of its own. Its particles are also far enough apart to be treated as individuals.
explanation: The defining property of a gas is distance: the particles are separated by many times their own size, which is why the volume of a gas changes readily with pressure and why the ideal gas law works as well as it does. It is also why a gas can be compressed — there is nearly empty space between the particles to close up — and why all gases mix with each other perfectly rather than sitting in layers.

definition: A metalloid at number 32, hard and brittle, used in infrared optics and in the semiconductor devices that were built before silicon proved cheaper. It was the substance the first transistors were made from.
explanation: Germanium is what silicon replaced, and the history is a lesson in how a materials decision becomes an industry. Its crystals were the basis of the first transistors, in 1947, and it worked better than silicon because the technology to grow a pure silicon crystal did not yet exist. Silicon caught up in the 1960s and germanium became a scarce, expensive substitute, and it is still indispensable where its properties differ usefully.

definition: A substance in which covalent bonds run from atom to atom in an unbroken network, so the whole crystal is effectively one molecule. Diamond, graphite and silicon are the three that matter, and their very different properties come from how the networks are arranged.
explanation: A giant covalent structure is what it sounds like: bonds running from atom to atom without end, so that the whole crystal is one macromolecule. There are very few of them — diamond, graphite, silicon, silicon carbide, boron nitride — and they are defined by having no intermolecular forces at all, which is why their melting points are so high and why, if they are brittle, they are brittle. The materials revolution of the last fifty years is largely the discovery of more of them.

definition: The metal at number 79, the most ductile and the least reactive of all, so it is found native rather than as a compound. Its yellow colour comes from relativistic effects in its electrons, which no other element's physics reproduces quite so well.
explanation: Gold is the least reactive element and the most ductile, and those two facts explain its entire history. It occurs native rather than as a compound, it never corrodes, it does not tarnish and it does not rust, so everything made of it that survives a thousand years survives intact. And a single gram can be beaten into a sheet a square metre across without tearing, which is how the earliest gold leaf was made.

definition: The surface between two differently oriented crystals in a polycrystalline metal. More boundaries means more grains means a finer crystal, and finer crystals are harder, because the boundaries are obstacles to dislocations moving.
explanation: Grain boundaries are the reason grain size is quoted as a material property. More boundaries means smaller grains, and each boundary is an obstacle to a dislocation moving, so more of them means more effort to deform the metal — which is why fine-grained steel is stronger. It also explains why a metal recrystallised by annealing is softer than the same metal worked cold: heating lets the grains grow, and there is less boundary left in the way.

definition: One thousandth of a kilogram, and the unit the periodic table uses for atomic weights. The masses in the table are averages over an element's isotopes and are therefore not the mass of any single atom.
explanation: The gram is the unit the periodic table uses, and there is a reason it is not the mole or the kilogram. Atomic weights were the first thing chemists standardised, because comparing masses was how the periodic law was found in the first place. They are also ratios, which is why they carry no unit at all — 'the atomic weight of iron is 55.845' is a statement about how iron compares, not about how much it weighs.

definition: The grey form of carbon in which each atom bonds to three others in flat sheets, and those sheets slide over each other. That is what makes it soft enough to write with and slippery enough to be a lubricant, and it conducts because it has electrons to move.
explanation: Graphite is the proof that a single element can be two materials. In diamond each carbon bonds to four neighbours in a rigid tetrahedral network; in graphite each bonds to three in flat hexagonal sheets, with the fourth electron delocalised across the sheet. Those sheets slide over each other, which is what makes graphite soft and slippery, and the same delocalised electrons make it conduct — the one element that does both, and the only solid that is both a lubricant and an electrical conductor.

definition: The SI unit of absorbed dose, one joule of radiation energy per kilogram of tissue. It measures what has been delivered; the sievert weights that dose by how much harm each kind of radiation does.
explanation: The gray is the absorbed dose and the sievert is the biologically effective one, and the difference between them is the whole reason both exist. A gray measures joules per kilogram; a sievert multiplies by a factor for the radiation's type, because neutrons do more damage per gray than X-rays do. That is why the same absorbed dose in a neutron therapy is quoted in a much smaller number than in an X-ray therapy of the same intent.

definition: The design of chemical processes to use less energy, produce less waste and safer products, rather than the cleaning up of a process that already wastes. Its first principle is that prevention is better than treatment, and atom economy is how the waste is measured.
explanation: Green chemistry is a set of principles about designing a process rather than about cleaning one up, and its sharpest idea is that prevention beats treatment — a reaction that makes no waste needs no treatment. The other principle that changed practice is that solvents count: using a solvent that has to be recovered and distilled is often the largest cost and the largest hazard in a process, so removing the solvent is a bigger win than making the product greener.

definition: The lowest-energy arrangement of a system, which is where an unexcited atom sits with its electrons in the orbitals of lowest energy. Every other arrangement is an excited state and is unstable.
explanation: A ground state is a minimum rather than just a low energy: energy can only be added to take a system out of it, and it will return. That is the whole mechanism of emission — an electron drops from a higher level into the ground state and gives up the difference as a photon. It is also why a ground-state atom cannot absorb a photon at all, since there is nowhere lower for an electron to fall from.

definition: A vertical column of the periodic table, holding elements with the same number of electrons in their outermost shell. That shared outer shell is why the group behaves alike, and why the group number predicts an element's chemistry as well as its atomic number does.
explanation: Group 1 elements have one outer electron, group 17 have seven, and everything else on the table follows from that. It is why the halogens form salts so readily — one more electron and they are done — why the alkali metals are uniformly violent, and why elements in a column behave alike despite having very different masses. The transition metals break the pattern, sharing their outer electrons with a partially filled d shell, and they are the reason group 3 to 12 does not behave as neatly as the rest.

definition: The industrial reaction of nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia, at high pressure and with an iron catalyst. It is run at about 200 atmospheres because equilibrium shifts towards the ammonia, and it feeds the nitrogen for roughly half the world's food.
explanation: The Haber process is the industrial process that made the twentieth century's food supply possible, and it is a good illustration of how much a reaction's conditions are a design decision. Nitrogen and hydrogen will not react appreciably at all without a catalyst and a great deal of pressure, and the process runs at about 200 atmospheres partly because pushing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia and partly because the volume of gas involved makes the economics work. The ammonia then feeds the nitrogen for roughly half the food humanity eats.

definition: The main iron ore, an oxide of iron whose red colour gives both the element's name and the colour of rust. Most of the world's iron is reduced from it in a blast furnace, and hematite itself is used as a pigment.
explanation: Haematite is the most important iron ore and also the source of red pigment going back to antiquity, because its colour is the colour of rust. The main impurity in it is silica, and removing silica is what a blast furnace's slag exists for. It is also the mineral that gives the red flush in some soils and the red bands in banded iron formations, which are the evidence for the oxygenation of the atmosphere.

definition: A metal at number 72 with an atomic radius almost identical to zirconium's, so it is always found with it and only separated from it by careful chemistry. It absorbs neutrons greedily, so it makes control rods for reactors.
explanation: Hafnium is the most annoying element on the table chemically, because it is chemically almost identical to zirconium and has an atomic radius within a few femtometres of it. That makes separating the two very difficult, and it means hafnium is found only in zirconium ores and treated as a nuisance impurity. Its usefulness is the opposite: it absorbs neutrons greedily while staying corrosion-resistant, which is exactly what a submarine's hull wants.

definition: The German chemist who in 1938 discovered nuclear fission by bombarding uranium with neutrons, in work he did not at first understand. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained what it meant; Hahn received the Nobel Prize alone, which she disputed for the rest of her life.
explanation: Hahn's discovery of fission is the clearest case in the history of science of a right result arrived at by a wrong route, and the episode is instructive because of what happened next. He bombarded uranium with neutrons, saw the products he expected, and wrote a paper describing them without recognising what had occurred. Meitner and Frisch, working in Sweden and in exile, read the paper and worked out that the nucleus had split. Hahn received the Nobel Prize alone; Meitner received none, and the explanation was with her for the rest of her life.

definition: The time it takes for half the atoms in a radioactive sample to decay. It is unaffected by pressure, temperature or chemical form, which is what makes it useful for dating rock rather than merely alarming.
explanation: Half-life is a measure of a population and not of an atom, which is the single most important thing to understand about it. An individual atom does not decay slowly or quickly; it either decays or it does not, and there is no way to predict which. What is predictable is the fraction of a large number that decays in a given time, which is why a hundred atoms and a hundred million both halve in the same interval and why a single atom's behaviour is irrelevant to a sample.

definition: Any of the six elements in group 17: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine and tennessine. They all need one more electron to fill their outer shell, which makes them the most reactive non-metals and the reason they form salts so readily.
explanation: The halogens are the most reactive non-metals because each is one electron short of a full outer shell, and that single fact governs their chemistry. It is why they form salts so readily, why they are all diatomic, why fluorine is more reactive than iodine despite iodine's larger size and stronger dispersion forces, and why they are found in seawater rather than in rocks — being reactive, they do not survive near anything else to react with.

definition: Water carrying dissolved calcium and magnesium, which it picks up as it passes over limestone. The minerals form scum with soap and scale in kettles and boilers, which is why hard water is softened before use in industry.
explanation: Hard water's cost is not the minerals but what they do to soap. Calcium and magnesium ions bind the carboxylate head of a soap molecule into an insoluble scum, so more soap is needed and the scum has to be scrubbed off, and the scale that builds up inside kettles and boilers is the same problem in solid form. Softening by ion exchange swaps the calcium and magnesium for sodium, which forms no scum, and costs almost nothing in detergent.

definition: How resistant a material is to scratching, abrasion or indentation. In minerals it is measured on the Mohs scale, an ordinal scale where diamond is ten and talc is one — a number that says which scratches which, not by how much.
explanation: Mohs hardness is an ordinal scale, which means diamond being ten does not mean it is ten times as hard as talc — the ratios are nothing like that. It says only which mineral scratches which, and the more useful modern measure, Vickers hardness, is a real load over a real indentation. The practical split is that metals are hard by deforming and ceramics are hard because they cannot deform at all, and only the first can be toughened without breaking.

definition: A synthetic element at number 108, and the heaviest element whose chemistry has actually been measured in solution, showing it to behave like osmium rather than like the gas the table predicts. It is named for the German state of Hesse.
explanation: Hassium is the heaviest element whose chemistry has been studied in solution, and the answer it gave was not the expected one. It sits in group 8 below iron, ruthenium and osmium, and experiments suggest it behaves more like osmium than like the gas that sits above it in its own period. That is one of the clearest experimental signs that the periodic table's predictions are beginning to fail at the top, and it is being found element by element rather than argued about.

definition: Energy transferred because of a temperature difference, measured in joules. It is a process rather than a property: a substance has internal energy, and heat is what moves when there is a difference.
explanation: Heat is energy in transit, which is why a temperature can be measured directly and a heat cannot be contained — an object at a temperature can transfer it but cannot be said to hold a quantity of it. The confusion with temperature is worth avoiding: a bath of warm water can release more heat than a small cup of hot water while being at a lower temperature, because it holds more of it.

definition: The energy needed to melt a unit mass of a substance without changing its temperature. It is a property of the substance, so the same amount of heat melts ice and melts lead by very different amounts.
explanation: Heat of fusion is the reason a fever feels worse at night, and it is a bigger number than intuition suggests: melting ice at 0 °C takes 334 kJ per kilogram, and evaporating that same water at 100 °C takes over 2,260. That is why sweating cools a body and why it works so well — the evaporating water takes the heat away with it, and the salt in sweat is there to make the evaporating easier.

definition: The physicist who wrote the uncertainty principle, that a particle's position and momentum cannot both be known exactly, and the first formulation of quantum mechanics in mechanics. It is also why the word orbit was eventually abandoned for orbital.
explanation: The uncertainty principle is usually misreported as 'you cannot know both at once', which is imprecise in a way that matters. It says the product of the uncertainties in a pair of conjugate quantities cannot go below a value set by ħ, so the uncertainty can be made small for position or for momentum but not both, and the sharper you define one the wider the other becomes. It is also why the word orbit was abandoned: no trajectory exists to be uncertain about.

definition: The noble gas at number 2, and the first element ever found in the Sun rather than on Earth. It is the only element named after a celestial body, it will not react with anything, and it is the reason a balloon lifts and a diver's mixture does not cause the bends.
explanation: Helium is the element with the most unusual origin story of the first hundred: it was found in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, twenty-seven years before anyone found it on Earth, and the name means 'of the sun'. On Earth it comes almost entirely from the alpha decay of uranium underground and is accumulating faster than the atmosphere is losing it. Its two liquid phases below about 2 K made it the liquid used in the early large Hadron Collider, and it is now found in MRI machines as a cryogen and in balloons as the only thing lighter than air.

definition: The SI unit of frequency, one cycle a second, abbreviated Hz. It is named after Heinrich Hertz, who demonstrated in 1887 that light is an electromagnetic wave rather than a particle of a special sort.
explanation: Hertz is one cycle a second, and its use is broader than acoustics even though the unit is named for radio. The frequency of a photon is related to its energy by a single constant, which is why light frequency is quoted as terahertz and energy as electronvolts and both describe the same photon. Heinrich Hertz demonstrated in 1887 that light is an electromagnetic wave, settling the question his contemporaries were arguing about in his favour.

definition: The rule that the enthalpy change of a reaction is fixed, and is the sum of the changes of whatever steps it is written as. It is how the enthalpy of a reaction nobody can run directly is calculated, by running the steps instead.
explanation: Hess's law is the reason reaction enthalpies can be known at all. A reaction that cannot be run directly — because it happens at 2,000 °C, or requires a hundred atmospheres, or does not happen at all without a catalyst — can still be calculated, by running steps that do work and adding their enthalpies. Every bond enthalpy table on this site is used that way, and the whole discipline of thermochemistry rests on it being exact.

definition: A rare earth metal at number 67 with the highest magnetic strength of any element, which is why it is used in the pole of a surgical laser. It also gives borosilicate glass a golden colour.
explanation: Holmium has the highest magnetic strength of any element and the magnetic moment of an atom or a material is used to say how much. Its practical use is a surgical laser: the glass containing it is pumped so that a particular wavelength is emitted, and that light is absorbed preferentially by tissue containing water and by the tissue's own particular concentration of water, which is what makes the cut precise. It is also what gives borosilicate glass a golden colour, which is why some glassware looks as it does.

definition: The rule that electrons filling degenerate orbitals spread out singly with parallel spins before any of them pairs up. It is why the d block is filled five orbitals at a time and why nitrogen's three unpaired electrons give it its magnetic character.
explanation: Hund's rule is why nitrogen has three unpaired electrons and therefore a magnetic moment, while fluorine has one. Electrons in degenerate orbitals spread out with parallel spins before any of them pairs, because pairing them costs repulsion energy and the exchange energy gained by spreading out is smaller but free. It also explains why the d block fills five orbitals at a time, and therefore why that block is ten columns wide rather than five.

definition: A substance in which water molecules are chemically joined rather than merely mixed in — copper sulfate has one bound in its crystal. The water can be driven off by heating, and the word describes a real bond rather than wetness.
explanation: A hydrate's water is chemically bound rather than merely mixed in, which is what distinguishes it from a wet solid and what makes it a compound with a fixed formula. The water can be driven off by gentle heating and is usually recoverable, which is how copper sulfate goes from blue to white and why it can be used to detect water. The colour change is the practical part: anhydrous copper sulfate is a good enough test for water in an unknown liquid.

definition: A compound of hydrogen with something less electronegative than itself. Saline hydrides react violently with water to release hydrogen, which is why they are kept away from moisture.
explanation: Saline hydrides react so violently with water that they must be stored under oil, and the reaction is simply the hydride taking a proton from water to release hydrogen. That is the reason they are dangerous and also the reason they are useful: a hydride is a compact source of hydrogen and a strong reducing agent. The naming distinguishes them from hydrates on purpose, and the two words sound more alike than they are.

definition: A compound of nothing but carbon and hydrogen. The whole family runs from methane up through the long chains that make petrol and oil, and its members are unreactive enough to be stored and are burned for heat.
explanation: Hydrocarbons are unreactive enough to store and burn, which is why almost all the fuel in the world is one. Their variety comes from three architectures — chains, rings and, with double and triple bonds, branching — and from chain length, which is what a refinery sorts them by. They are also largely responsible for the ozone problem, because the C–H bonds are tough enough that combustion can proceed at temperatures where NOx is generated as well.

definition: The lightest element, number 1, and the most abundant in the universe though not in the earth's crust. It is a gas, it burns to make water, and fuel cells consume it to make electricity with nothing but water as the waste.
explanation: Hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe and a fairly minor one in the earth's crust, because it is so reactive it is nearly always bound into water or organic matter. Its three isotopes are the exception worth knowing: protium, deuterium and tritium, with tritium being radioactive and being what most fusion fuel is actually made of. Free hydrogen is also the hardest gas to store, because it is the smallest and leaks through almost everything.

definition: The weakening and cracking of a metal caused by hydrogen atoms getting into it, which can happen during pickling or plating. It is the reason some high-strength steels and titanium alloys cannot be electroplated.
explanation: Hydrogen embrittlement is the reason some high-strength steels and titanium alloys cannot be electroplated, and it is one of the few places where a process step destroys a part invisibly. Hydrogen atoms get into a metal during pickling, plating or welding and migrate to stressed regions, where they lower the energy needed to open a crack. The failure appears later, under load, with no surface sign that anything went wrong during manufacture.

definition: A reaction in which water breaks a bond in another substance. It is how soap works, how esters are broken back down, and how the body's digestion starts with starch — all of them reactions with water rather than with acid or heat.
explanation: Hydrolysis is a reaction with water rather than with acid or heat, and it is how a great deal of chemistry actually happens — digestion is its first step, soap works by it, and an ester goes back to its acid and alcohol by it. It is also how many minerals weather, which is the slow chemistry behind soil formation and the release of phosphate from rock. Where it is rapid it is usually enzyme-catalysed, since water alone is a feeble reagent.

definition: A polyatomic ion made of an oxygen and a hydrogen, written OH−, and the ion the alkalis dissolve to. Its concentration in solution is what the pH scale actually measures.
explanation: The hydroxide ion is what the pH scale measures, which is worth stating plainly: pH is a logarithmic measure of hydrogen ion concentration, and the hydroxide concentration follows from it by the water dissociation constant. So an alkali solution is not 'negative hydrogen ions' but a real ion. Its concentration is also what makes alkalis corrosive — they react with fats and proteins, which is why a caustic soda spill and a strong acid spill both burn.

definition: A hypothetical gas obeying the simple pressure–volume–temperature law exactly, with no forces between its particles and no volume of their own. Real gases approximate it well at high temperature and low pressure, which is most of the time.
explanation: The ideal gas is a useful fiction and it is worth knowing exactly which assumption is doing the work. The molecules are assumed to have no volume and no forces between them, so they hit the walls hard and follow the simple law; real gases approximate it well at high temperature and low pressure, and badly when either condition fails. Those failures are not noise — the condensation of a real gas is a consequence of the attractions the ideal gas denies.

definition: A soft metal at number 49, so soft it can be scratched with a fingernail, and the element in the indium tin oxide coating that makes touchscreens work. It is also used as a dopant in the semiconductor layers of solar cells.
explanation: Indium is soft enough to mark paper and is used to make touchscreens work: indium tin oxide is a coating that is transparent and conducts at once, which almost nothing else does. It is also the dopant that makes thin-film solar cells work, absorbing more light than plain silicon. The uncomfortable part is that indium is a by-product of zinc refining, so its availability is tied to how much zinc the world happens to want.

definition: Another name for the noble gases, from their reluctance to react with anything. Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon all have a full outer shell, and none of them needs to gain an electron from anywhere.
explanation: Inert gas is another name for the noble gases, from their reluctance to react with anything. The name is doing less work than it used to: xenon, krypton and radon all form compounds, and xenon chemistry is substantial. What is true is that they do not react spontaneously and cheaply, so they are inert in the practical sense — a gas that will not react under the conditions available is inert, whatever else it can be made to do.

definition: A dark solid at number 53 that sublimes to a violet vapour on warming, which is how it is recognised. It is essential to the thyroid, and the sea's richest source is seaweed.
explanation: Iodine is one of the few elements that sublimes visibly: warm crystals go straight to a violet vapour with no liquid phase involved, and the vapour is what you see on heating it. The thyroid gland takes up iodide and makes two hormones that regulate metabolism, which is why iodine deficiency causes goitre and why table salt is iodised in much of the world. Seaweed concentrates it enormously, which is why kelp is a traditional source and also why some seaweed exceeds safe limits.

definition: An atom or molecule carrying a net electric charge because it has gained or lost electrons. Losing them makes it a cation and gaining them makes it an anion, and in solution it is the ion rather than the substance that does the chemistry.
explanation: Ions are why a great deal of chemistry happens only in water or when molten. In a solid ionic lattice the ions are locked in place and cannot move, so the substance conducts nothing; dissolved or melted, they are free to carry charge, which is the difference between salt as a solid and salt as a conductor. That is also why electrolysis works — the ions have to be mobile to be driven anywhere.

definition: A bond in which electrons move from one atom to another and the resulting opposite charges hold each other together. It is what holds salts like sodium chloride together, and it works best when the two atoms differ a lot in electronegativity.
explanation: An ionic bond is really an arrangement rather than a link: a lattice in which every cation is surrounded by anions and vice versa. There is no discrete pair, which is why the term formula unit exists, and the attraction is not between specific atoms but between opposite charges throughout the crystal. That difference explains why ionic compounds conduct when molten or dissolved but not when solid — the ions are fixed in place until something lets them move.

definition: About half the distance between the nuclei of two touching ions of opposite charge. An anion is always bigger than the atom it came from, because it has gained an electron, and a cation is always smaller for the same reason reversed.
explanation: Ionic radii are quoted for ions that do not exist except in a crystal, and the convention is half the closest distance between two touching opposite ions, which means the number depends on which compound it came from. The trends are reliable even so: an anion is larger than its parent atom and a cation is smaller, because gaining an electron expands the electron cloud while losing one contracts it, and the charge is doing the work.

definition: The energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom. It rises across a period and falls down a group, and it is high enough in the noble gases to explain why they do not react with anything.
explanation: The first ionisation energy of the elements is the shape of the table, if you plot it. It rises across a period because the same shell is filling and holding its electrons more tightly, and it drops down a group because an outer electron is further from the nucleus and better shielded. The peaks are the noble gases and the dips are the group 1 metals, and the discontinuities — beryllium above boron, nitrogen above oxygen — are where an electron is pairing for the first time.

definition: The most corrosion-resistant metal at number 77, used in the crucibles that grow single crystals of silicon and in spark plug electrodes. The thin iridium layer marking the end of the Cretaceous is why we know the impact happened at all.
explanation: Iridium is the most corrosion-resistant metal there is, which is why it is in the crucibles that grow single crystals of silicon and in the electrodes of spark plugs that have to survive thousands of hours. Its other claim to fame is geological: the iridium layer at the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary is unusually concentrated worldwide, and that is the strongest single piece of evidence that something arrived from outside and finished the dinosaurs.

definition: The most-used metal on Earth, the main ingredient of the planet's core, and the atom that carries oxygen in your blood. It loses rust readily and gains it back, and steel — iron with a little carbon — is the backbone of buildings, bridges and ships.
explanation: Iron is the element that both built and ruined civilisations, and the reason is a thermodynamic loop that carbon closes: smelting iron needs coke, which needs wood, and the land grows back while people are making charcoal from it. Steelmaking also gives off slag, so the waste is enormous — the reason iron became cheap in the first place is the same reason it became a pollutant. Its alloy with carbon is the single most useful substance anyone has produced.

definition: Two nuclides with the same mass number but different atomic numbers. Only such pairs can occur in a nuclear chain as one decays into the other without emitting a particle.
explanation: An isobar sits at the top of the beta-decay series, because a beta decay changes the atomic number and not the mass number, so it moves a nucleus along a line of constant mass. That is what makes a decay chain traceable: each beta step is a move sideways at the same mass, and the alpha steps between them are the ones that lose four. Chains like uranium-238's are followed by walking this ladder rather than by identifying each daughter separately.

definition: Two molecules with the same formula and the same connections in different arrangements. They have different properties, and sometimes different colours and different smells.
explanation: Isomers are the reason a structural formula matters and the reason a molecular formula alone is never enough to predict anything. The two isomers of butane differ only in the branching of the same four carbons, yet one is a gas and one is a liquid. Ethanol and dimethyl ether have the same formula and completely different structures, which is why one is a drink and one is not.

definition: Describing solutions with the same osmotic pressure, so water does not move between them across a membrane. It is what makes intravenous fluid a saline solution and not plain water, which would swell red blood cells.
explanation: Isotonic solutions have the same osmotic pressure, which means water has no reason to move between them across a membrane — and that is the whole basis of intravenous therapy. Plain water is hypotonic relative to body fluids, so it would move into red blood cells and swell them; a saline solution is isotonic, so nothing moves. The word describes a solution rather than a substance and is less commonly met than hypotonic and hypertonic, which describe the same relationship from the other side.

definition: One of two or more atoms of the same element differing only in neutron count. Their masses differ while their chemistry does not, because the electron arrangement that governs chemistry is the same for all of them.
explanation: Isotopes share an atomic number and differ in neutron count, which means their chemistry is identical and their masses are not — and almost everything interesting about isotopes follows from that one sentence. Carbon-14 and carbon-12 behave the same chemically and are separated by mass alone; uranium-235 and uranium-238 are chemically almost identical and the difference between them decides whether a reactor works. Because the electrons never see the neutrons, an isotope's reactions need no adjustment.

definition: The French physicists who in 1934 showed that a stable nucleus could be made radioactive by bombardment, which opened the whole field of artificial radioactivity and produced the radioisotope tracers that medicine is built on.
explanation: Artificial radioactivity opened the field of tracer chemistry, which is a larger contribution than it first appears. If you can put a few labelled atoms into a system and follow them, you can find out where something goes rather than only how much of it ends up in each place, and that is how the Calvin cycle mapped carbon fixation and how a drug can be followed through a body. It also created a hazard that did not exist before 1934 and was understood too slowly.

definition: The SI unit of energy or work, one newton-metre. Heat, work and electrical energy are all measured in it, which is why a calorie is 4.18 of them and why the SI prefixes matter for the very small and very large quantities chemistry deals in.
explanation: The joule ties the three things a chemist measures together. Heat is in joules, work is in joules, and an electrical energy delivered in joules is a charge times a voltage — which is why a 12-volt car battery is described in amp-hours, a unit of charge. It is a derived unit, one newton-metre, and the prefixes matter here more than anywhere: bond energies are a few hundred kilojoules and nuclear ones are a few hundred megajoules.

definition: The SI unit of temperature, and the only one on an absolute scale — zero is the temperature at which thermal motion stops. It is the same size as a degree Celsius with the numbers shifted by 273.15, so 0 °C is 273.15 K.
explanation: The kelvin is the only temperature scale with an absolute zero, and it is the only one on which ratios are meaningful. Zero kelvin is the temperature at which thermal motion stops, which is why it is written on every thermodynamic law and why it is not reachable — quantum mechanics puts a floor about a billionth of a degree above it. Its size equals a Celsius degree with the numbers shifted by 273.15, so 0 °C is 273.15 K and the two scales share no origin.

definition: The study of how fast a chemical reaction goes, and of what controls that rate. It is a question separate from thermodynamics, which asks whether a reaction will run at all: a reaction can be energetically favourable and still far too slow to matter.
explanation: Kinetics and thermodynamics answer different questions and disagree constantly. Thermodynamics says whether a reaction will run and what the equilibrium is; kinetics says how fast, and a reaction can be thermodynamically favourable and take a geological age. Diamond is the standing example — carbon's arrangement at the surface is less stable than graphite's, so diamond is slowly converting, and the barrier is high enough that a diamond keeps its shape for a very long time.

definition: A noble gas at number 36, used in some high-performance light bulbs and in the lamps that project the definition of the metre. It was once measured against a spectral line, and the metre has since outgrown it.
explanation: Krypton-86 was the basis of the definition of the metre from 1960 until 1983, which is the clearest example of an element being repurposed as a standard. Its orange-red emission line was counted in interference fringes to fix the length, and it was superseded by a speed of light and then by a distance defined by a time interval. It still has a real use in flash lamps and in insulating window panes, where it lowers heat loss.

definition: Any of the fifteen elements from lanthanum to lutetium, filling an inner 4f subshell. They are chemically so alike that separating them is difficult and expensive, which is why they are called the rare earths.
explanation: The lanthanides are fifteen chemically near-identical elements, and that identity is an economic problem rather than a scientific one. Separating them requires dozens of stages of fractional crystallisation or solvent extraction because their chemistry differs by a fraction of a per cent, which is why they used to be cheaper to discard than to recover. It is also what makes their compounds so useful in catalysis and phosphors — the near-identity lets one substitute for another.

definition: A soft silvery metal at number 57, and the element from which the lanthanides take their name. It is used in the lenses of camera objectives, because its glass has a high refractive index.
explanation: Lanthanum is named for the village of Lanthasylis in Sweden, from the oxide first separated there, and it is the element the lanthanide series is measured from. Its high refractive index is what makes it useful in camera lens glass — the lenses in professional photography have used lanthanum-containing glass since the 1930s because it bends light more without adding the colour other heavy glasses add. It is also a component of the catalysts that crack crude oil.

definition: The energy a substance absorbs or releases while changing phase without any change in temperature. Water at boiling point stays at 100 °C for as long as it takes to become steam, and all of that extra heat is going into breaking bonds rather than into temperature.
explanation: Latent heat is the energy a substance absorbs while changing phase with no temperature change at all, and it is a large term that the temperature does not reveal. Water at 100 °C stays at 100 °C while it boils, and all of the energy going in is breaking the hydrogen bonds holding the liquid together. It is why a kettle takes as long to come to the boil as it does, and why the amount of steam needed to scald is not the same as the amount of water.

definition: The repeating three-dimensional arrangement of atoms or ions in a solid crystal. It is the lattice that gives a material its hardness and its melting point, and it is why diamond and graphite are so much harder than they are, being the same element arranged differently.
explanation: A lattice is the repeating arrangement that gives a solid its properties, and it is the variable that decides most of what a material does. Diamond and graphite have the same atom and the same bonding and different lattices, and one is the hardest substance known while the other is a lubricant. The arrangement also determines density, melting point and whether the solid conducts, which is why crystal structure is the first thing to look up for an unfamiliar compound.

definition: The eighteenth-century French chemist who insisted that burning and rusting involve combination with a gas from the air, and who called that gas oxygen. He also introduced the law of conservation of mass into chemistry as a working rule, and framed the whole subject as one of measurement.
explanation: Lavoisier's contribution was not a discovery but a rule — the law of conservation of mass — and it is the rule that turned chemistry from observation into measurement. Before it, a chemist could not tell whether something had been created or destroyed, so there was no such thing as a balance on the outcome of a reaction. He also named oxygen and defined an element as a substance that could not be decomposed further, which is a better definition than any before it.

definition: The rule that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, only rearranged. It is why a sealed flask weighs the same before and after, whatever happens inside it.
explanation: The law says mass is rearranged rather than created or destroyed, and it is the foundation every equation rests on: balancing an equation is enforcing it. It has one celebrated apparent exception, in a reaction where a gas escapes an open vessel and the products seem lighter than the reactants, which is not an exception at all. It was revised for nuclear reactions, where a small amount of mass becomes a very large amount of energy, and it holds there too.

definition: A synthetic actinide at number 103, the last member of the actinide series and named for Ernest Lawrence, who invented the cyclotron. Only a few dozen atoms have ever been assembled, enough to establish that it behaves as a heavier lutetium.
explanation: Lawrencium is the last actinide and the heaviest element whose chemistry has been studied in solution, and the result confirmed the series closes properly: it behaves as a heavier lutetium rather than as a transition metal. That is a real finding rather than a formality, because the alternative was live — that the actinides ended earlier. Only a few dozen atoms have been made, and it was named for Ernest Lawrence, who invented the cyclotron that made it possible.

definition: The rule that a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose a disturbance put to it. Add heat and an endothermic reaction is favoured; remove a product and making more of it is favoured; and raising pressure favours whichever side has fewer gas molecules.
explanation: The principle is a qualitative statement that a system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by opposing it, and it is the reasoning tool for every equilibrium problem. Raise the temperature and an endothermic reaction is favoured; remove a product and making more of it is favoured; raise the pressure and whichever side has fewer gas molecules is favoured. It works because the shift that opposes the disturbance is the one that lowers the system's free energy, and it is only qualitative — the equilibrium constant tells you how far, not which way.

definition: A soft, heavy metal at number 82 that resists corrosion, and the metal of lead-acid car batteries and of solder. Its density and its softness have served plumbing and roofing for two thousand years, and its toxicity has ended both.
explanation: Lead's story is a long fall from ubiquity, and every stage of it was a good idea at the time. It is soft, dense, malleable, corrosion-resistant and it alloys well, and the Roman water pipes that still stand are a fair summary of its virtues. It was in paint until leaded petrol put it into the air and made it a neurotoxin, and it was in solder until electronics found it poisoned workers. Almost all of it now goes into batteries, which are the one application that recycles well.

definition: The American chemist who proposed that a covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons and drew it as two dots, and who explained the octet rule in terms of that. He also introduced electron dot structures, still the fastest way to sketch a molecule's bonding.
explanation: Lewis's dot structures are still the fastest way to sketch a molecule's bonding, and they are the reason the octet rule can be drawn rather than merely stated. His larger contribution is the idea that a chemical bond is a shared pair of electrons, which is what unified organic and inorganic chemistry under one picture. The one thing his model cannot do is account for why some molecules are stable at all, which is the question that led to molecular orbital theory.

definition: A substance that accepts a pair of electrons in the course of a reaction. Broader than the Brønsted–Lowry definition of an acid, which is specifically a proton donor, and it is the one that explains catalysis.
explanation: The Lewis definition is broader than the one it replaced, and the broadening is the point. Brønsted–Lowry defines an acid as a proton donor, which handles aqueous reactions neatly and misses most of the chemistry that does not happen in water. Lewis defined an acid as an electron-pair acceptor, which captures catalysis, the metal-ammonia complexes and most of what happens in an organic reaction. Under that definition every Lewis base is also a Brønsted base, and not every Lewis acid is a proton donor.

definition: A substance that donates a pair of electrons in the course of a reaction. Most bases are Lewis bases, and the lone pair on ammonia is what makes it one.
explanation: A Lewis base is anything with an electron pair to offer, which is a very large class: ammonia with its lone pair, water, and any anion. The strength of a base in this sense tracks how available that pair is, so it depends on what the pair is shared with, which is why the same ammonia is a strong base towards a proton and a weak one towards boron. It is also why a carbonyl group is nucleophilic at the oxygen and not at the carbon, and why that governs most of its chemistry.

definition: The reactant that runs out first and so decides how much product can form. It is rarely the one in shortest supply by mass, because the equation gives the ratios — which is the trap in the question.
explanation: The limiting reagent is the one whose stoichiometric ratio runs out first, and the trap is that it is rarely the one in shortest supply by mass. A recipe calling 50 g of something and 500 g of something else may be short of the first, because the equation says they react in a ratio of 1:20 and not 1:10. The calculation is always: divide each amount by its coefficient, and the smallest quotient identifies the limiter.

definition: A state in which particles are close together but can still slide past one another, so a liquid has a fixed volume and takes the shape of its container.
explanation: A liquid is a solid's order partly broken: the particles are still close enough to stay in step with their neighbours over a short range but not over a long one. That is why a liquid flows and why it has a surface, because molecules at the surface have fewer neighbours and are less tightly held than those inside.

definition: The lightest metal, and the only one of the alkali metals less dense than water. It is soft enough to cut with a knife, and its salts are used in the batteries of phones and laptops because they give up and take back a charge well.
explanation: Lithium is the alkali metal that behaves least like one: it is the hardest, the least reactive, and the only one dense enough to float on oil. Its 1s shell is filled at two electrons, so lithium's nucleus holds its small set of electrons more tightly than the others' and it keeps them longer. That is the whole of its difference — and it is enough that lithium grease works where sodium would not, and lithium batteries dominate because of the same ionic behaviour.

definition: A dye that turns red in acid and blue in alkali, used for centuries as a rough test and now largely replaced by indicators with sharper ranges. It works because the molecule's shape changes with pH, and the shape changes the colour.
explanation: Litmus works because its molecule changes shape with pH and a different shape absorbs a different colour, which is the general mechanism behind every acid–base indicator. What changed is the precision: litmus switches across roughly pH 5 to 8, while methyl orange and phenolphthalein each switch over about two units, and a potentiometer measures the number itself. Litmus survives as a classroom demonstration and in microbiology, where its absence of colour at neutral pH is useful.

definition: A unit of volume of one thousand cubic centimetres, or about a kilogram of water. It is not an SI unit — the SI unit is the cubic metre — but it is the one used in chemistry wherever a solution's volume is quoted.
explanation: The litre is not an SI unit, which surprises people who write it as though it were. The SI unit of volume is the cubic metre, and a litre is a derived unit accepted for use with it — a cubic decimetre, or a kilogram of water by a very good approximation. In chemistry it is the unit that matters, because solutions are made up by volume and a molar concentration is moles per litre, which is a convention rather than a law but a universally kept one.

definition: A synthetic element at number 116, named after the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory that made it. It sits below polonium in group 16, and only a few atoms have ever been made.
explanation: Livermorium is one of three elements named after the American laboratory that made them rather than after a person, which is a departure from the convention that held for eighty years. Only a few atoms have been produced and its chemistry is predicted rather than measured. It sits below polonium in group 16, and the prediction that matters is that it may not resemble it — the relativistic effects that distort the heaviest elements' chemistry make the table's groupings unreliable here.

definition: The last and heaviest of the lanthanides, at number 71, and chemically the most like a transition metal of them all. Its oxide is the catalyst in the petroleum cracking of every barrel of petrol.
explanation: Lutetium closes the lanthanides and is the last of the fifteen, and chemically it is the least lanthanum-like of them — its 4f shell is completely full, so it behaves more like a transition metal.
