That is why its oxide is the catalyst in essentially every refinery cracking plant: it is one of the few solid acid catalysts that will survive the temperatures and the coke that petroleum cracking produces. Lutetium-177 and lutetium-177-PSMA are used in targeted cancer therapy.

definition: A light metal at number 12 that burns with a brilliant white flame and sits at the centre of every chlorophyll molecule. It is alloyed into aluminium for laptops and into cars to make them lighter.
explanation: Magnesium is the metal at the centre of every chlorophyll molecule, so it is in the mechanism of photosynthesis and in the diets of everything that eats plants. It burns with a brilliant white flame, which is why it was in flashbulbs, and it is alloyed into aluminium to make it both lighter and easier to weld. It is the second metal to become common enough to matter after copper and the first to be mined primarily for its own properties rather than its ore.

definition: The ability of a metal to be hammered or rolled into a sheet without cracking, which comes from the same sliding layers of atoms as ductility. Gold is the most malleable of all — a gram can be beaten into a sheet a square metre across.
explanation: Malleability and ductility are the same mechanism applied in two directions — layers of atoms sliding past one another — and they are what separate the metals from everything else. Gold is the extreme case: a gram beaten into a square metre without tearing, which is how the earliest gold leaf was made and how the gold leaf on an icon came to be. The same sliding is also why a metal can be work-hardened, and why it eventually needs annealing to be worked further.

definition: A hard, brittle metal at number 25, added to steel to remove sulphur and to make it tougher. In the form of MnO₄⁻ it is the purple permanganate, which is oxidising enough to disinfect water.
explanation: Manganese appears in steel for the unglamorous reason that it removes sulphur, and iron sulphides would otherwise make the steel brittle. It also strengthens steel directly, and its compound permanganate is the purple oxidant used in water treatment and in a demonstration of how fast reaction rates can be. In the ocean floor it accumulates as nodules that are both a resource and a serious ecological question, because they take millions of years to form and a century to mine.

definition: The total of an atom's protons and neutrons, and therefore roughly its atomic mass. It is a whole number for a given nuclide, which is why it is a different thing from atomic weight.
explanation: The mass number is a count, not a measurement, which is why it is always a whole number and why a given nuclide has exactly one. It is protons plus neutrons, and the two can be separated because they are not interchangeable: changing neutron count gives an isotope and changing proton count gives a different element. The mass number is written as a superscript before the symbol and it is what identifies a nuclide unambiguously.

definition: The Austrian-Swedish physicist who, in 1938, explained that a uranium nucleus split by a neutron could release energy, and named it nuclear fission. She worked out the whole thing in a letter to her nephew, and it took physics some years to catch up with it.
explanation: Meitner is the most instructive case of a person losing credit for their own work, and the details are worth knowing because the error was ordinary rather than malicious. Her and Frisch's explanation of Hahn's fission results, produced in Stockholm in 1938 and 1939 while the war made travel impossible, was the physics that made the bomb possible — and it took until the 1950s for the community to credit her, and Nobel nominations for her came decades too late. She was also the one to apply nuclear physics to medicine, founding the first radiotherapy unit in Europe.

definition: A synthetic element at number 109, named for Lise Meitner, who explained nuclear fission in 1938 and whose work Otto Hahn carried out without fully recognising what he had produced. The element honours the theorist rather than the experimenter.
explanation: Meitnerium is named for the theorist who explained nuclear fission rather than for the chemist who discovered it, and that is the justification the IUPAC gives when a name honours a person rather than a place. Only a few dozen atoms have been made and its chemistry has not been measured in solution. It sits in group 7 below technetium and rhenium, and the expectation is that it behaves like them, which is itself untested.

definition: The temperature at which a solid becomes a liquid, and — for a pure substance at a given pressure — a fixed one. It varies with pressure only slightly for most solids, and falls to nearly nothing as the pressure rises for water, which is unusual.
explanation: Melting point is one of the most useful numbers in the table and one of the least simple. A perfect crystal has a sharp melting point and a real sample does not, because a polycrystalline material melts over a range as different grains melt at slightly different temperatures. Tungsten's is 3,422 °C and mercury is, uniquely, liquid at room temperature; and gallium is a metal that melts in a warm hand, which is the exception that proves the range is a real property and not a law.

definition: The Russian chemist who arranged the elements by atomic weight in 1869 and left gaps where elements were missing, naming the gaps and predicting their properties. Eka-aluminium became aluminium and eka-boron became scandium, and both predictions were confirmed within fifteen years.
explanation: Mendeleev's achievement was not the table but the gaps. He arranged the elements by atomic weight, noticed the regularities, and left spaces where an element ought to be — naming them eka-aluminium, eka-boron, eka-silicon and giving each a predicted atomic weight and a list of predicted properties. When germanium turned up twenty years later with essentially the properties he had written down, the table stopped being a classification and became a prediction machine. He was also wrong about the noble gases, which he had no room for.

definition: A synthetic actinide at number 101, named for Dmitri Mendeleev, who arranged the periodic table in the first place. Only a few atoms have ever been made at a time, which is how its existence was confirmed at all.
explanation: Mendelevium is the element named after Mendeleev, which is the obvious choice and the one the IUPAC ratified. Only a few atoms have ever been made, in experiments repeated over years because the yield was about one atom at a time. Its discovery mattered out of proportion to the atom count: it was the element that proved the actinides carried on past the point the chemistry changed, which is what eventually ended the actinide series.

definition: The only metal that is a liquid at room temperature, at number 80, and it was once in thermometers, mirrors and dental amalgam. It is toxic and its vapour is dangerous, which is why it has been withdrawn from most of those uses.
explanation: Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature, and the reason is unglamorous: it has filled its 6s shell and holds its electrons unusually tightly, so the forces between atoms are weak. That combination of low melting point and high density made it useful in thermometers, and it is also what makes it toxic — elemental mercury vapour is absorbed through the lungs and its ions bind sulphur-containing groups in proteins. It is being phased out almost everywhere it was used.

definition: An element that is a good conductor of heat and electricity, is lustrous, and is malleable and ductile. Those properties all follow from having valence electrons that are free to move through the structure rather than locked into bonds.
explanation: What makes a metal a metal is a shared property with a shared cause: enough valence electrons that they are not localised. They move through the structure, which is why metals conduct and why they are malleable and ductile; they also hold each atom's neighbours less tightly than a covalent network does, which is why metals have lower melting points than the ceramics of similar bonding. That one free-electron picture predicts most of what a metal does.

definition: An element with properties between a metal's and a non-metal's, and used as a semiconductor for exactly that reason. Boron, silicon, germanium and arsenic are the four most important, and silicon's position is what the whole electronics industry rests on.
explanation: The metalloids are the elements where the answer to 'is this a metal?' is genuinely ambiguous, and the ambiguity is not a failure of classification — it reflects a real crossover in bonding. Each has more valence electrons than a metal and fewer than a non-metal, so it shows a bit of both: silicon's oxide is an acid, its elemental form is a brittle shiny solid, and it conducts more than a non-metal and far less than a metal. Which is why they are used where a half-way behaviour is wanted.

definition: A naturally occurring solid with an ordered crystal structure and a definite chemical composition. Nearly every rock is made of them, and the ones that matter here are named for what they contain: haematite for iron, galena for lead, bauxite for aluminium.
explanation: A mineral is defined by having an ordered crystal structure and a fixed composition, not merely by being a natural substance, and that is why almost every rock is a mixture of minerals rather than one thing. The ones that matter to chemistry are named for their contents — haematite, galena, bauxite, chalcopyrite — which makes an ore's name a reliable statement about what can be extracted from it.

definition: Two or more substances together without joining, each keeping its own properties and separable by physical means. Air, sea water and steel are all mixtures, and the distinction from a compound is that no new substance has formed.
explanation: A mixture is worth distinguishing from a compound for a practical reason as much as a definitional one: its components can be separated by physical means, while a compound's cannot. Air, sea water, brass and petrol are all mixtures, and a chemist who calls one of them a compound has made an error that predicts the wrong separation method. The exception worth remembering is a mixture that happens to have a fixed ratio — a mixture is not automatically variable.

definition: The mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole, and numerically equal to its relative atomic or molecular mass. It is the bridge between a mass on a balance and a number of particles on a page.
explanation: Molar mass is the mass of a mole in grams, and it is numerically equal to the relative atomic or molecular mass, which is why the two are interchangeable in practice and not quite the same thing. It is what converts between a mass and an amount: 18.0 g of water is very nearly a mole, and 18.0 g of anything else is not. Its reliability depends on isotopes, so the molar mass of an element is a weighted average and its most abundant isotope is not necessarily the one that sets the number.

definition: The concentration of a solution in moles of solute per litre of solution, written M. A 0.1 molar solution contains 0.1 moles in every litre.
explanation: Molarity is defined per litre of *solution*, not per litre of solvent, which is the detail that catches people and which is why a solution made from a solid and a solution made by dilution can end up with different molarities for the same nominal recipe. It also means molarity changes with temperature, since the volume does, which is why a standard solution's concentration is quoted with the temperature it was made at.

definition: The amount of a substance containing 6.022 × 10²³ particles — the chemist's dozen, but six sextillion of them. It exists because counting atoms directly is hopeless and weighing them is easy, and the mole converts between the two.
explanation: The mole is the reason chemistry can count. Atoms are too small to count and too light to weigh individually, so the mole converts between them: weigh a sample, divide by molar mass, and you have the number of moles, and Avogadro's constant converts that to the number of particles. Its modern definition fixes the number of entities rather than the mass, which is unusual — a definition that starts from a constant rather than from a measurement.

definition: An orbital spread over two or more atoms rather than confined to one, which is the accurate picture of a covalent bond. The number of them equals the number of atomic orbitals combined, and their energies decide whether a bond forms at all.
explanation: A molecular orbital is the quantum-mechanical reason a covalent bond exists, and it replaces the shared-pair picture with something less comfortable: the electrons occupy a wavefunction spread over both nuclei, and for the same atom that spread has a node through the middle. Two atomic orbitals combine into two molecular orbitals, one bonding and one antibonding, and whether a bond forms depends on filling the bonding one. It also explains why O₂ is paramagnetic, which Lewis structures cannot.

definition: Two or more atoms joined into a discrete unit with its own properties. Molecular substances are usually gases, liquids or soft solids, because the forces between the molecules are much weaker than the bonds inside them.
explanation: A molecule is a discrete unit, and that discreteness is what gives molecular substances their character: the forces between molecules are much weaker than the bonds inside them, so they have low melting and boiling points and they sublime readily. The exceptions are the giant covalent structures — diamond, graphite, silicon — which have no discrete molecules at all and whose properties are those of a solid rather than of a compound.

definition: A metal at number 42 with the highest melting point of any element, used to strengthen steel and in the filaments of older light bulbs. It is also essential to nitrogenase, the enzyme that lets bacteria fix nitrogen.
explanation: Molybdenum has the highest melting point of any element, which is what made it the filament metal before incandescent bulbs were overtaken. It is also one of the few elements biology cannot do without: nitrogenase, the enzyme that lets bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen, contains a molybdenum centre, and the element is therefore part of the nitrogen cycle. Its ore is almost always a by-product of copper mining, which is why its supply tracks copper's.

definition: The turning effect of a force about a point, which is the force multiplied by its distance from that point. A heavy door opened near its hinges is far harder to move than the same door opened at the handle.
explanation: A moment is a force times its distance from the pivot, which is the whole of it, and it is the reason a heavy door is easy or hard to move depending on where you put your hand. It also explains why levers work: a small effort far from the pivot can move a large load near it, and the trade is exact — you gain force and lose distance by the same ratio. The same quantity, measured about the centre of mass rather than a pivot, is what makes a molecule tumble.

definition: A synthetic element at number 115, named for the Moscow region where one of the two laboratories that made it stands. Only a few dozen atoms have been produced and its chemistry is predicted rather than measured.
explanation: Moscovium is the heavier of the two elements discovered in Russia's Dubna laboratory and named for the Moscow region, and both were found in the same experiment in 2003. Only a few dozen atoms exist and none of its chemistry has been measured. It sits below antimony in group 15, and the prediction that matters is that it may not behave like antimony: at these atomic numbers relativity distorts the shells enough that group membership becomes unreliable.

definition: The physicist who in 1913 showed that an element's X-ray spectrum depends on its atomic number and not on its atomic weight, which settled a standing argument and made the periodic table's basis explicit. He volunteered for the army in 1915 and was killed at the Somme the following year.
explanation: Moseley's work settled a standing argument that had lasted twenty years and cost a career. The periodic table was arranged by atomic weight, which put tellurium at 127 next to iodine at 127 and so in the wrong group, and several pairs sat wrongly. Moseley showed in 1913 that an element's X-ray spectrum depends on its nuclear charge and not on its weight, which fixed the ordering and gave the table the basis it now has. He volunteered for the army in 1915 and was killed at the Somme the following year, at twenty-five, and his method went on to identify elements nobody had found yet — technetium, hafnium, rhenium.

definition: A rare earth metal at number 60 used in the strongest permanent magnets there are, which is why it is in headphones, windscreen wipers and MRI scanners. Its glass also colours glass a deep violet.
explanation: Neodymium magnets are the strongest permanent magnets available and the reason electric vehicles and wind turbines exist at their present size. The strength comes from combining neodymium with iron and boron in a specific crystal structure, and the cost is brittleness — a neodymium magnet is a hard, dense, easily cracked ceramic-looking material that has to be plated and handled carefully. Add dysprosium and you get heat resistance at the price of more of a scarce element.

definition: A noble gas at number 10, glowing red-orange when an electric current passes through it. The signs in every high street are filled with it because it emits so much visible light for so little electricity.
explanation: Neon's advertising signs work because of a feature that makes it nearly useless elsewhere: at low pressure the emission is concentrated in a few very narrow lines rather than spread across the spectrum. That narrowness is why the red-orange glow is so efficient — almost all the electrical energy goes into visible light instead of into invisible heat or ultraviolet. The same property that makes a good sign makes it a poor general lamp.

definition: The first transuranic element to be made, at number 93, in 1940. It occurs naturally in uranium ore in tiny amounts, and it is the feedstock for making plutonium-239.
explanation: Neptunium is the first transuranic element ever made and the only one that occurs naturally in appreciable amounts, because neptunium-237's half-life is long enough for some to survive since the earth formed. That makes it a genuinely rare case: an element heavier than uranium, present in uranium ore without anybody having built it. It is also the feedstock from which plutonium-239 is produced, which is what gave it its historical importance.

definition: An acid reacting with a base so that neither is left in excess, giving a salt and water. The pH of the result is seven only for strong acid–strong base pairs, which is the detail school chemistry tends to leave out.
explanation: Neutralisation is an acid meeting a base and neither being in excess, and the pH that results depends on the pair. A strong acid with a strong base gives 7 at 25 °C, but a strong acid with a weak base gives an acidic solution and a weak acid with a strong base gives an alkaline one, because the conjugate ion that is left over hydrolyses. That is why neutralising a gastric upset with sodium bicarbonate works differently from the same with milk of magnesia.

definition: A neutral particle in the nucleus, found by Chadwick in 1932 and about the same mass as a proton. Having no charge is what lets it pass through atoms without being deflected, which is what makes it both a projectile and the hardest thing to shield.
explanation: The neutron's lack of charge is the property everything else follows from. It passes through matter without being deflected, which makes it penetrating and makes it hard to detect; it also means it is not held by electromagnetic attraction and is not attracted to anything in particular, so it must be found by collision rather than by steering. Its mass is very nearly the proton's, and that near-equality is why a nucleus's neutron-to-proton ratio is a meaningful number rather than an arbitrary one.

definition: The SI unit of force, the push needed to accelerate one kilogram by one metre per second squared. Gravity gives an average person about 700 newtons of weight, which is a different quantity again.
explanation: The newton is force per unit definition that is worth knowing for one reason: it is derived from the second law, so it is a unit that says a standard object under a standard acceleration produces it. In chemistry it appears less often than the joule, but it underlies the pressure unit, since a pascal is a newton on a square metre. Newton's own units were based on a particular planet and his own gravity, and they had to be redefined when the metric system was agreed.

definition: A metal at number 28, silvery and hard, used as an alloy with copper for electrical contacts and in stainless steel. Among the transition metals it is unusually resistant to corrosion, which is why coinage and plating both use it.
explanation: Nickel is the element that makes a coin, a battery and a bolt all different from one another. Pure nickel resists corrosion well but is expensive, so it is used where the surface matters — coinage, electrical contacts, plating — and alloyed with copper where the metal has to be affordable. In a lithium-ion cell it is one of the two electrode metals and is increasingly a constraint, because the supply is concentrated in Indonesia and there is no easy substitute for it in a cell.

definition: A synthetic element at number 113, named for Japan where it was made, and the first element discovered in Asia. It is a few rows below thallium and is predicted to be more stable than it, which is the same relationship mercury has to lead.
explanation: Nihonium is the first element discovered in Asia and the lightest of the three whose predicted chemistry departs sharply from the element above it. It sits below thallium in group 13, and where thallium prefers the +1 state, nihonium is predicted to prefer +3 — the same inversion mercury shows relative to lead. Only a few atoms have been made and none of its chemistry has been measured, so that is currently a prediction resting on a calculation.

definition: A soft, ductile metal at number 41 used in the superconducting alloy in MRI scanners and in the cabling of particle accelerators. It was called columbium for decades, and the older name is still common.
explanation: Niobium's two uses are both cases of a material being chosen for a property nothing else has. It stays superconducting at temperatures a few times higher than the alloys that came before, which is what makes an MRI scanner's magnet possible at all. And it superalloys nickel for turbine blades, because niobium carbide pins the grain boundaries and stops them moving at temperature. It was called columbium for sixty years and both names are still in use.

definition: Hardening a metal's surface by heating it in nitrogen so that nitrogen diffuses in and forms a hard compound. Unlike carburising it does not distort the part, which matters for anything that has to stay within a tolerance.
explanation: Nitriding hardens a surface by letting nitrogen diffuse in, and the reason to choose it over carburising is the temperature. Nitriding happens some 200 °C below carburising, so the part distorts far less, which matters for anything with a tight tolerance or a ground bearing surface. It is slower as a result — the same case depth takes days — and it is the standard treatment for crankshafts, gears and cylinder liners.

definition: The gas making up 78% of the air, so inert that it is used wherever something must not react. Its triple bond is exceptionally strong, which is why nitrgen gas is so unreactive and why fixing it — turning it into something plants can use — is one of chemistry's central problems.
explanation: Nitrogen's unreactivity is a bond-strength story and not an inertness story: the triple bond is one of the strongest in chemistry, so breaking it costs a great deal and the atoms are locked together. That is why fixing it — converting atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia — is one of the hardest reactions industry performs, why it needs a catalyst and 200 atmospheres, and why it feeds roughly half the world's food. Burning fossil fuel has also put a third of the atmospheric oxygen there, and that is the carbon cycle.

definition: A synthetic actinide at number 102, named for Alfred Nobel. Only a few atoms exist at a time, and the evidence for it in the early 1960s was thin enough that for years it was thought the element had not really been made.
explanation: Nobelium has the shortest history of any element: it was claimed in the 1960s on evidence thin enough that for years other groups said it had never really been made. It is now accepted, at about half a milligram produced in total, and only its atom count and a couple of chemical properties are known. Its longest-lived isotope lives for minutes, which is the practical definition of the edge of what a neutron-bombardment programme can reach.

definition: One of the six elements in group 18 whose outer shells are full and which therefore form almost no compounds. Argon gives the faint glow in an ordinary fluorescent tube, and helium is what makes a balloon float.
explanation: The noble gases are the elements the periodic table's original version had no room for, and Mendeleev did not predict them — he predicted an empty space at zero. Their later discovery was the confirmation that the table was right and incomplete at once, and the fact that they sit in a whole column rather than scattered is what showed the octet rule was structural. Xenon and krypton do form compounds, so 'inert' has always been a practical term rather than an absolute one.

definition: A heat treatment that refines the grain of steel by heating it and letting it cool in air. It raises toughness and tensile strength by making the structure uniform, and it is the standard treatment given to a casting before it is used.
explanation: Normalising is the heat treatment that fixes a casting. A casting has large, irregular grains because it cooled slowly and unevenly, and those are weak spots; heating it above its recrystallisation temperature and letting it cool in air produces a fine, uniform structure. It costs a dimension change, which is why it is done before machining and not after — and it is why a normalised steel part is dimensionally predictable in a way an as-cast one is not.

definition: Radioactive material left over from nuclear power or weapons production, classified by how long it stays dangerous. High-level waste is usually spent fuel; low-level waste is gloves and filters from a plant, and it is a hundred thousand times less voluminous.
explanation: Nuclear waste is classified by how long it stays dangerous, and the categories are less reassuring than they sound. Low-level waste — gloves, filters, contaminated tools — is a hundred thousand times less voluminous than high-level waste and needs decades of controlled storage. High-level waste is spent fuel, and the difficulty is not that it is immensely large but that it must be isolated for a hundred thousand years with no repository yet built anywhere.

definition: A proton or a neutron, the two particles that make up a nucleus. The count of them in a nucleus is the mass number.
explanation: Nucleon is the collective word for protons and neutrons, and it is useful mainly because nuclear quantities are quoted per nucleon. Binding energy per nucleon is the quantity that explains both fission and fusion: it rises towards iron and falls either side, and every reaction that moves a nucleus towards iron releases the difference. Quoting total binding energy per nucleus instead gives a curve that says almost nothing.

definition: The dense central part of an atom, holding its protons and neutrons and carrying almost all of its mass. It is around 10,000 times smaller than the atom and about 100,000 times heavier per unit volume.
explanation: The nucleus is about 10,000 times smaller than the atom and holds over 99.9% of its mass, which is why an atom is mostly empty space and why alpha particles pass through gold foil without deflecting. Almost all of it is protons and neutrons bound by the strong force, which is the strongest force known and which resists being screened by anything. The result is a set of very dense, very tightly packed objects with a very short range of stability.

definition: A specific atom described by its proton and neutron counts, which fixes its mass and its radioactivity. It is a more precise word than isotope, which allows for a nucleus that is the same atom but in a different energy state.
explanation: A nuclide is a nucleus specified exactly, and the word exists because 'isotope' is not quite enough. Two nuclei of the same isotope can be in different energy states, and a nuclide names the state as well as the proton and neutron counts — which matters in spectroscopy, where a metastable isomer like technetium-99m is a genuinely different nuclide with a different half-life from the ground state of the same element. M and A together fix a nuclide.

definition: The tendency of atoms to gain, lose or share electrons until they have eight in their outer shell. Noble gases satisfy it and do not react, which is the whole reason the rule exists.
explanation: The octet rule is a statement about stability rather than about a law, and its exceptions are what make it useful. Noble gases have full shells and do not react; anything with seven valence electrons wants one more; anything with one wants to lose it. But the transition metals routinely exceed eight because their d orbitals hold ten, and boron routinely falls short with six, because there are not eight electrons to reach in its second shell. Every exception has the same explanation: there were not eight there to have.

definition: The heaviest element yet made, at number 118, named for Yuri Oganessian. It completes the seventh period, and it may not behave like a noble gas at all: predictions suggest a solid, reactive element, which would mean the table's last column is a pattern rather than a rule.
explanation: Oganesson may not be a noble gas, and that is the most interesting claim attached to any element on this site. It sits at the bottom of group 18, but relativistic effects at this atomic number are large enough that its seven valence electrons are predicted to be relatively inert while its eight are not — which is backwards. If that is right, the last column of the periodic table is a pattern that happened to hold for seven rows rather than a rule.

definition: A region around a nucleus in which an electron is likely to be found, described by three quantum numbers rather than by a path. There are seven in the fourth shell, which is why a period of the table can be that wide.
explanation: An orbital is a probability description, not a thing, and it cannot be drawn: what the pictures in textbooks show is a surface enclosing most of the probability, and there is an equal chance of the electron being outside it. That is why the s orbitals are drawn as spheres and the p and d orbitals as lobed shapes — the shapes are the shapes of the region, and they are what decide a molecule's geometry.

definition: The power of ten nearest a quantity, and how far atomic and nuclear things are usually compared. Atomic radii are about a nanometre, nuclei about a femtometre, and the periodic table spans about seven orders of magnitude in density.
explanation: Order of magnitude is the comparison that makes atomic-scale numbers meaningful. Atomic radii are about 10⁻¹⁰ m, nuclei about 10⁻¹⁵ m, and the periodic table spans about seven orders of magnitude in density from hydrogen gas to osmium. It is also how you should read every other number on this site: the last digit of an atomic weight is real, and the last digit of a nuclear radius usually is not.

definition: A rock from which an element is profitably extracted. An element's abundance says nothing about whether there is any ore of it, because ore is about concentration and cost: aluminium is the third most abundant element in the crust and was once worth more than gold.
explanation: Abundance and oreness are different questions, which is the whole point of the word. Aluminium is the third most abundant element in the crust and was once more valuable than gold, because the ore was not known how to be reduced; gold is a few parts per billion and was worth a fortune precisely because of that. An ore is defined by concentration and cost, and both change with technology — which is why a metal that was unexploitable in 1800 may be common now.

definition: A concentration of an element in rock rich enough to be worth mining. Where it forms depends on the chemistry — veins around granite intrusions, layers in sedimentary basins, or nodules on the sea bed — and the whole of economic geology follows from those mechanisms.
explanation: Where an ore deposit forms follows from the chemistry, and the three settings account for most of them. Veins come with granite intrusions, where hot fluids carry metal ions upwards and deposit them as they cool. Sedimentary layers form where the element is more soluble in one condition than another, as with evaporite deposits. And nodules on the sea bed precipitate directly from seawater. The setting predicts both the metal and the extraction method, which is why geologists prospect for one and not the other.

definition: The densest of all the elements at number 76, slightly heavier than platinum per unit volume. It is used for the tips of fountain pen nibs and for making very hard alloys, and it stains almost black on the skin.
explanation: Osmium is the densest element there is, slightly heavier than iridium per unit volume — a difference of a fraction of a per cent, and one of the few things on this site where the answer depends on whether you mean by mass or by volume. Its practical uses are all about hardness and wear rather than density: fountain pen nibs and instrument pivots, because it takes an extremely long time to wear away.

definition: Losing electrons. It is not the same as combining with oxygen, though that was the original meaning and the word has outgrown it — iron rusting is oxidation and so is a cell discharging.
explanation: Oxidation has nothing to do with oxygen and everything to do with electrons. The original meaning — combination with oxygen — was a special case that happened to be the commonest one, and the word outgrew it. Any loss of electrons is oxidation, whether the partner is oxygen, chlorine or another element, which is why iron rusting is oxidation and so is a battery discharging. And because electrons cannot simply vanish, everything that is oxidised is matched by something being reduced.

definition: The charge an atom would have if its bonds were all ionic, worked out by giving shared electrons to the more electronegative atom. It is a bookkeeping device rather than a real charge, and it is how compounds get named.
explanation: Oxidation state is a bookkeeping convention, not a real charge, and the distinction is worth holding on to. It is computed by pretending every bond is ionic and giving both electrons of a shared pair to the more electronegative atom; the result is a number used to name compounds and to balance equations. In an ion it coincides with the charge, and in the covalent molecules where the method is a fiction the number is still useful — but a non-integer oxidation state is not an atom carrying a fraction of a charge.

definition: A compound of oxygen with one other element, and the commonest of all compound types on Earth's crust. The oxides of metals are usually basic and those of non-metals usually acidic, which is a rough but useful predictor.
explanation: Oxides are the most common compounds in the earth's crust, and their acid–base behaviour follows a pattern worth knowing: metal oxides are usually basic and non-metal oxides usually acidic, so sodium oxide reacts with water to an alkali while sulfur dioxide reacts with water to an acid. The exceptions are informative — aluminium's and zinc's are amphoteric, which is a property of the metal's position rather than of the oxide's formula.

definition: A substance that takes electrons from something else, and is itself reduced. It is the partner of a reducing agent, and the pair is what a redox reaction consists of.
explanation: An oxidising agent's job is to take electrons, and it is reduced in doing it — so it is called an oxidising agent by what it does to the other substance, not to itself. Oxygen in the air is one, and so is hydrogen peroxide; the halogens are strong ones. The strength of an oxidising agent is measured against the standard electrode potential, which is a table of exactly these pairings.

definition: The element at number 8, the most abundant in the earth's crust and the one every combustion depends on. It is a gas with no colour or taste, and it is roughly a fifth of the air by volume.
explanation: Oxygen is the most abundant element in the crust and roughly a fifth of the air, and almost every combustion and every corrosion process is a reaction with it. Its two allotropes are not interchangeable: ozone is more reactive and is what the upper atmosphere is made of, and it is also what destroys most rubber and most biological tissue. And it took two billion years of photosynthesis to put the atmospheric oxygen there, which is why the carbon cycle and the oxygen cycle are the same cycle.

definition: A platinum-group metal at number 46 that absorbs hydrogen gas readily, which is what makes it the catalyst in a hydrogen fuel cell. About half of all the palladium ever mined has gone into recycling rather than being discarded.
explanation: Palladium absorbs hydrogen gas into its own lattice, reversibly, and that is what a hydrogen fuel cell runs on. The gas goes into the metal on one side of the membrane and comes out on the other, so the cell delivers electricity with water as its only waste. It is also the palladium that catches carbon monoxide and unburnt hydrocarbons in a catalytic converter, which is roughly half of what is spent on it. Most of the palladium ever mined has been recovered rather than discarded, largely because it is this expensive.

definition: The SI unit of pressure, one newton on a square metre, and abbreviated Pa. A standard atmosphere is about 101,325 of them, and sea-level pressure is 211,000 Pa written as 211 kPa.
explanation: The pascal is one newton on a square metre, which is a definition rather than a measurement, and it is the unit that makes pressure comparable across contexts. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is 101,325 Pa, so quoting it as 101.3 kPa is the same number in a friendlier form — and the prefix is doing real work, since the pressures in a reaction vessel or at the top of Everest differ by two orders of magnitude from that.

definition: A surface becoming resistant to corrosion because a thin, adherent, impermeable oxide layer has formed on it. Iron does it in concentrated nitric acid but not in dilute, and the layer is what makes aluminium usable despite being reactive.
explanation: Passivation is a surface deciding to protect itself, and the two cases behave differently. Iron passivates in concentrated nitric acid and rusts in dilute, because the concentrated acid grows an adherent oxide layer while the dilute one does not. Aluminium passivates in air, which is why it survives weather despite being reactive — the oxide is only microns thick and self-repairs as long as oxygen and water are both present.

definition: The physicist who proposed that no two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers, and that electrons of the same kind repel each other. The exclusion principle is what gives each shell its fixed capacity, and so what gives the periodic table its shape.
explanation: Pauli's other contributions are worth remembering alongside the exclusion principle. He predicted the neutrino — an uncharged particle that carries away the energy missing from beta decay — before anyone had evidence for one, and that prediction is what made the conservation of energy work for nuclear reactions. The spin of the electron was named for him, and Pauli being the man who thought of the neutrino and then of the principle that governs every atomic shell is an unusual pair of achievements for one physicist.

definition: The rule that no two electrons in an atom can share all four quantum numbers, which is why a shell holds only two electrons per orbital and why the second shell holds eight rather than some larger number. Electrons also differ in spin, which is how two fit in one orbital without repelling.
explanation: The exclusion principle is the reason a shell holds what it holds, and therefore the reason the periodic table has the shape it has. It says no two electrons can share all four quantum numbers, which caps each orbital at two — one spin up and one spin down — so the first shell holds two, the second eight, the third eighteen. It was formulated from spectroscopic evidence with no knowledge of the electron's wavefunction, and it worked.

definition: The chemist who put electronegativity on a numerical scale in 1932, so that bonds could be classed as ionic, polar covalent or non-polar rather than left as a description. It is one of the most used numbers in chemistry and one of the vaguest, since it is not directly measurable.
explanation: Pauling's electronegativity scale is one of the most used numbers in chemistry and one of the least well founded, and it is worth knowing both of those things. It is a scale built by contrast: fluorine is fixed at 4.0 and the rest derived from bond dissociation energies, which makes it a comparative judgement rather than a measurement of anything. It has been revised several times, other scales exist, and the ordering is stable while the third decimal place is not — so it is quoted to two places and used qualitatively.

definition: A horizontal row of the periodic table, holding elements whose outer electrons occupy the same shell. Periods get longer down the table as that shell gains room for more electrons, from two in the first to thirty-two in the seventh.
explanation: Periods are the horizontal rows, and their length is entirely determined by how many electrons can sit in the outer shells. Two in the first, eight in the second, eighteen in the third, and thirty-two in the fourth — which is why a period is seven columns wide for most of its length and why the f-block elements have to be lifted out below to keep the table printable. A period also corresponds to filling one shell, which is what makes it a genuine unit of structure and not a way of drawing.

definition: The rule that an element's properties repeat in a regular cycle as atomic number increases, and the observation on which the whole table rests. It was noticed before the structure of the atom was known, and explaining why it is true came a century later.
explanation: The periodic law was noticed before anything was known to explain it. The progression of properties across a row and their repetition down a column was obvious from atomic weights, and it was stated as a fact of nature with no mechanism at all — and then it sat unexplained for fifty years until the electron was discovered and the shell structure made it inevitable. It is the clearest case in chemistry of a pattern being found first and understood second.

definition: The arrangement of the elements by atomic number, with periods running across and groups down. Its shape is a direct consequence of electron configuration: seven electrons in the second shell is why a period is seven columns wide.
explanation: The table is the most successful predictive device in science, and its authority comes from that rather than from its layout. Mendeleev's version was arranged by atomic weight and left gaps; Moseley's basis was atomic number, which fixed the ordering; and the blocks, the periods and the groups are all consequences of the shell structure rather than choices about drawing. What it does not yet do is predict, reliably, the behaviour of the heaviest elements — which is a live question rather than a solved one.

definition: A number from 0 to 14 describing how acidic or alkaline a solution is, on a logarithmic scale. Each whole step is a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration, which is why small differences in pH are large differences in acidity — and why the scale cannot be measured beyond about 0 and 14 in water.
explanation: pH is a logarithmic scale, which means every whole step is a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration and that small differences matter a great deal. It is also conventionally measured only in water, where it runs about 0 to 14 — outside that range you are measuring something else, and in a non-aqueous solvent the scale is a different one with a different neutral point. And neutral pH is 7 only at 25 °C, because the water dissociation constant is temperature-dependent.

definition: The scale pH is measured on, running from strongly acidic at one end to strongly alkaline at the other, with 7 as neutral. Pure water sits at 7 because it contains equal amounts of hydrogen and hydroxide ions, and it is 7 at 25 °C rather than at any temperature.
explanation: The scale is logarithmic and centred on neutral water, and those two facts explain its range and its temperature dependence. Neutrality sits at 7 at 25 °C and shifts at other temperatures, because water's own ionisation is temperature-dependent — so a solution neutral at 25 °C is slightly basic at 100 °C. Strong acids and alkalis fall outside 0 and 14, which is a limit of the scale in water rather than of acidity.

definition: A physically distinct, uniform part of a system — the liquid in a bottle and the vapour above it are two phases of the same substance. A mixture of phases is what most things actually are, which is why the states are worth telling apart.
explanation: A phase is a physically distinct, uniform region, which is why most things are not one. A glass of water with ice in it is two phases of the same substance, an oil and water mixture is two, and a partly melted metal is two. The phase rule says that the number of phases that can coexist in equilibrium is fixed by the number of components, which is a surprisingly tight constraint and the reason a two-component system cannot have three phases except at one temperature and pressure.

definition: Glow that continues after the exciting light is switched off, because the energy was stored rather than radiated straight away. It differs from fluorescence, which stops the instant the light does, and the difference is how long the excited state lasts.
explanation: Phosphorescence and fluorescence differ only in how long the excited state survives, and the boundary is drawn at about a nanosecond — a convention rather than a law. Phosphorescent materials are what remain legible in a dark after switching off the light, which is why they are used on safety signage and on the dials that used to glow in the dark. Genuinely long-lived emission is not as common as the word suggests; the classic examples involve introducing a rare earth ion, and the rare earths are rare mainly because they are hard to separate.

definition: The element at number 15, essential to DNA and to ATP, and dangerous enough that the pure white form ignites in air. It is one of the few nutrients that cannot be recycled, so the phosphate in rock is worked out from agriculture to geology.
explanation: Phosphorus is one of very few elements with no biological recycling: phosphate is worked out from rock to agriculture to food and is never returned in a useful form, which is why phosphate rock is mined like an oil field. Pure white phosphorus ignites in air at 30 °C and is stored under water; the red form is stable and non-toxic; and the black form is the one with a layered structure and conducts electricity. All three are the same atoms arranged differently.

definition: A dense, silvery-white metal at number 78, resistant to corrosion and used as a catalyst, in jewellery, and in the pins of spark plugs. Spanish conquistadors found it as a contaminant of Colombian gold and called it platina, little silver.
explanation: Platinum is the most inert of the common metals and the most valuable, and the two facts are connected: nothing attacks it, so a reaction vessel lined with it survives almost anything. That inertness is what made it the catalyst of choice for a century, and its scarcity is why rhodium, palladium and platinum appear together in a catalytic converter. It was known to the pre-Columbian Egyptians and used by them for jewellery, and Columbus's third voyage was partly to find more of it.

definition: A radioactive actinide at number 94, made by bombarding uranium and fissile enough for a chain reaction in a reactor. It is warm to the touch from its own radioactivity, and it is the element that makes both nuclear power and nuclear weapons possible.
explanation: Plutonium is the element that makes both nuclear power and nuclear weapons possible, and it is defined by a property rather than by a discovery: it is fissile, so it can sustain a chain reaction on its own without the help of a heavier isotope. It is also warm to the touch, because its own radioactivity does the heating, and that heat has been used as a source of power in spacecraft. Its half-life is 24,000 years, which sets the timescale for everything else about it.

definition: Any of the group 15 elements: nitrogen, phosphorus, arsenic, antimony and bismuth, and moscovium. The word comes from the Greek for choking, because of what happens when arsenic or antimony is deliberately inhaled.
explanation: The pnicogens get their name from the Greek for choking, which records what arsenic and antimony do when their fumes are inhaled — a hazard that was occupational and known for centuries before it was measured. Their chemistry is otherwise ordinary: they need three more electrons to close a shell, so they form three bonds and a large family of oxoacids. Two of them, arsenic and antimony, are metalloids and the third, nitrogen, is a gas, which is the widest spread in any group.

definition: A covalent bond in which the shared electrons are pulled unevenly toward one atom, giving it a slight negative charge and the other a slight positive one. Every bond between different elements is polar to some degree, and the difference between them is a matter of degree rather than of kind.
explanation: Every bond between two different elements is polar to some degree, so polar and non-polar is a matter of degree rather than of kind. What matters is the polarity of the whole molecule, which need not follow from its bonds: carbon dioxide has two strongly polar bonds and is non-polar overall, because the molecule is linear and the dipoles cancel. Water is bent, so they do not, and that single geometric fact is why water dissolves salt.

definition: The uneven distribution of charge across a bond or a molecule, arising from a difference in electronegativity. It is why water dissolves salt and oil does not dissolve in it, and why a molecule can have ends that behave differently.
explanation: Polarity is the uneven distribution of charge that follows from a difference in electronegativity, and it is the single most useful concept for explaining why substances mix the way they do. Polar molecules attract each other and dissolve polar things; non-polar ones do not, which is why oil and water separate and why a non-polar solvent cannot dissolve a polar solute in any useful amount. Polarity also explains melting points: more polarity, more intermolecular attraction, higher melting point.

definition: A highly radioactive metal at number 84, discovered by Marie Curie and named for her homeland. It is intensely radioactive, self-heating enough to glow, and dangerous enough that handling it requires shielding and remote control.
explanation: Polonium is named for Marie Curie's homeland and was the substance with which she began her work, and it is among the most toxic materials known — lethal in amounts measured in micrograms. It self-heats to above 300 °C from its own radioactivity, which made it the first substance to demonstrate that radioactivity is itself a source of heat. It has been studied as a heat source for space missions and is otherwise avoided.

definition: A very large molecule built by repeating a smaller one thousands of times. Starch, DNA, nylon and polystyrene are all polymers, and their properties follow from the length of the chain and how its monomers are arranged.
explanation: A polymer's properties follow from three things: how long the chain is, how it branches, and how the chains sit relative to one another. Long and linear gives strength, as in polyethylene; branched chains cannot pack closely, which gives low-density flexibility; cross-linked gives rigidity and heat resistance, as in vulcanised rubber. The same monomer therefore yields quite different materials depending only on how the chains are arranged after polymerisation.

definition: Joining small molecules together into a chain, usually with a catalyst and often with nothing given off. Addition polymerisation opens a double bond; condensation polymerisation joins molecules and loses a small one each time.
explanation: The two kinds of polymerisation build different backbones and lose different things. Addition polymerisation opens a double bond and adds a monomer with nothing given off, so the product's mass is the sum of the monomers' — the reason nearly all of a plastic's mass came from crude oil. Condensation polymerisation joins molecules and releases a small one each time, so the product is lighter than its inputs, and it is how PET and nylon are made.

definition: An alkali metal at number 19, slightly less dense than water and prone to reacting with it. Its flame is the lilac that the flame test identifies it by, and its ions do a great deal of the work of keeping nerves and muscles working.
explanation: Potassium's flame is lilac, which is how the flame test distinguishes it from sodium's yellow, and the sodium in any sample will otherwise mask it completely — which is why the test is viewed through cobalt glass. Its ions do a great deal of the work of maintaining the resting membrane potential, and its shortage in soil is one of the commonest nutrient deficiencies, visible in a field as leaf scorching at the edges of older leaves. It reacts with water violently enough to ignite the hydrogen it releases.

definition: Energy stored in a position or a structure rather than in motion. A bond holds potential energy, releasing it as heat when the bond breaks, and an electron in a higher level holds more of it than one in a lower one.
explanation: Potential energy is energy held in a structure rather than in motion, and chemistry has three kinds of it that matter. Bonds hold energy that is released when they break. Electrons in higher levels hold more than electrons in lower ones, which is what an emission is. And a charge separated from an opposite one holds energy, which is what a battery has and what a lightning discharge releases. All three are released as heat or light when the structure relaxes.

definition: Making a part by pressing metal powder into a shape and sintering it. It produces parts that would be difficult to machine and uses less material than removing metal from a billet would.
explanation: Powder metallurgy makes parts by pressing metal powder into a shape and sintering it, and it exists because of what it avoids. No molten metal, so no tooling to withstand the heat; very little waste, because there is no billet to cut down; and a fine microstructure, because each powder particle starts small and does not grow. It is the standard route for small complex parts and for materials that would be difficult to machine in solid form.

definition: A rare earth metal at number 59 whose salts are green, and which is used in the glass of welding goggles to absorb infrared. The name means green twin, for the colour of its didymium salts.
explanation: Praseodymium's name means green twin and records a piece of history about how elements get named. Its salts are green, and when it was separated from what was then called didymium — a mixture of two elements with almost identical chemistry — the halves were named praseodymium and neodymium, green and new twin. Separating the two required dozens of fractional crystallisations, and they remain among the hardest of the rare earths to separate from each other.

definition: An insoluble solid that forms in a solution when two dissolved substances react, and settles out. Silver chloride is the classic case: mixing silver nitrate with sodium chloride turns the clear liquid cloudy at once.
explanation: Precipitation is a reaction producing an insoluble solid, and it is the clearest test for whether ions are present: silver chloride from silver nitrate and sodium chloride turns a clear solution cloudy at once. The direction depends on solubilities rather than on anything special about silver, and the same argument explains why barium sulfate works as a radiographic contrast agent — its solubility is low enough for the gut to clear it entirely. A precipitate is always a compound and never a mixture of the two ions.

definition: Force per unit area, measured in pascals, which is one newton on a square metre. Gas pressure is the constant push of the particles striking a surface, so it rises with temperature and falls as a gas is given more room.
explanation: Gas pressure is the constant bombardment of a surface by moving particles, which is why it rises with temperature and falls when a gas is given more room. That is also why pressure has a units problem that mass does not: it is force per area, so a gas squeezed into a smaller container at the same temperature has the same pressure if the same number of particles hit the same area — which is Boyle's law, and the first quantitative result in the field. The standard atmosphere is 101,325 Pa because that is what a barometer measures on a particular day.

definition: The English chemist who isolated oxygen in 1774 by heating mercuric oxide, a discovery he made while working on what he thought was an air. He also discovered the mild anaesthetic properties of nitrous oxide, and never thought either discovery was important.
explanation: Priestley found oxygen in 1774 by heating mercuric oxide, which he did while investigating what he thought was a kind of air, and he reported it as a curious property of a particular substance rather than as a new element. Joseph Priestley was also the inventor of soda water, the discoverer of the anaesthetic effect of nitrous oxide, and a chemist of such standing that Lavoisier, who did recognise the discovery's significance, had to argue the case for treating it as a new substance. He was also, and not separately, a political figure of some prominence, and his last years were shaped by that.

definition: A substance formed when a reaction happens, written after the arrow. The products of a reaction are new substances with their own properties, which is the whole test of whether a chemical change has occurred.
explanation: A product is what a reaction forms, and the distinction from a reactant is a one-way arrow rather than a matter of opinion. In an equilibrium reaction both sides are products and reactants simultaneously, which is why the notation changes. And what is written after the arrow is not necessarily what was isolated: a reaction may give three products where only one is wanted, which is why selectivity is one of the recurring difficulties in synthesis.

definition: The only radioactive lanthanide, and the only rare earth with no stable isotope, so it is made artificially in small amounts. It was once used in luminous paint, which is why it is found in abandoned factory sites.
explanation: Promethium is the only radioactive lanthanide and the only rare earth with no stable isotope, so it is made artificially in milligram quantities by irradiating neodymium. It was used in luminous paint in the 1960s and abandoned once its radioactivity was understood, which is why it is found in measurable quantities at abandoned factory sites. Its element name is the one place on this site where the periodic table reaches into mythology, and it was chosen deliberately: the element was taken from the earth, and named for the titan who stole fire.

definition: A radioactive actinide at number 91 that sits between thorium and uranium, and is rare because it decays quickly on both sides. It was one of the last elements to be isolated, which took a tonne-scale effort in the 1960s.
explanation: Protactinium sits between thorium and uranium in the actinide series and is rare because it decays quickly at both ends — its parents make it and its children consume it. It was one of the last elements to be isolated, and the achievement took a tonne-scale effort, which is a reminder that a rare element's practical limit is often the mass available rather than the difficulty of the chemistry. Protactinium-231 from uranium-238 decay is what led to the age of the earth being worked out.

definition: A positively charged particle in an atom's nucleus, whose count is the element's atomic number. It is about 1,836 times heavier than an electron and is itself made of two up quarks and one down quark.
explanation: The proton is a stable composite particle, two up quarks and one down, and it is one of the very few things in particle physics that does not decay. Its charge is positive by convention and its mass is about 1,836 electron masses, which is the reason a nucleus is so dense. In chemistry its count is the element; in acid–base chemistry 'proton' is shorthand for a hydrogen ion, which is a hydronium in water and the reason the pH scale exists.

definition: The movement of a hydrogen nucleus from one molecule to another without the electrons moving with it, which is the mechanism of every Brønsted–Lowry acid–base reaction. Water is unusually good at it, which is why it is the solvent for so much of chemistry.
explanation: Proton transfer is the mechanism of every Brønsted–Lowry acid–base reaction, and it is a separate step from electron transfer even though the two often happen together. Water is unusually good at it — its oxygen is small and its O–H bond is polar enough to give a proton up or take one — which is why so much chemistry happens in water and why water is a decent catalyst for reactions that do not obviously involve it. It is also why the proton has no independent existence in solution: it is always solvated.

definition: Separating a wanted substance from everything else, whether by recrystallisation, distillation, chromatography or washing. Almost any chemistry result is only as good as this step, and it is the step most often reported as done without being done.
explanation: Purification is the step that most often decides whether a result is real, and the step most often reported as done without being done. Recrystallisation for solids, distillation for liquids, washing for precipitates and chromatography for anything close — each is chosen by what the impurity is rather than by habit, since a procedure that removes one impurity frequently adds another. The honest test is a melting point or a boiling point that matches the literature, which is how you tell a pure compound from a clean-looking one.

definition: How completely a sample is the one substance it is claimed to be. Chemistry is measured in percentages of purity because almost nothing is entirely pure, and a 98% sample and a 99.9% sample can behave differently enough to matter.
explanation: Purity is quoted as a percentage and almost never means 100%, because almost nothing is entirely one substance. The distinction that matters in practice is between an impurity that is chemically inert and one that is not: 1% water in a solvent changes a reaction's rate and a 1% inert gas may change nothing. Analytical chemistry is largely the business of telling those two apart, and the phrase 'probably pure' usually means that nobody measured.

definition: The smallest discrete amount of a physical quantity that can exist independently, written for energy as E = hc/λ. In chemistry it is the reason electrons occupy energy levels rather than any energy at all.
explanation: Quantisation is why the periodic table has the shape it does. Electrons in an atom can only occupy particular energies, so an atom absorbs and emits light at particular wavelengths rather than at all of them, and the set of wavelengths is its spectrum. That discreteness also means an electron cannot sit at zero energy in an atom, which is one of several reasons the classical picture of an electron spiralling into a nucleus cannot be right.

definition: Heating steel and cooling it very rapidly in water or oil, which traps carbon in a hard, brittle structure. It is then followed by tempering, because quenched steel on its own would crack.
explanation: Quenching gives steel martensite, a structure in which carbon is trapped in the iron lattice rather than forming a compound, and martensite is hard and brittle. That brittleness is the problem: a quenched tool would crack under load, so tempering follows every time. The whole sequence — austenitise, quench, temper — is about getting hardness and toughness at once, which no single structure gives.

definition: The spontaneous breakdown of an unstable nucleus into a smaller one, emitting radiation as it goes. A given atom has a fixed chance of decaying in a given interval, which is why a sample's radioactivity falls rather than stopping at once.
explanation: A nucleus that decays does not do it slowly or on a schedule; each individual nucleus has a fixed chance in a fixed interval, and nothing about it can be predicted for a particular atom. What is predictable is the fraction of a large number that decays, which is why a sample's activity falls smoothly while its atoms behave randomly. Decay is also unaffected by temperature, pressure and chemical form, which is what makes it useful for dating rock and useless as a variable to control.

definition: A small amount of a radioactive isotope added to something so that its path can be followed. A tracer of a few atoms is enough to track where nitrogen ends up in a plant, or where iodine goes in the body, which no weighing could show.
explanation: A tracer follows a substance rather than measuring it, and its power is that a handful of atoms is enough. You cannot weigh the nitrogen a plant takes up, but you can feed it nitrogen-15 and follow that with a mass spectrometer. The technique is limited by the need for the isotope to be available and for the element to be one the body or the system does not treat specially, which is why carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and phosphorus are the usual choices.

definition: The spontaneous emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus. It does not depend on temperature or chemical form at all, which is why a radioactive sample stays radioactive whether it is frozen, dissolved or on the other side of the Earth.
explanation: Radioactivity is a property of the nucleus and is completely independent of what the element is doing chemically. A sample stays radioactive whether it is frozen, dissolved, ground up or on the other side of the Earth, because no chemical process reaches the nucleus. That is what makes it so useful for dating and for tracers, and it is also why it cannot be switched off — a fact that has done more to shape the last eighty years of politics than any chemical property.

definition: A radioactive alkaline earth metal at number 88, discovered by Marie Curie and named for radium's glow. It was painted onto watch dials in the 1920s and its unshielded workers suffered badly; it has no uses now beyond a few medical treatments.
explanation: Radium's history is one of the clearest cases of a discovery celebrated before it was understood. The Curies separated it from tonnes of pitchblende in 1902, and it was painted onto watch dials, added to toothpaste and put in patent medicines, because the glow was thought harmless and it was not. The women who worked with it suffered badly and the women who painted the dials suffered later; it is essentially abandoned now apart from a few narrow medical uses.

definition: A radioactive noble gas at number 86, produced in the ground by the decay of uranium and which seeps into basements. It is the second commonest cause of lung cancer after smoking, and the only one that is easily measured before it matters.
explanation: Radon is the second commonest cause of lung cancer after smoking and the only one that is straightforward to measure before it does harm, which is an odd combination for a hazard. It is produced by the decay of uranium in rock and soil and seeps into buildings through floors and cracks, so the amount varies enormously between neighbouring houses on the same street. The mitigation is simple and cheap — sealing the floor and ventilating the space — and it is not done often enough.

definition: How much reactant turns into product each second, which depends on concentration, temperature, surface area and any catalyst present. Raising the temperature speeds it up because more particles have the energy to get over the activation barrier.
explanation: A rate is a change in concentration over time, which means it is never a constant for a real reaction: reactants are used up, so the rate falls as the reaction proceeds unless something is continuously replacing them. It depends on concentration, temperature, surface area and catalyst, and the temperature dependence is large because it goes through the Arrhenius expression — which is why a ten-degree rise often roughly doubles a reaction's rate. A rate constant is a different quantity and does not depend on concentration.

definition: A substance that takes part in a reaction and is used up, written before the arrow. When a reactant runs out the reaction stops, however much of the other one is left.
explanation: A reactant is what goes in, and the stoichiometric ratio is what decides whether any of it is left over. A reaction scaled up from a test tube keeps the ratios and not the amounts, so doubling the largest quantity is what scales it — and using exactly the stoichiometric amounts is the hardest part of doing that in practice, because one reagent is usually a solution of known concentration and the other is a solid weighed out. Whatever is left over is the excess.

definition: A process in which one or more substances are turned into others, with bonds broken and others formed. It is written with reactants before an arrow and products after it, and the coefficients are the ratios in which they react.
explanation: A chemical reaction is defined by what changes at the electron level, not by what a reader notices. Bubbling, colour change and precipitation are evidence that something happened; the actual criterion is that different substances with different properties came out. That is why a reaction can happen with no visible sign at all, and why dissolving and burning are reactions while stirring water is not.

definition: Purifying a solid by dissolving it in hot solvent and cooling, so that the wanted substance crystallises out while impurities stay in solution. It works because solubility normally rises with temperature, and most impurities are present in too little to crystallise.
explanation: Recrystallisation purifies a solid by dissolving it in hot solvent and letting it cool, and it works for a reason that is worth stating: the solubility of most solids rises steeply with temperature, while impurities are present in too small an amount to crystallise at all. So the wanted substance comes out and the impurities stay in. It is why the crystals are large when the solution cools slowly and fine when it is cooled quickly, and why a good crystal is grown over days.

definition: Returning a material to use as raw material rather than discarding it. For metals it is often cheaper than extraction, because the ore has already been dug and refined once — which is why a tonne of aluminium scrap makes a tonne of new aluminium.
explanation: Recycling a metal is usually cheaper than extracting it, because the ore has already been dug, concentrated and refined once, and that fixed cost is not repeated. It is not always: aluminium recycling saves 95% of the energy of primary smelting, but lead recycling and lithium-ion battery recycling are harder and have been done in earnest only recently. The economics also depend on the price of the metal, which is why recycling a rare earth is harder than recycling gold.

definition: A reaction in which electrons move between two substances, so that one is oxidised and the other reduced at the same time. Rusting, burning and the working of a battery are all redox reactions, and so is respiration.
explanation: A redox reaction is a reaction in which electrons move, and every reaction of this kind has an oxidation matched to a reduction somewhere in the equation. That is not a convention but a consequence of charge being conserved: electrons do not appear from nowhere. Practically it means the pair must always be identified together — you cannot say what is oxidised without saying what is reduced — which is the single most common mistake in balancing redox equations by inspection.

definition: A substance that gives electrons to something else, and is itself oxidised. It is the partner of an oxidising agent.
explanation: A reducing agent is oxidised while reducing something else, which is the whole of its role and the reason the two names are always used together. Carbon and hydrogen are the commonest reducing agents in metallurgy, where their job is to take metal ions out of an ore. In the body, the reducing power of NADH is what carries electrons to the reactions that make ATP.

definition: Gaining electrons. It is not the same as losing mass, and the two ideas are locked together: whatever loses electrons in a reaction has to gain them elsewhere, so reduction always accompanies oxidation.
explanation: Reduction is gaining electrons, and the word contains an historical trap: it was coined when the theory said metals were reduced from their oxides by loss of oxygen, so the name came to mean loss of oxygen. When Lavoisier showed that it was gain of a gas instead, the name was kept because it had become too established to change. The partner to oxidation is unavoidable, and so reduction and oxidation always occur together.

definition: The proportion of light a surface sends back rather than absorbs. Metals reflect most visible light and absorb the rest, which is why they look shiny, and why their absorption heats them.
explanation: Metals' reflectivity is a consequence of having free electrons, and the same property makes them absorb what they do not reflect — which is what heats them. The correlation between a metal being shiny and being a good conductor is therefore not a coincidence but the same fact twice. Polishing increases reflectivity by removing the oxide layer that scatters light rather than returning it, so a polished metal and a freshly cleaned one are optically different in a way that a dull surface hides.

definition: What is left over once a reaction or an evaporation has finished. It is also the term for the ring of amino acids a protein folds into and the motif a protein needs in order to bind to a partner, which is the same word doing two quite different jobs.
explanation: Residue in chemistry means what is left once a process is finished, and its usefulness depends entirely on what it contains. A distillation's residue is the less volatile component, often still holding most of the material; a crystallisation's mother liquor holds everything that did not crystallise; and an organic reaction's residue is a mixture that has to be worked up before anything can be said about the product. Calling something a residue is a statement that the work is not finished, not that it is finished badly.

definition: One that can run forwards and backwards, the two reaching an equilibrium rather than finishing. It is written with a double arrow, and the conditions matter: ammonia needs high pressure to go towards ammonia rather than towards its elements.
explanation: A reversible reaction is written with a double arrow because it runs in both directions, and at equilibrium both are happening at the same rate. Three things determine where it settles — the equilibrium constant, the temperature, and any change in concentration — and the lever that industrial chemists reach for is almost always removing a product as it forms. The Haber process removes ammonia continuously, which is why it converts more than a batch equilibrium would and why it needs a continuous plant.

definition: One of the rarest elements in the earth's crust at number 75, and the last element to be discovered among those with a stable isotope. It is used in the superalloys of jet engine blades, and a few grams in a fleet is worth a considerable sum.
explanation: Rhenium has two remarkable scarcity facts that are worth knowing together. It was the last stable element to be discovered, in 1925, and it is one of the rarest in the crust — a few parts per billion. Yet it is in almost every jet engine, because superalloys containing rhenium hold their strength at turbine temperatures where every other alloy fails. The consequence is an aviation supply chain entirely dependent on one element found in a few places, recovered from turbine blades that have to be sent back for it.

definition: The rarest and most expensive of the platinum metals, and the main ingredient in the three-way catalytic converter, where it turns nitrogen oxides back into nitrogen. Platinum has been used as a catalyst since the 1830s and rhodium since the 1970s.
explanation: Rhodium is the rarest and most expensive of the platinum metals and it is there for one job: converting nitrogen oxides back into nitrogen in a catalytic converter. Platinum did that job alone until the 1970s, when rhodium proved substantially better and the whole fleet was retrofitted. That is why the price of rhodium has behaved as it has, and why emissions regulations written in terms of what a converter must remove have a direct effect on the price of a metal.

definition: Heating a sulfide ore in air so that the sulfur burns off as sulfur dioxide and the metal is left as its oxide. It is the first step in most metal extraction, and it is why sulfur dioxide from smelters is an air-pollution problem.
explanation: Roasting is the first step in most metal extraction and it is where the sulfur goes. A sulfide ore is heated in air and the sulfur burns off as sulfur dioxide, leaving the metal's oxide — which is why smelter emissions are a long-standing air-pollution problem and why sulfur dioxide from copper smelting is a regulated pollutant. What is left is then reduced, usually by carbon, in the smelter proper.
