definition: A synthetic element at number 111, named for Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays. It is the heaviest element to have had its chemistry studied in solution, which showed it behaving like the gold group above it.
explanation: Roentgenium is the heaviest element whose chemistry has been studied in solution, and it behaved as expected for once — like its group members rather than like the gas above it. That result is scientifically useful precisely because it was expected: it bounds where the table's predictions stop working, and the elements either side that do not behave are the interesting ones. Only a few dozen atoms have ever been made and it took months of beam time per atom.

definition: An alkali metal at number 37, the second-softest element and one of the two that ignite spontaneously in air. It has no stable isotope, which is why a rubidium–strontium clock, used to calibrate satellite navigation, measures it by counting decays.
explanation: Rubidium is one of the two elements that ignite spontaneously in air, and it is used as a rubidium–strontium clock in the navigation satellites because its decay is so regular it can be measured against itself — there is no stable isotope to use instead. That clock is why a GPS receiver knows where it is without being corrected by anything on the ground. On the ground, rubidium is used in photocells and in some lasers, and it is separated from caesium by a very small margin of chemistry.

definition: A hard, corrosion-resistant platinum-group metal at number 44, used to harden electrical contacts and as a catalyst. It hardens platinum so effectively that a few per cent makes an alloy that lasts far longer.
explanation: Ruthenium's value is that a few per cent of it makes platinum far more durable, and it does so by pinning the grain boundaries that would otherwise let the metal wear. That is why the catalytic converters and the fuel-cell anodes that are expected to last years contain it. It also hardens electrical contacts, which is why a connector rated for a high current may have a ruthenium contact where a cheaper alloy would not survive.

definition: The New Zealand physicist who discovered the atomic nucleus by firing alpha particles at gold foil and finding a few bounced almost straight back. He concluded the atom is mostly empty space, named the proton and the neutron, and split the atom deliberately in 1917.
explanation: Rutherford is the experimentalist who made the atom real, and the experiment was almost accidentally simple. Alpha particles fired at gold foil mostly went straight through, which killed the plum pudding model on its own, and a very few bounced back — implying an enormous mass concentrated in something much smaller than the atom. He went on to name the proton and the neutron, discover the atomic number, and split the nucleus deliberately in 1917; he was also the first to articulate artificial transmutation.

definition: The first of the transactinides, at number 104, and the first element made by colliding nuclei in a cyclotron rather than by neutron bombardment. It was named for Ernest Rutherford, who discovered the nucleus it sits in.
explanation: Rutherfordium is the first of the transactinides and the first element made by colliding nuclei in a cyclotron rather than by neutron bombardment, which is a change of technique as much as of discovery. Its chemistry has been studied in solution and it behaves like a heavier hafnium, as its group predicts. That is not a formality: at these atomic numbers the expectation could have gone the other way, and the elements either side it that behave unexpectedly are the ones being argued about.

definition: Containing salt, or saltier than seawater. A saline solution is the one isotonic with body fluids, which is why an intravenous drip is saline and not plain water.
explanation: Saline means saltier than seawater, and it is used both of a solution and of the practice of giving one. An intravenous drip is saline because a solution isotonic with body fluids is the only one a vein will accept — plain water moves into cells through the membrane and swells them, and concentrated saline pulls water out of them. It is also the base of the oral rehydration solution that has saved more lives than almost any other simple intervention in medicine.

definition: Any ionic compound whose ions are not hydrogen and hydroxide. Table salt is sodium chloride, but the definition is far wider than the kitchen: sodium carbonate and calcium nitrate are salts, and so is a compound of any metal and any acid.
explanation: Salt is not sodium chloride; it is any ionic compound whose ions are not hydrogen and hydroxide. Sodium carbonate, calcium nitrate and ammonium sulfate are all salts, and the term is a formal category rather than the kitchen one. That broader definition is what lets a chemist say a salt can be acidic or alkaline — ammonium chloride is a salt and its solution is acidic, because the ammonium ion is a weak acid.

definition: A rare earth metal at number 62 used in magnets that keep working at temperatures where neodymium magnets lose their strength. It was the element that made magnets with no nickel or cobalt possible.
explanation: Samarium's magnets are the ones that keep working when neodymium's do not. Neodymium loses its strength as the temperature rises; samarium-cobalt holds it several hundred degrees further, at the cost of being heavier and more brittle and much more expensive. That trade is worth it in a motor or a turbine and not in a pair of headphones, which is why the two appear in different machines rather than competing.

definition: The state of holding as much dissolved solute as can stay dissolved at that temperature. Adding more will not dissolve, and the extra sits at the bottom as undissolved solid until the solution is warmed.
explanation: A saturated solution is holding as much as it can and will take no more at that temperature, and the excess sits undissolved rather than refusing to go in. Raising the temperature usually lets more dissolve — so the solubility of most solids rises and that of most gases falls, which is why a warm soda fizzes more on opening and why a warm bottle of beer is flatter. Saturating a solution and then filtering is also a way of purifying it, since the impurities stay behind.

definition: A soft, light metal at number 21, rare and expensive, used in small amounts to make aluminium alloys stiffer. It is the first of the transition metals and the only one with no practical use of its own.
explanation: Scandium is the first transition metal and the one that turned out to be almost useless in its own right, which is an awkward result for an element in the middle of the d block. It is used in small amounts to make aluminium alloys stiffer, at a few tenths of a per cent, and that is genuinely the whole of the market. It is more abundant in the crust than lead and was not discovered until 1879, because it is so difficult to separate from the other rare earths.

definition: The Swedish chemist who discovered oxygen, chlorine, manganese, barium and hydrogen all at once, in the eight years before he died at fifty-one. He never got the credit, because he published in Swedish and because he was too poor to be listened to.
explanation: Scheele discovered oxygen, chlorine, hydrogen, manganese and barium in about eight years and got almost none of the credit. He published in Swedish, he was too poor to be taken seriously, and he insisted on publishing without the apparatus notes that would have let others verify him — so Priestley and Lavoisier got oxygen and he got a chapter nobody read. He died at fifty-one. It is the standard example in the history of chemistry of being right and not being heard.

definition: The physicist whose equation replaced Bohr's orbits with orbitals — regions where an electron is likely to be rather than paths it follows. It gives the shapes and relative energies of s, p, d and f orbitals, which is the whole basis of the orbital-configuration table on this site.
explanation: Schrödinger's equation replaced Bohr's orbits with orbitals and is the reason the orbital-configuration table on this site is not just a convention. It gives the shapes and relative energies of s, p, d and f orbitals from first principles, and the d orbital's five-fold degeneracy is why that block is five columns wide and why Hund's rule fills them singly first. It also produces the absurdity of the cat, which he intended as an argument against the Copenhagen reading rather than as a piece of physics.

definition: The first element named after a living person, at number 106, honouring Glenn Seaborg. The proposal was controversial and the naming of elements after people had been thought unlikely to happen again — it then happened twice more.
explanation: Seaborgium was the first element named after a living person, which at the time was considered impossible — the convention was that an element was named after something, a place or a property, and never after someone still able to be offended. The naming committee's reasoning was that the heavy elements had been produced by an international effort of the sort that needed the credit, and once the precedent was set it happened twice more: within a few years, roentgenium and oganesson were named for living people.

definition: The element at number 34, a semiconductor whose conductivity changes with light, which is what makes it useful in photocells. It is also toxic in concentrated form, so supplements are dosed carefully.
explanation: Selenium's conductivity rises sharply with light, which is what makes it a photoconductor and what put it in the first photocopy machines as the drum. It is also an essential trace element, required in small amounts and toxic in larger ones, so the same property that makes supplements necessary makes them dosed. Its compounds are red and poisonous — a drop of selenium bromide on the skin burns, which is a legacy of glass manufacture and metallurgy.

definition: A material that conducts electricity far better than an insulator and far worse than a metal, and whose conductivity can be controlled by doping. Silicon is the one the whole electronics industry is built on, precisely because it has this middle behaviour.
explanation: A semiconductor is defined by being neither conductor nor insulator and, crucially, by having a conductivity you can set deliberately. Adding a few phosphorus atoms to silicon gives it free electrons in a controlled concentration; adding boron gives free holes. That tunability is what makes a chip possible — the whole of digital electronics is the business of arranging two types of semiconductor into switches, and no other material offers that combination of control and reliability.

definition: An element with properties between a metal's and a non-metal's, such as silicon, germanium and arsenic. Some are semiconductors rather than semimetals in the strict sense, and the term is used loosely for both.
explanation: A semimetal in the strict sense conducts less well than a metal and more than an insulator, and the elements usually meant are silicon, germanium and arsenic. The term is used more loosely for the metalloids, and the overlap is a reminder that the metal–non-metal boundary is a real physical gradient rather than a line. The practical consequence is that a metalloid's oxide is acidic where a metal's would be basic, and its elemental form is brittle where a metal's would be malleable.

definition: One of the energy levels around a nucleus, holding a set number of electrons: two in the first, eight in the second, and more in the rest. The outermost shell and its occupancy decide which group an element belongs to and how it reacts.
explanation: A shell is an energy level, and its capacity is set by how many orbitals it holds and how many electrons fit in each: two, eight, eighteen, thirty-two. That sequence is the whole reason the periods of the table have those lengths. The outermost occupied shell is the one that matters chemically, since it is the only one taking part in bonding, and the number of electrons in it is what puts an element in a group. Inner shells are nearly inert and are why the heavier elements in a group behave alike despite very different masses.

definition: The SI unit of biological effect, one joule per kilogram weighted for the type of radiation. It is the unit radiation limits are written in, and a whole-body dose of about five sieverts is usually fatal.
explanation: The sievert is the unit radiation limits are written in, and it is the unit that accounts for biological effect rather than merely for energy deposited. A gray of alpha and a gray of X-rays do very different amounts of damage, so the sievert multiplies by a factor for the type of radiation — which is why a neutron therapy is quoted in a much smaller number of sieverts than an X-ray therapy of the same intent. Five sieverts to the whole body is usually fatal.

definition: A covalent bond formed by orbitals overlapping head-on along the line between the two atoms. It is the strongest kind and every single bond is one, which is why a triple bond is one sigma and two pi rather than three sigma.
explanation: A sigma bond is a bond formed by orbitals overlapping along the line between the two atoms, and there is one in every single bond. It is the strongest kind because the overlap is head-on, so any double or triple bond is one sigma plus weaker pi bonds rather than two or three sigmas. That is the reason a double bond is more reactive than a single one and not twice as strong: the extra bond is the weak one and it sticks out sideways where an attacking molecule can reach it.

definition: The metalloid at number 14, and after oxygen the most abundant element in the earth's crust. Nearly every integrated circuit in the world is grown from it, and it is also the main ingredient of sand and of silicones.
explanation: Silicon is the material the electronics industry is made of, and its pre-eminence is a result of four properties rather than one: it is the second most abundant element in the crust, it forms a near-perfect oxide, its oxide is a good insulator, and it can be grown as a crystal of extraordinary purity. Those together made it possible to grow a crystal with no defects at the scale of a wafer, which is the actual requirement. It is also the main component of sand and of the silicones.

definition: The best conductor of heat and electricity there is, and the element at number 47. Its conductivity is beaten only by copper among practical metals, and unlike copper it does not corrode, which is why contacts and plating use it.
explanation: Silver conducts heat and electricity better than any other element, which is a persistent puzzle, because it is not the most mobile electron and it is not the lightest atom. The answer involves how tightly the conduction electrons are bound and how the lattice scatters them. Silver is also the most reflective element, which is why it was the mirror coating until glass replaced it, and its antibacterial activity has put it in catheters and dressings, where it works by disrupting the bacteria's chemistry rather than by killing it chemically.

definition: Heating a compacted powder until its particles bond without melting, which is how ceramic parts and some metal parts are made. It gives a very fine structure, and the shrinkage during sintering has to be allowed for in the die.
explanation: Sintering joins a compacted powder without melting it, so the part does not go through a liquid stage — which means no shrinkage beyond what the densification itself causes, and a very fine microstructure. That microstructure is why sintered parts are strong: the grain size is limited by the powder particle size, which can be micrometres. The trade is that porosity has to be controlled and the shapes must be simple, so sintering is usually followed by a machining step for the critical dimensions.

definition: The solid waste that floats on top of molten metal during smelting, made of the flux and of the impurities it carried off. It is glassy and much less dense than the metal, which is why the two separate so cleanly.
explanation: Slag is the reason a blast furnace is a chemical plant rather than a kiln. The iron comes down as a molten metal and the unwanted silica comes up as a glassy mass with the flux, and the two separate because one is much less dense than the other. Some slag is used — as a cement component, as road aggregate, and as a source of vanadium and rare earths — and the rest has to be dealt with, which is a large waste stream for every tonne of iron made.

definition: Heating an ore with something to combine with the unwanted part so that the metal comes out. Almost every metal extraction is a redox reaction of this sort, and the carbon monoxide generated is the same reaction in reverse.
explanation: Smelting is a reduction carried out in a furnace, and it is the step that separates metallurgy from mining. The metal is usually reduced by carbon or by carbon monoxide, and that is exactly the reaction that happens when carbon burns — so the exhaust of a smelter is largely the same gas that heats it. Where a metal is too reactive for carbon to reduce, as with aluminium, the melt has to be electrolyzed instead, which is a different process with the same goal.

definition: A soft, reactive alkali metal at number 11, soft enough to cut with a knife and stored under oil because it reacts with damp air. Combined with chlorine it gives the one compound everybody uses every day: table salt.
explanation: Sodium is the metal that makes the alkali metals look tame. It is soft enough to cut with a knife and it reacts with water so violently that the hydrogen it releases usually ignites, so it is stored under oil and handled with a dry tool. In seawater it is present at about 10,000 times the concentration of its element in the crust, which is the clearest demonstration of how thoroughly the world's water has been processed by geology.

definition: A resin or acid that clears oxidation off a metal before solder will wet it. Solder does not stick to an oxide layer, which is why flux is essential to the joint rather than a convenience.
explanation: Flux exists because solder will not wet a clean metal and will happily stick to an oxide — which is the opposite of what a soldered joint needs. Tin and lead solders alloy with the copper and form a metallurgical bond, but only where the surface is bare, so the flux removes the oxide as part of the operation. A fluxless solder is possible in electronics and works in a controlled atmosphere; on a workbench you want the acid or resin flux.

definition: A state in which particles are held in a fixed arrangement and can only vibrate in place. That gives solids a fixed shape and volume, and it is why a solid can have a melting point rather than a range.
explanation: A solid is defined by its particles having fixed positions and only vibrating in place, and that gives it a shape and a volume rather than merely a volume. It also gives it a melting point rather than a range — in a pure substance, since a real polycrystalline solid melts over an interval as different grains melt at slightly different temperatures. Diamond is solid because its particles are fixed by covalent bonds; sand is solid because its particles are fixed by friction and are not chemically bonded at all.

definition: A solid in which atoms of one element sit in the lattice of another without changing it — brass is copper with zinc dissolved in it. Above a solubility limit the phases separate, and the alloy becomes brittle.
explanation: A solid solution is one element dissolved in another's lattice without changing it, and it is the basis of every alloy that is not an intermetallic compound. Brass is copper with zinc in it; steel is iron with carbon dissolved and in part bonded. Above a solubility limit the two separate into distinct phases, and the alloy becomes brittle — which is why a solder's composition matters and why some of them are specified to a narrow range.

definition: How much of a substance dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature. It is usually quoted in grams per 100 grams of water, and for most solids it rises with temperature while for gases it falls.
explanation: Solubility is quoted in grams per 100 grams of solvent at a stated temperature, and the temperature is not optional: it rises steeply with temperature for most solids and falls for gases. The gas case has a familiar consequence — a warm bottle of beer fizzes more when opened, because the gas was less soluble and stayed in solution under pressure. What solubility cannot do is separate two dissolved substances, which is why it is often combined with filtration or crystallisation rather than used instead of them.

definition: The equilibrium constant for a sparingly soluble ionic compound dissolving, written as the product of the ion concentrations raised to their powers. It is constant at a given temperature and says nothing about how fast the dissolving happens.
explanation: The solubility product is the equilibrium constant for a sparingly soluble salt dissolving, written as the ion concentrations raised to their powers, and it is constant at a given temperature and independent of how much solid is present. Its practical use is that it lets you predict a precipitate: add two solutions and compare the ion product with Ksp, and if it exceeds it something comes out. It also explains why a common-ion effect suppresses solubility — adding more of one ion makes the salt want to come out of solution.

definition: The substance that has dissolved in a solvent — the sugar in a solution of sugar in water. What it dissolves in is the solvent, and the result is the solution.
explanation: A solute is what has dissolved, and the distinction between a solute and a solvent is about relative amount rather than about any chemical property. Water dissolving salt gives salt the solute and water the solvent, but dissolve water in a lot of salt and the roles reverse. What does matter chemically is the particle size: dissolved at the molecular or ionic level is a solution and cannot be filtered, while dispersed in larger particles is a suspension and settles.

definition: A mixture in which a solute is dispersed through a solvent at the particle level, so that neither can be separated by filtering. It is clear and homogeneous, which distinguishes it from a suspension, which settles.
explanation: A solution is homogeneous at the particle level, which is the test that distinguishes it from a suspension and from a colloid — both of which scatter light and both of which will eventually separate. A true solution also has a fixed composition at a given temperature, which is why it can be quoted as a concentration and why a saturated solution has a maximum. Anything clear is not necessarily a solution: gin and vodka are solutions, orange juice is a colloid.

definition: The substance a solute dissolves in, and the one present in the larger amount. Water is the usual one, and its polarity is the reason it dissolves so many ionic and polar compounds and so few non-polar ones.
explanation: Water is the default solvent because of its polarity and its hydrogen bonding, and both point the same way: it dissolves ions and polar molecules and very little else. That is why salt dissolves and oil does not, and why an ionic compound only conducts when dissolved or molten — the ions need to be free to move. Organic solvents are chosen for the opposite property, dissolving things water cannot, and they are nearly all flammable.

definition: The energy needed to raise one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius. Water's is unusually high, which is why a hot pan of water cools slowly and why it is such an effective coolant.
explanation: Water's specific heat capacity is about ten times that of most substances, and that single fact shapes a surprising amount. It makes water a good coolant, it makes oceans slow to heat and slow to cool, and it is why a hot pan of water does not scald as badly as a hot pan of metal while feeling far hotter. The units are per gram per degree, so a kilogram of water needs 4.18 kilojoules to move one degree, which is about the energy in a teaspoon of tea.

definition: Identifying a substance by the wavelengths it absorbs or emits, and finding how much of it is present from how strongly it absorbs. It is the most direct evidence there is for what a bond is doing, because it measures light rather than inferring it.
explanation: Spectroscopy is the most direct evidence in chemistry because it measures light rather than inferring from what happened. The wavelengths an atom absorbs and emits come from its energy gaps, so the spectrum identifies the element and the intensity says how much is there. That combination — identification and quantification from the same measurement — is why it displaced wet chemistry for most of what it now does, and why flame emission and UV–visible absorption are now standard analytical tools.

definition: Nuclear fuel that has been used in a reactor and must be stored or disposed of. A tonne of it contains less heat energy than a litre of oil but remains dangerously radioactive for thousands of years, and no country has yet opened a permanent repository.
explanation: A tonne of spent fuel holds less usable energy than a litre of oil and stays dangerously radioactive for thousands of years, which is the central awkwardness of nuclear power and not a flaw in the fuel. It is also small in volume — a reactor's entire lifetime output is a few cubic metres of it — so it is not a space problem. The problem is that no country has yet opened a permanent repository, which means every reactor's waste is stored on site while the argument continues.

definition: An intrinsic angular momentum of an electron, quantised in two values, which is not a literal rotation of anything. It exists so that two electrons can share an orbital without being in identical states.
explanation: Spin is an intrinsic property rather than a rotation, and it was introduced to explain an observation — the doublet lines in the spectrum of sodium — that the existing model could not. What it buys is the Pauli exclusion principle: two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins, so an orbital holds exactly two, and that is where every shell capacity on this site comes from.

definition: A fixed temperature and pressure at which gas volumes are quoted so that numbers can be compared, conventionally 0 °C and 1 atmosphere. The abbreviation matters because there is also a modern convention of 25 °C, and the two give different volumes.
explanation: There are two conventions in use and they give different numbers, which is worth knowing before comparing a figure to a textbook. The older one is 0 °C and 1 atm, and it is what a gas volume quoted at STP uses; the newer is 25 °C and 1 bar, which is more nearly a real laboratory. A molar gas volume is 22.4 dm³ at the old conditions and 24.0 at the new, and the difference is entirely the temperature.

definition: The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is made from its elements in their standard states. It is tabulated as zero for the elements themselves, which makes it possible to calculate the enthalpy of any reaction that follows.
explanation: Every tabulated standard enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change for making one mole from the elements in their standard states, which is why every element's own value is defined as zero. That single convention makes any reaction's enthalpy a sum of tabulated numbers rather than a measurement. The 'standard' matters: one bar, usually at 25 °C, and the state of each substance has to be the one actually used — gaseous water and liquid water differ by 2 kJ per mole, which matters when you are adding them up.

definition: Whether a substance is a solid, liquid or gas. Which one it is depends on the balance between the forces between its particles and the energy they have, and adding heat usually moves it along the sequence.
explanation: The three states are distinguished by how much energy is going into motion rather than into breaking attractions. In a solid the energy goes into vibration; in a liquid some goes into motion as well, so particles slide past one another; in a gas most of it does, and particles separate entirely. That is why heating a solid past its melting point raises the potential energy first — the temperature does not change during the transition, which is what latent heat is.

definition: The arithmetic of a chemical equation: working out from the balanced equation how much of each substance is needed or produced. It is bookkeeping with the whole point that atoms are conserved, and it is how a reaction is scaled from a test tube to a plant.
explanation: Stoichiometry is the arithmetic of a balanced equation, and it rests entirely on the law of conservation of mass. The coefficients give the ratio of moles, molar masses convert those to masses, and a molarity converts them to a volume. Almost every calculation in practical chemistry is one of these three operations, and the commonest mistake is to convert a mass to moles and then to treat it as a volume.

definition: An acid that gives up its hydrogen ions almost completely in water. Strong does not mean concentrated — the two are independent, and a dilute strong acid is a weaker acid than a concentrated weak one.
explanation: Strong and concentrated are independent, and confusing them is the standard error. A strong acid is one that dissociates essentially completely in water, which is a statement about its Ka and not about how much of it there is. A dilute solution of a strong acid is a weaker acid than a concentrated solution of a weak one, and the pH of a strong acid approaches zero as it becomes concentrated rather than rising.

definition: A base that takes up protons completely in water, so its solution ends up with hydroxide ions at full concentration. Sodium hydroxide is one; ammonia is a weak base for the opposite reason.
explanation: A strong base is one that takes up protons essentially completely in water, so the solution ends up with hydroxide ions at full concentration. Sodium hydroxide is strong; ammonia is weak, and it is weak precisely because it is a small uncharged molecule rather than an ion, so it has to be deprotonated to react. That is why ammonia's solution is basic at all — a small equilibrium that runs a little way rather than a large one that runs all the way.

definition: A metal at number 38 that burns with a crimson flame, which is what gives fireworks and road flares their colour. Its compounds were once used in toothpaste and are now avoided for that reason.
explanation: Strontium's crimson flame is what makes it the ingredient in road flares, fireworks and the red in a warning flare, and it comes from the same two lines in the spectrum that give lithium its red and barium its green. Its salts were in toothpaste for decades as an anti-sensitivity agent and were removed once it was shown to be carcinogenic at the concentrations used — a case where a compound's usefulness and its safety are entirely separate questions. Strontium-90 is a particularly unpleasant fission product, because bone and milk concentrate it.

definition: A solid turning straight to vapour without passing through a liquid. Iodine does it on purpose, and dry ice does it by necessity, because carbon dioxide has no liquid phase at ordinary pressure at all.
explanation: Sublimation is a solid going straight to vapour, and it happens because the intermolecular forces are weak enough that a molecule can escape from the solid surface without melting. Iodine does it visibly, and the violet vapour is how iodine is identified. Carbon dioxide does it because it has no liquid phase at atmospheric pressure at all, which is why dry ice chills rather than cools. It is also a preservation method, because the water leaves with nothing behind for microbes to grow on.

definition: A reaction in which one atom or group is swapped for another in a molecule while the rest stays put. It is the main way organic molecules are modified, and it is why halogenated compounds are so useful in pharmaceuticals.
explanation: Substitution is the main way organic molecules are modified, because it swaps one group for another while leaving the framework intact. That is what makes the halogenated compounds so useful in drugs — a hydrogen is replaced by a chlorine and the molecule's shape changes in a small, predictable way. It also produces a hydrogen halide as a by-product, which is why substitution needs a base to mop it up and why it competes with elimination.

definition: A yellow solid at number 16, one of a handful of elements known since antiquity and the main component of vulcanised rubber. It burns to a choking gas, which is most of what is unpleasant about it.
explanation: Sulphur is one of a handful of elements known since antiquity, yellow, and it is the crosslinker that turns sticky natural rubber into the durable material it is on every tyre. That reaction needs about 30% sulphur by mass, which makes rubber the largest single use of the element by far. Burning it gives the choking sulfur dioxide that makes it a poor fuel, and its compounds go into fertilisers, sulphuric acid and pesticides.

definition: A nickel-based alloy that keeps its strength at temperatures where ordinary metals would melt or soften, and so goes in turbine blades. It is a deliberately expensive material used where a failure would stop an aircraft.
explanation: A superalloy is defined by holding its strength at temperatures where ordinary metals would have softened, and the design problem is that strength usually comes from precipitates that dissolve at exactly the temperature you need them at. The alloys in a turbine blade are therefore engineered to be stable where they are used, and their lives are quoted in cycles and hours rather than in years. It is a deliberately expensive material used where a failure would stop an aircraft.

definition: A material that conducts electricity with no resistance at all below a critical temperature. Some also expel magnetic fields, which is why a magnet hovers above them, and this is what makes MRI scanners and maglev trains possible.
explanation: A superconductor conducts with no resistance below a critical temperature, and some also expel magnetic fields, which is the second and more visible property. That expulsion is why a magnet hovers above one, and it is what makes MRI scanners possible: a superconducting magnet at a few kelvin is far stronger than a permanent magnet and needs no cooling power once it is cold. The barrier has always been the critical temperature, and the last thirty years have been about raising it.

definition: A process that can be kept up indefinitely without exhausting its inputs or ruining its surroundings. For an element this usually comes down to whether it can be recycled, and whether its ore will last.
explanation: Sustainability for an element usually reduces to two questions that are easy to confuse: is the ore going to last, and can the material be recovered when it has been used. Recycling answers the second and it very often answers the first too, since recycled metal does not consume ore at all. Titanium, rare earths and lithium are the ones where both answers are currently unfavourable, and they are the ones most likely to constrain a technology before the geology does.

definition: Making a substance from simpler ones, whether that means joining elements in a laboratory or assembling molecules from precursors in living cells. A synthesis is only a synthesis if the new substance did not exist in the starting materials.
explanation: A synthesis builds a substance from simpler ones, and the chemist's word for the desired compound being made is the target. Synthetic chemistry is distinguished from what the cell does in one important respect: a synthesis is planned backwards from the target, disconnecting bonds to find something you can make, and that planning is most of the intellectual work. It is also distinguished from isolation, which merely separates something that already exists.

definition: A metal at number 73 that is completely immune to body fluids and does not corrode, which is why surgical implants and capacitor plates use it. It is named for Tantalus, whose punishment was water he could never drink.
explanation: Tantalum's oxide is one of the most chemically inert substances known — it resists acids and alkalis and is unharmed by body fluids, which is why surgical implants are made of it. Capacitors use it for the same reason: a thin layer of tantalum oxide is an excellent dielectric, and it is what makes small high-value capacitors possible. Its ore is coltan, and the supply chain from the Congo has made the metal a subject of conflict regulation and of conflict.

definition: The dulling of a metal's surface by a thin layer of oxide or sulphide — silver going black with hydrogen sulphide, copper going green. Unlike rust it usually stays bonded, so the metal underneath is protected rather than eaten away.
explanation: Tarnishing is the dulling of a metal by a thin layer of its own oxide or sulphide, and unlike rust it usually stays bonded to the surface, so the metal underneath is protected rather than eaten away. Silver blackens with hydrogen sulphide in the air, copper greens with a carbonate patina, and both are stable. That is why a copper roof outlasts the fasteners holding it — and why the fasteners, being a different metal, corrode instead.

definition: The lightest element with no stable isotope, so it occurs only as decay products and must be made artificially. Its isotope technetium-99m is used in medical imaging because it decays in about six hours, leaving almost nothing behind.
explanation: Technetium has no stable isotope and its longest-lived, technetium-98, lasts about four million years, so any technetium present now was made recently. It matters because technetium-99m decays in about six hours while emitting gamma rays, which is close to ideal for medical imaging: enough radiation to be detected from outside the body, gone within a day. That combination is why it displaced the older tests, which required days of exposure.

definition: A rare metalloid at number 52, brittle and toxic, used in thermoelectric materials and in a compound that has become one of the more effective solar cells ever made. The name comes from tellus, the earth.
explanation: Tellurium is a rare metalloid and the element with two of the most useful compounds in solar cells: one of the first cadmium telluride panels is still among the highest-efficiency ones in production. It is also among the rarest elements in the crust, and cadmium telluride's supply chain runs through tellurium's, which is a constraint on a technology that is otherwise made from silicon. Its name comes from tellus, the earth, which is a rare piece of honest naming.

definition: A measure of how energetic the particles of a substance are on average, on a scale where the reading is proportional to that energy. It is measured directly, and it is not the same quantity as heat.
explanation: Temperature measures the average motion of the particles and heat measures how much energy they carry, so a large body at a low temperature can hold more heat than a small one at a high one — which is why a swimming pool is harder to heat than a bath and harder to cool. Absolute temperature is proportional to that average energy, which is why the kelvin scale's zero is meaningful and the Celsius scale's is not.

definition: Reheating quenched steel to a lower temperature and cooling it again, which softens it slightly and relieves the internal stresses that would otherwise crack it. Steel is never finished by quenching alone.
explanation: Tempering is what makes quenched steel usable. Quenching traps carbon in the iron lattice and gives martensite, which is very hard and very brittle; reheating it to a few hundred degrees lets some carbon precipitate out as a carbide, relieving the internal stresses and reducing the brittleness. The temperature sets the final properties and is quoted as a trade-off — lower for hardness, higher for toughness — so 'tempered to 200 °C' is a specification rather than a step.

definition: A synthetic element at number 117, named for Tennessee, and the second-heaviest element yet made. It sits below astatine in group 17, where its properties were predicted to differ from astatine's because of relativity's effects on its electrons.
explanation: Tennessine is the second-heaviest element yet made and the second element named after a place in the United States, following tennessine's heavier partner. It sits below astatine in group 17, and the prediction that matters is that it may not behave like astatine: relativistic effects at this atomic number are large enough that the valence electrons are differently bound, so its chemistry may resemble a metalloid rather than a halogen. Only a few atoms exist and none of its chemistry has been measured.

definition: A rare earth metal at number 65 used in the green phosphor of older displays and in magnetostrictive materials that turn shape when magnetised. It is rare and expensive because separating it from its neighbours is difficult.
explanation: Terbium is used in the green phosphor of older displays and in magnetostrictive materials that change shape when a magnetic field is applied, which is how some sonar transducers and ultrasound probes work. It is also the element that moves a neodymium magnet's operating temperature, in the form of a diffusion alloy that raises its Curie point. All of that depends on separating it from gadolinium and dysprosium, which is expensive and which makes terbium one of the more supply-constrained elements in use.

definition: A soft grey metal at number 81 that is almost indistinguishable from lead, and was therefore used as rat poison for decades until it was banned. It is also among the most toxic of all elements by mass.
explanation: Thallium was used as rat poison for decades because it was tasteless and had no antidote, and its replacement was a matter of will rather than of efficacy — the ban was long overdue. It is among the most toxic elements by mass, and its danger comes partly from looking enough like potassium to be taken up by cells in its place. Modern uses are few, though thallium-201 is still used in some medical imaging because of the way its gamma emission behaves.

definition: How well a substance carries heat. Metals do it well because their electrons are free to move and carry energy with them, and diamond does it well for the opposite reason, through stiff lattice vibrations — the same value as an electrical insulator and a good thermal conductor is one of chemistry's nicer oddities.
explanation: Diamond conducts heat about five times better than copper and conducts no electricity at all, which is the most useful single fact about it as a material. The reason is that its atoms are small and identical and bonded stiffly, so a temperature difference is carried away by lattice vibrations with very little scattering. Copper conducts well because its free electrons carry the energy. Both are conduction, and they have almost nothing in common — which is why 'conductivity' has to say which.

definition: The increase in volume a substance undergoes when it is heated. Most expand, because the particles move further apart; water is the exception between 0 and 4 °C, which is why a lake freezes from the top down and pipes burst in winter.
explanation: Most substances expand when heated, because the particles move further apart and the average separation grows. Water is the exception between 0 and 4 °C, where its density is maximal — which is why a lake freezes from the surface down, and why aquatic life survives a winter under a lid of ice while water in a pipe freezes and splits the pipe. The expansion also has to be allowed for in bridges and railway rails, which is why they have joints.

definition: The study of energy, heat and the direction changes run in. Its two laws say energy cannot be destroyed and that entropy tends to increase, which together explain why some reactions are spontaneous and others will not run however long one waits.
explanation: Thermodynamics answers whether a process will run and where it settles; kinetics answers how fast. The first law says energy is conserved, the second says entropy of a system plus its surroundings increases, and between them they explain why some reactions go to completion, some stop at an equilibrium, and some will not run at all however long one waits. Their scope is narrower than it looks — they say nothing about rate, which is why a thermodynamically favoured reaction can be too slow to matter.

definition: The physicist who in 1897 showed that the cathode rays emitted by a tube are streams of particles a thousandth the mass of a hydrogen atom, and that the atom therefore has parts. His name is now also the SI unit of magnetic flux density.
explanation: Thomson is the physicist who showed the atom had parts, and the measurement was the elegant part. He found cathode rays bent by magnetic and electric fields and computed the mass-to-charge ratio of the particles, obtaining a value about 1,800 times lighter than a hydrogen atom. So the atom had to contain something much smaller than itself, and that something was the electron. He is also the namesake of the SI unit of magnetic flux density, and he deserved it.

definition: A radioactive metal at number 90, three times as abundant as uranium and once used in gas mantles. Molten salt reactors are designed to burn it, which is what makes it a possible fuel rather than a waste.
explanation: Thorium is about three times as abundant as uranium in the crust and it breeds fissile material, which is why molten salt reactors are designed to burn it. It was also used in gas mantles until the thorium dioxide in them proved mildly radioactive. It cannot be used as a bomb fuel without breeding first, which is exactly what makes it attractive as a reactor fuel and a bad actor's choice — a fact that has been publicly discussed by people who should know better.

definition: The least abundant of the rare earths, at number 69, and the last one before lutetium. It is used in portable X-ray sources, which is a consequence of an element nobody has much of.
explanation: Thulium is the least abundant of the rare earths, at a few parts per million, and it is used in portable X-ray sources — which is a consequence of an element nobody has much of. Its most efficient transition is also unusually clean, which is why a tunable laser using it exists at all. The scarcity is a consequence of the same separation difficulty as every lanthanide: thulium sits between two heavier ones with almost the same chemistry.

definition: A soft, silvery metal at number 50, one of the first metals anyone worked because it melts at such a low temperature. Its alloys with copper give bronze and with lead give solder, and it plates the steel of food cans.
explanation: Tin has been worked since about 3,500 BC, which is remarkable given that it melts at 232 °C — low enough for a bronze-age furnace. Alloys with copper give bronze, which is what made metal tools possible; alloys with lead give solder, which is what made electronics possible. It has one notorious property: tin pest, in which tin below about 13 °C slowly turns to a grey powder, which is why old soldered joints on cathedral organs fail and why lead-free solder exists.

definition: A metal at number 22, as strong as steel at half the weight, and inert enough to be used in implants that stay in the body for decades. Its oxide layer is what makes it so hard to corrode.
explanation: Titanium has the strength-to-weight ratio of steel and is inert enough to be implanted in the body, which is why it is in hip joints, dental implants and aircraft. The oxide layer is the reason: a few nanometres of titanium dioxide is stable, self-repairing and impermeable, so the metal underneath does not corrode. Making it affordable was a twenty-year problem, since extracting it from ore requires the Kroll process, and that difficulty is why titanium is still not used structurally in cars.

definition: Adding a solution of known concentration to one of unknown until a colour change marks the endpoint, then working out the amount present from the volumes used. It is how the concentration of an acid or a peroxide is found to four figures.
explanation: Titration is the most accurate technique in practical chemistry and the one that depends least on judgement, because it ends in an unambiguous colour change rather than a judgement about shade. What it measures is concentration, by adding a solution of known concentration until the reaction is exactly complete. Volumetric glassware is calibrated to contain a stated volume at a stated temperature, which is why a titration done with warm glassware gives a slightly wrong answer.

definition: A quantity present at the limit of what can be detected, usually below a part per million. It is the level at which an element is present in the environment but not in anyone's diet, and where most of the periodic table's rarest elements actually are.
explanation: A trace amount is at the limit of detection, and it is where most of the periodic table's rarest elements actually are: present, measurable with care, and irrelevant to any chemistry that happens. It is also the level at which an element's effect changes character — essential in parts per million and toxic in parts per thousand, which is a real and frequently exploited distinction in nutrition. Reporting a detection limit alongside a result is what makes the number mean anything.

definition: An element present in a body or the environment at a tiny concentration, in parts per million or less. Some are essential in those amounts and toxic in larger ones, which is the same element behaving differently by quantity rather than by nature.
explanation: A trace element is present at a tiny concentration, and the interesting cases are the ones where essential and toxic differ only in quantity. Selenium, chromium, copper and iodine are all required in fractions of a milligram and harmful in tens. It is also the level at which a deficiency disease and a poisoning look identical in their early stages, which is part of why they are confused in medicine. Copper deficiency and Wilson's disease are the same condition with different causes.

definition: An element in the d block whose atoms or ions can use more than one of the d electron numbers. It is why these elements form coloured compounds, catalyse reactions, and give tough alloys — several unrelated properties from one unfilled shell.
explanation: The transition metals are defined by a partly filled d shell, and that one fact gives them colours, catalysis, variable oxidation states and tough alloys. The colours come from d–d transitions absorbing visible light; the catalysis from surfaces holding intermediate states; the variable oxidation states from the d electrons being close enough in energy to move. None of that applies to a metal with a full shell, which is why aluminium and zinc behave so much more predictably than their neighbours.

definition: Turning one element into another by changing its nucleus. It cannot happen by ordinary chemical means, because the electron arrangement is untouched by chemistry — it needs bombardment with neutrons or other nuclei, as the reactors and accelerators do.
explanation: Transmutation means changing one element into another by changing the nucleus, and no chemical process can do it because chemistry never reaches the nucleus. It requires neutrons or other nuclei, which is what a reactor and an accelerator both provide. The consequences are practical as well as military: transmutation can destroy long-lived waste and breed fuel from thorium, and those two applications are the reason research reactors and accelerator-driven subcritical systems are of interest.

definition: The metal at number 74 with the highest melting point of any element, and still liquid where iron boils. That is why filaments were tungsten until LEDs replaced them, and why it is used for the parts of a rocket that have to survive re-entry.
explanation: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any element, 3,422 °C, and it is still liquid at temperatures where iron boils. That is why it was the filament in every incandescent bulb for a century and why it is used where a part must survive re-entry. It has two odd properties worth knowing: it is brittle at room temperature and ductile above about 350 °C, the reverse of most metals; and tungsten is the heaviest element that has a stable isotope, which is why the technical definition of 'stable' is not available past it.

definition: A dense, radioactive actinide metal at number 92, the fuel of nuclear power stations and of weapons. It is about as common in the crust as tin, and nearly all of it is the fissile isotope uranium-235 at roughly one part in a hundred.
explanation: Uranium is about as common in the crust as tin and is the only element whose practical use depends on its own instability. The fissile isotope, uranium-235, is about 0.7% of natural uranium, which is why reactors use enriched fuel and why enriching it is the step with the greatest proliferation consequence. Its density is nearly the same as gold's, which is why it is found by geochemical methods rather than by washing, and its half-life is long enough that it will still be here when the sun burns out.

definition: The number of electrons an atom can gain, lose or share to reach a full outer shell, and so the number of bonds it tends to form. Hydrogen and the halogens have valence one, oxygen two, and the noble gases zero.
explanation: Valence is the number of bonds an atom tends to form, and it is a consequence of the electron count. Hydrogen and the halogens want one, oxygen wants two, carbon wants four, and the noble gases want none — which is the same octet rule seen from the atom's side. Valence and oxidation state are different quantities and are routinely confused: valence is how many atoms an atom bonds to, oxidation state is a bookkeeping charge, and for carbon in methane those numbers are four and minus four respectively.

definition: An electron in the outermost occupied shell, which is the only one that takes part in bonding. Change it and the element's chemistry changes, which is why elements in a group behave alike despite having different numbers of electrons in total.
explanation: The valence electrons are the ones in the outermost occupied shell, and they are the only ones that take part in bonding. That is why elements in a group behave alike despite having very different total electron counts — lithium and caesium differ by thirty electrons and share one valence electron between them. It is also why the group number often predicts an element's chemistry directly, and why the transition metals are the exception: their d electrons participate too.

definition: A weak attraction between molecules arising from temporary uneven distribution of their electrons. It is much weaker than a bond and it is what gives molecular solids a low melting point, and what lets a gecko cling to a wall.
explanation: Van der Waals forces are the weak attractions between molecules that come from temporary asymmetry in their electron distributions, and they are the reason molecular substances have low melting points. They are strong enough to make a gecko cling to a wall and to give graphene its remarkable strength, and they are strong enough to matter and far too weak to explain bonding. London dispersion, the main one, scales with polarisability, which is why iodine sticks to itself more readily than helium.

definition: A transition metal at number 23, used to strengthen steel and, in its compounds, as the working element in flow batteries. Its oxidation states give solutions in every colour from violet to yellow.
explanation: Vanadium's compounds give solutions in almost every colour from violet to yellow, because its oxidation states differ by one electron each and each gives a different absorption. That makes it a test for oxidation state in the laboratory and a nuisance in industry, since the same chemistry has to be controlled in a refinery. It strengthens steel for tools and springs, it is the working element in flow batteries, and the ore is a slag that the iron industry would otherwise discard.

definition: A gas given off by a liquid or a solid. The distinction between a vapour and a gas is one of origin rather than of kind, kept in British usage: water vapour is what the atmosphere calls a gas too, and there is no sharp boundary between the two.
explanation: Vapour and gas are the same state and the distinction is one of origin rather than of kind: water vapour is steam, and steam is what the atmosphere calls its water too. The British usage keeps the distinction, and it is a useful one because a vapour is what a liquid has just produced and a gas may never have been liquid. There is no sharp boundary and no sharp critical point at which one becomes the other; the difference is entirely in what the substance was doing before.

definition: How resistant a fluid is to flowing. Glycerol is several thousand times more viscous than water, which is the difference between a drizzle and a downpour once the droplets are the same size.
explanation: Viscosity is resistance to flow and it varies enormously between substances that are chemically similar. At room temperature glycerol is several thousand times more viscous than water and honey more so again, and the difference is entirely in hydrogen bonding between the molecules. Viscosity is also temperature-dependent and strongly so — a liquid roughly halves in viscosity for every 10 °C rise, which is why engine oil is graded by temperature behaviour rather than by viscosity alone.

definition: Easily turned to vapour. It means the substance evaporates readily at room temperature, not that it is explosive: acetone and ether are volatile in this sense and neither is remotely reactive.
explanation: Volatile means readily converted to vapour at room temperature, and it says nothing about reactivity. Acetone and diethyl ether are among the most volatile common liquids and neither is remotely reactive; conversely a non-volatile compound can be highly hazardous to handle. The confusion is probably from flammable, which is about ignitability. What volatile does predict is that a substance will have a strong smell, since the vapour reaching your nose is exactly what volatilising means.

definition: The SI unit of potential difference, one joule per coulomb, and abbreviated V. It is the push that drives charge around a circuit, and a single dry cell provides about one and a half of them.
explanation: A volt is one joule per coulomb, so it is an energy per charge rather than an energy. That is why a battery is described by a voltage and a capacity and neither alone tells you what it can do: 12 volts says the push, amp-hours says the charge, and the energy is the product. Voltage also fixes what chemistry a cell can do — the electrode potentials of the materials involved determine the cell voltage, which is why the periodic table's standard electrode potentials are the starting point for designing one.

definition: The compound of two hydrogen atoms to one oxygen, and the most abundant liquid on Earth. Its bent shape and its hydrogen bonding give it a higher boiling point than its mass suggests, an unusually high heat capacity, and the ability to dissolve both salts and sugars.
explanation: Water's properties are nearly all consequences of its bent shape and its ability to hydrogen bond, and a bent shape is itself a consequence of the two lone pairs on oxygen repelling the O–H bonds. Hydrogen bonding gives water a boiling point 100 °C above what its molar mass predicts, a high heat capacity, high surface tension, and its ability to dissolve both ionic compounds and polar molecules. That combination is why it is a solvent for most chemistry and why life found it convenient enough to evolve in.

definition: Water dispersed through oil as droplets rather than oil through water, which is what forms when water is shaken into crude. It can be stable enough to survive a pipeline, and breaking it can cost a refinery more than extracting the oil did.
explanation: A water-in-oil emulsion is oil with water dispersed through it rather than water with oil, and the practical problem is that it is stable enough to survive a pipeline. Crude from a water-bearing field arrives as an emulsion, and a refinery that cannot break it is processing a mixture whose properties it cannot predict. Demulsifiers, heat and centrifugation all help, and the cost is sometimes greater than the value of the oil, which is how a field gets abandoned.

definition: The SI unit of power, one joule a second, and abbreviated W. It is a rate rather than an amount, which is why a 100 W bulb left on for ten hours has used one kilowatt-hour of energy and not a thousand watts.
explanation: A watt is a rate, not an amount, and the distinction is the one people get wrong with appliances. A 100 W bulb left on for ten hours has used a kilowatt-hour of energy and not a thousand watts, and an electricity bill is measured in the first. It is also worth knowing that the unit was named for James Watt, who improved the steam engine rather than inventing it, and that the horsepower he used to market it is about 746 watts.

definition: An acid that only partly gives up its hydrogen ions in water, so the solution settles at an equilibrium between the acid and its ions. Weak refers to the degree of dissociation, never to the amount present.
explanation: Weak and dilute are independent, and the difference is about what fraction of the molecules ionise. A weak acid only partially gives up its protons, so the solution settles at an equilibrium between the acid and its ions and the pH changes very little when a little more acid is added. Acetic acid is the standard example, and the strength of vinegar comes almost entirely from its dilution rather than from the acid being stronger.

definition: A base that only partly takes up protons from water, leaving most of the base unreacted. Ammonia is the standard example, and its weak basicity is why it gives off so little smell compared with sodium hydroxide.
explanation: A weak base is one that only partly takes protons from water, and the reason is usually size and charge rather than weakness of the bond. Ammonia is a small uncharged molecule, so it must become an ion to react, and only a fraction does; sodium hydroxide is already an ion and reacts essentially completely. That is why ammonia gives off so little smell compared with caustic soda despite being a base, and why weak bases need much higher concentrations to reach a given pH.

definition: Joining metals by fusing them, either with the parts touching and heated, as in gas welding, or with a filler metal, as in arc welding. It makes a joint as strong as the metal, and the weld is the part most likely to fail.
explanation: A weld has to match the metal it joins in strength, and that is the standard it is judged by — a joint that is 90% of the parent metal's strength can still be the weakest part of the structure. Welding is also a metallurgical process rather than a mechanical one: the filler and the base metal fuse and form a new structure across the joint, and that structure is where defects such as inclusions and cracks live. Nondestructive testing exists because of that.

definition: A noble gas at number 54, heavy enough to be denser than air and the first of the group that forms real compounds. Its flash tubes are used to light stadium pitches, and its isotopes generate the light in some plasma displays.
explanation: Xenon was the first noble gas shown to form compounds, in 1962, and it did so in exactly the way that should have been impossible — with fluorine, the most electronegative element there is. Its use in ion propulsion is now more significant than its flash lamps: an ion thruster pushes xenon out the back of a spacecraft and produces more thrust per kilogram of propellant than any chemical rocket, which is why deep-space missions use it and why the Apollo launch plume photographs show what it looks like.

definition: The amount of product a reaction actually gives, compared with the amount the equation predicts. A yield below 100% is normal and is usually due to an incomplete reaction or to loss while the product is being separated.
explanation: Yield and atom economy answer different questions and are routinely confused. Yield is how much product you obtained compared with how much the equation predicts; atom economy is how much of the reacting mass could have ended up as product, and it is fixed by the equation before you start. A reaction with a poor atom economy cannot be made perfect by working harder, and it is that figure rather than the yield that tells you whether a synthesis route is worth pursuing.

definition: The amount of product the balanced equation predicts from the reactants used. Actual yield is always lower, and the ratio of the two is the percentage yield, which measures how well the experiment went.
explanation: The theoretical yield is what the balanced equation says you should get from the reagents you used, and the percentage yield is the ratio of the two. Anything below 100% is normal, and the commonest causes are an incomplete reaction and loss during work-up — a product that precipitates in the filter or stays dissolved in the filtrate. A yield much over 100% is not good news: it means the product was wet, or impure, or that the limiting reagent was misidentified.

definition: A rare earth metal at number 70, soft and silvery, used in pressure gauges because its electrical resistance changes predictably with pressure. It is also a dopant in some lasers.
explanation: Ytterbium is a soft, silvery rare earth whose electrical resistance changes predictably with pressure, which is what makes it useful in pressure gauges and in the diamond anvil cells that reach pressures of millions of atmospheres. Its ions have a very narrow energy gap, so they are efficient emitters, which is why it appears in some lasers. It is one of the four rare earths named for a Swedish village — Ytterby, where the element was separated in the 1870s and which gave the elements their collective name.

definition: A metal at number 39 used in the phosphors that make older displays and in the ceramics of fuel pellets. Its oxides glow, which is where the element's name came from — yttria, separated in a Swedish village.
explanation: Yttrium's oxides glow, and that is where the element's name comes from: yttria, separated from a village in Sweden and named for it, and the source of the word 'yttrium' that the rare earths inherited. Its practical uses are in the phosphors of older displays and in the ceramics of nuclear fuel pellets, where it improves the pellet's thermal conductivity and therefore how much power can be extracted from it.

definition: A metal at number 30 that protects steel by corroding in its place, which is what galvanising is. Every dry cell has a zinc casing, and brass is copper with zinc in it.
explanation: Zinc is the only metal used as a sacrificial anode on a large scale, and galvanising steel is the largest single use of the element. Its role is to corrode in place of the iron, which means the coating protects the steel even where it is scratched — the opposite of a paint film, which protects only where intact. It is also the anode in a dry cell, where that same sacrificial behaviour is the cell's mechanism rather than a protective measure, and it is essential in the body for hundreds of enzymes.

definition: A metal at number 40 that absorbs neutrons without absorbing many, so nuclear fuel is clad in it. It is nearly as hard as steel, far lighter, and its oxide diamond is used as a substitute for diamond itself.
explanation: Zirconium's two remarkable properties are related. It absorbs neutrons without absorbing many — which is why submarine hulls and reactor control rods use it rather than steel — and its oxide is so hard it is sold as a diamond substitute. It is also chemically almost identical to hafnium, with an atomic radius differing by a few femtometres, so the two are exceptionally hard to separate and hafnium is always found alongside it. Zirconium is the main component of zircon, the mineral in a diamond's typical rough is actually often zircon.
